#2777. Jonah Jackson on Luke Goedeke's grievances: "This is football, man"

After Sunday night's game between the Buccaneers and Bears, Tampa Bay tackle Luke Goedeke had some grievances to air about Chicago defensive tackle Jeffery Simmons. Bears guard Jonah Jackson was unpersuaded by Goedeke's complaints about Simmons launching himself at and/or holding Bucs linemen.

"The guys on his team tried to launch themselves at us on every play," Jackson said on 104.3 The Score. "I don't know any different. That's on him how he feels. It is what it is. This is football, man. Especially in the trenches. It gets rough and rowdy. . . . Did you see that big guy, number 50 [Vita Vea], launching at us? . . . It is what it is. We signed up for this."

As to Simmons holding Goedeke, Jackson was equally blunt.

"They all do it. It is what it is. You've got find ways to combat it," he said.

It really is anything goes when it comes to line play, subject to what the officials see and are willing to call. Especially when there are so many uncalled holding penalties on offensive linemen, arguably since defensive ends are so good and the powers-that-be prefer to keep quarterbacks in one piece.

The best, most recent example of that came in Carolina on Sunday, on the play when Broncos linebacker Nik Bonitto forced a fumble by Panthers quarterback Bryce Young to seal the game. Bonitto was being held the entire play. And he still got it done.

That's the message for all offensive and defensive linemen. Do whatever you have to do to get it done. It's only a foul if a flag is thrown.

#2775. KIRK SPEAKS: Purdue

Fresh off of a decisive road victory against the Northwestern Wildcats, the Iowa Hawkeyes continue to control their own destiny for a spot in the College Football Playoffs. However, as we all know, the team almost certainly needs to win out in order for that to become a reality.

The remaining schedule is favorable on paper, but the Hawkeye cannot afford to let their guard down at all in any of the remaining games, and that starts this weekend against the Boilermakers. Let's see what Kirk Ferentz has up his sleeve to prep the team, shall we? Check out the full transcript HERE and my commentary below.

Q. I know you're not a stat guy, but Iowa has had a 97-yard offensive touchdown drive in each of the last three games. The first team since 2015 to do that. I know with this group, I wouldn't call them young now that they've almost played a full season together, but what about this group makes them not flinch when they're pushed back against their own goal line? It seems like they aren't pressing. They're calm in the way they execute. I know you told Hank and the offense before they went out against Northwestern: Hey, you did this last week; just go out there and do it again. What makes them so composed?

KIRK FERENTZ: I wish it was that easy. Take a shot there. Sometimes they listen.

It's all about execution. I think I said Saturday night, the goal was just to get the ball out of there, so if you do have to punt, you can at least flip the field position a little bit. That's what you're hoping to do. The opponents are trying to keep you where they get the ball back midfield or less.

There's percentages with all that stuff, but I got to tell you, I've been impressed with that three straight weeks. I lost track about three weeks ago, but the other two I knew.

It's really impactful if you can do that certainly because, again, as a defensive team, you're thinking, okay, we have a chance to pin them down, get the ball back, and at minimum, get three points. If you can take that and then, flip it around the other way, that's a double bonus there.

I wish I could tell you what the magic formula is, but it's a real credit to the players just for sticking to it and doing the execution part of it.

KIRK FERENTZ SAYS EXECUTION – TAKE A DRINK!! But in all seriousness, the offense has truly been such an improvement this year. The fact that we're able to confidently move the ball, confidently throw on first down in a lot of these scenarios…that says something. Iowa is taking some really big steps forward this year under Tim Lester, and it's paying off tremendously.

Q. I don't mean to beat a dead horse here, but I know the fumbles have kind of continued. I know you said there's not exactly a perfect drill to maybe fix that or to work on it, but I guess is it just business as usual, or how do you address that?

KIRK FERENTZ: I mention it, and you're not beating a dead horse either. Believe me, we're on the same page. Twelve loose balls, that's way too many. Our interception rate could be better, but it's about average, I'd say, league-wide, and it's not alarming. But 12 loose balls, that's a lot for, like, three seasons, I'd say.

To me it's concentration. It's like tackling too. Some games we tackle better than others, but we tackled really, really well last week, but we pretty much do the same stuff routinely, whether it's ball security drills or tackling. I think a lot of it's just concentration.

Sometimes you can't explain what happens in a game, but a couple of weeks ago, eight loose balls, I mean, that's just ridiculous, quite frankly. It gets down to concentration, in my opinion.

Experience factors in there, but we're nine games into it, so everybody is a veteran at this at this point, unless you just got out there. I'd give you a hall pass there maybe, but we have to do a better job. I think we will, but we have to do it.

12 loose balls on the season seems like the most I can ever remember in a season under Kirk Ferentz. Surely I'm wrong on that stat, but this has definitely been a problem this year, without question. In a rare moment here, I agree completely with Kirk that it does seem like a matter of concentration, particularly in the Minnesota game. The team just didn't show up that game, and it showed. This is something that needs to have been fixed yesterday.

Q. Related to the ball security question, you're going to obviously mention it to the group, but is it something you maybe put on your assistant coaches to reemphasize, if you will, in meeting rooms? Hey, you're running here with the ball out like this. I guess that would be my first question.

KIRK FERENTZ: Yeah. There was something we saw a week ago with a particular player about just some of the maybe technique that could have been changed, and I think that was addressed last week and really didn't show up Saturday. That's encouraging.

But, yeah, everybody has ownership, and then we talk about turnovers too. Sometimes it's somebody missing a block or not blocking well enough where a guy gets caught in a compromising position, so everybody has a hand in that.

Yeah, we continue to coach it, and we will continue to coach it and emphasize it. Those old adages are true. What you emphasize is usually what you get. There's a fine line too.

I'm thinking of a story. I worked with a guy who worked with another guy. I was coaching at Stanford and overdid it. They were playing Oregon State I think. They had buckets of water out there and the whole nine yards, and they went out there and proceeded to turn the ball over like seven times because they had the players just talked into it. You want to be careful about where that line is, that's for sure.

Lol "a particular player" does his name happen to start with X and does he play running back? If what you emphasize is what you get in a game…what is being emphasized in practice??

Q. I know all offseason we talked to you about the young defensive line that you had and everything you lost, a very talented linebacker corps. Maybe outside of Jayden, really have not been tested. You guys have 30 sacks. I think it's seventh in the country. How much of that is just execution, the different schematics by Seth or Phil? How much of them are coverage sacks? How have you been able to extract the best out of a young group that continues to gain experience by the week?

KIRK FERENTZ: I'm afraid to be too complimentary because you end up regretting it. A good friend of mine said, "Don't brag on anybody but dead folks." A pretty good motto, actually.

That was an area of concern, that and our specialists were two big areas of concern, and probably the offensive line coming into the season just because of inexperience. To that point, I think we're doing okay up front there, and to me it's the whole front seven.

I didn't lie, but cheated a little bit. We had a feeling that Cam Buffington was going to be a pretty good player. We knew Jayden was. We had that part locked down pretty good, but the development of what's going on up front has been really pleasing.

We were counting on Bryce to be an anchor and a leader up there, and he's done that. Hawthorne has done a really good job there.

Kenny didn't play that many snaps relative to the other guys last year, but he's a veteran guy with a great attitude, and he's adopted a good, strong leadership role, too, so that's helping in that room. Then everybody else is kind of doing what they can to catch up.

We're getting all we could ask for out of Luke and Will in their rotation. Kahmari Brown is starting to get comfortable in our defense and the way we do things, so that's good to see. Then you have Epenesa and Campbell, two young guys that are starting to gain a little confidence and getting the feel for what it is. Collectively it's more of a collective thing, to answer your question. Then you have Ries on the sub packages and Van Kekerix is playing really well.

It has been a collective thing. All the things you talked about are true. The schematics have been good, giving guys a chance to be in position where maybe they have opportunity. Then historically we have a fair number of coverage sacks where we'll be rushing four guys, but if you can make a quarterback hold the ball a little bit more than he wants to, that gives you a chance maybe to flush him and have something good happen. I think that's kind of been an understated strength for us over the years is if we can make it hard for them to have an easy throw, then maybe some good things will happen up front.

The defense started out a little questionable at times, but I'll be damned if they haven't turned into one of the finest units in the country. They're downright scary. The quarterback pressure was fantastic last weekend. Sure, it was a backup, but still, the defense was all over the place. They will need to keep playing like that every single game to come out of these remaining games without a loss.

Let's end with this interesting nugget from Kirk about the CFB Playoff expansion:

Q. I know you said you're not worried about future College Football Playoff stuff years down the road, but is there maybe some sadness the loss of the Big Ten Championship game? I know that's been a pretty special event in the past.

KIRK FERENTZ: I have to tell you — yes and no. I'm not feeling real collegiate anymore. If I was, we'd still be playing with 10 or 11 teams in the Big Ten. That stuff is all gone by the wayside.

The world has changed dramatically in this arena, so you have to roll with it. I don't want to dissertate too much about the playoff thing because it's already been said, but to me, when they went from two teams to four, my attitude at that point was the more the merrier. I really meant that. I would rather have it be two or 22 or in this case 24 because you're always going to have that argument, we should have been No. 4, not No. 5 and all that stuff.

As soon as we went to four, the bowl games — it started to diminish the value of bowl games traditionally, which is unfortunate in my opinion. But, again, that's 20 years ago. All that stuff is kind of in the rearview mirror.

I think our Commissioner has kind of led the way on the 24 thing, and it made perfect sense. He talked about relevance of these games in November nationally, and you have to shift your mentality because that's really what it's all about. You know, here's the new world, and that one we'll deal with next year. Right now we're dealing with this year, and really none of it matters.

I don't dislike any of these shows, but they just don't mean anything to me right now because I know enough that the accuracy rate of what gets said tonight or last week or next week won't be real impressive. It's the way it goes.

Guess what, in a month we'll all know. We'll all know the answers. Suspense is killing me, I have to tell you.

I for one will definitely miss crowning a conference champion, but at the same time, with the diminishing values of the bowl games that Kirk mentions here, the expanded playoff does make a lot of sense. I'm still of the thought that the end game here is that college football will turn into two conferences (most likely Big Ten and SEC) and you'll have all your teams that used to make up the Big 12 or ACC or what have you will be different divisions in the conferences. You then get divisional championships and a spot in the playoffs, like the NFL. It just makes sense at this point for it to go in this direction, even if it means we may not get a definitive conference champion.

#2772. 5 NFL trade deadline moves we wish happened, including Jonathan Taylor

The 2026 NFL trade deadline has officially passed, and it was one of the most exciting in recent memory.

The reason for this is simple. For the first time in a long while, a significant quarterback trade happened ahead of the deadline. The Las Vegas Raiders sent their starting quarterback, Kirk Cousins, to the Minnesota Vikings, who surrendered a third-round pick to reacquire the veteran who spent six seasons with the team from 2018-23.

The Cousins deal wasn't the only major move. The Indianapolis Colts also traded a couple of receivers, Keenan Allen and Josh Downs, ahead of the deadline while the Jacksonville Jaguars were aggressive in adding three pieces to their defense to put a bow on the NFL's trade season.

Even so, there were still plenty of trades that didn't end up happening. Most notably, running back Jonathan Taylor – who was subject to many trade rumors in the lead-up to the deadline – remained with the Colts while the Los Angeles Chargers decided to hang on to most of their veterans despite sporting a winless record.

With that in mind, here's a look at five deals we would have liked to see that didn't ultimately happen as the dust settles on the 2026 NFL trade deadline.

NFL TRADE GRADES: Which team won every major deadline deal?

There's little doubt the Vikings made the most impactful deadline deal by acquiring Cousins from the Las Vegas Raiders to address their quarterback woes. Still, Minnesota could have taken it a step further and tried to pry Taylor away from the Colts.

The Vikings' rushing offense has ranked 27th in EPA per play this season, per the NFL's Next Gen Stats. Aaron Jones and Jordan Mason have formed a solid but unspectacular duo at the position, and adding a true three-down playmaker could have made an even bigger difference for Minnesota's offense.

Taylor would have been an excellent fit, and bringing him in to play alongside Cousins could have given Minnesota's offense an even bigger shot in the arm. Getting that unit to play at an above-average level could be all it takes to turn the Vikings, who sport an elite defense under Brian Flores, into a true Super Bowl contender.

As such, it would have been fun to see the Vikings try to make an all-in move to get Taylor. But at the same time, it isn't shocking to see first-year general manager Nolan Teasley take a more measured approach – especially given the Colts' high asking price for Taylor – while treating Cousins as the team's marquee acquisition.

The Jaguars opted to keep Thomas ahead of the 2026 NFL trade deadline. That isn't a major surprise considering Jacksonville was a big-time buyer, swinging deals for a trio of defensive players – safety Jessie Bates III along with defensive tackles Jordan Davis and Davon Godchaux – to bolster their chances of making a Super Bowl run.

Even so, Thomas has struggled to make much of an impact in Liam Coen's offense, posting just 10 catches for 117 yards and two touchdowns across eight games this season. The 2024 first-round pick could use a change of scenery, and landing with a Rams team in desperate need of help at the position could've proven to be a nice fit.

The Rams are currently without both Puka Nacua and Davante Adams, who are each on IR, so Matthew Stafford is going to have to make use of a receiving corps whose top options are Konata Mumpfield and Tutu Atwell. Thomas would have been a big-time upgrade to that group and could have completed a formidable receiving trio along with Nacua and Adams in Sean McVay's offense.

The Patriots are currently dealing with key injuries at running back. Rhamondre Stevenson is dealing with a knee injury that is expected to sideline him short-term, while TreVeyon Henderson is still dealing with the aftermath of an "unusual medical emergency" that briefly hospitalized him.

Because of those issues, New England is left with only Corey Kiner and Lan Larison among the healthy running backs on its 53-man roster. Kiner has flashed in limited action, but it may have been wise for the Patriots to add another proven running back to the rotation as they look to make a playoff push.

Pollard is on pace for a fifth consecutive season with at least 1,000 rushing yards, and he ran for 246 yards and five touchdowns in his two games leading up to the 2026 NFL trade deadline. The 29-year-old veteran would have been a perfect option as a steady, plug-and-play fit for the Patriots who could help take pressure off Drake Maye.

The 49ers were active ahead of the trade deadline, acquiring defensive tackle DeForest Buckner and wide receiver Keenan Allen from the Colts, but they still could have used additional help for their pass rush.

San Francisco ranks 30th league-wide in pressure rate, per the NFL's Next Gen Stats, and has only produced 15 total sacks this season. Just one team with a winning record, the Kansas City Chiefs, has fewer sacks than the 49ers thus far this year.

The 49ers could certainly see an uptick in production with Nick Bosa healthy and Buckner now in the fold. Still, adding a proven veteran like Mack to help them chase a title could also have been a good play. The 35-year-old has played 69.3% of the Chargers' defensive snaps this season while generating three sacks and 19 pressures. Placing him across from Bosa could have added a welcome layer of depth and talent to San Francisco's pass rush.

And hey, it also would have been nice to see Mack, a pending free agent, get a chance to play with a contender instead of languishing through a lost season with the 0-8 Chargers.

The Chiefs rank middle-of-the-pack league-wide in pressure rate, but they have struggled to turn those pressures into sacks. Kansas City has just 14 sacks in eight games and endured a three-week stretch without recording a single sack.

The Chiefs have performed better of late, racking up 10 sacks over their last four games. Still, adding a player like Sweat, who had a career-high 12 sacks last season and has posted three this season despite playing for a struggling Cardinals defense, could have improved their baseline production and given more assistance to George Karlaftis and Chris Jones.

Instead, the Chiefs focused on grabbing a "Josh" for their offense: Colts wide receiver Josh Downs. The move was sensible given the team's injury issues at the position and Xavier Worthy's inconsistent performance, but it still would have been nice to see Kansas City try to upgrade the defensive side of the ball as well.

#2771. Game Preview: Pittsburgh Penguins @ San Jose Sharks 11/11/2026

Who: Pittsburgh Penguins (6-10-2, 14 points, 8th place Metropolitan Division) @ San Jose Sharks (8-11-1, 17 points, 6th place Pacific Division)

How to Watch: Locally televised game on Sportsnet Pittsburgh and NBCSCA, streaming for out of market at ESPN+

Pens' Path Ahead: Monday kicked off a slack part of the schedule for the Pens, who only have three games from Nov 9 – 20. They'll go back home and see Ottawa on Saturday night then get quite a few days off before the following game next Thursday 11/19 against St. Louis.

Opponent Track: It's been a long November for the Sharks, who at least were able to break a five-game losing streak with a win on Monday at home against the Islanders, though it required a shootout to get there. To amend the Counting Crows line from the first sentence, there's not much reason to believe the rest will be better than the last with games this month still to go against Utah, Minnesota, Anaheim, Vegas and Colorado.

Season Series: It won't be too much longer before the Sharks make their trip for the year to Pittsburgh, playing the Pens again on December 6th.

Hidden Stat: The Penguins are 4-1-0 in their last five visits to the SAP Center, per Penguins PR.

Michael Misa – Macklin Celebrini – Will Smith

Mason Marchment – Alex Wennberg – Kiefer Sherwood

Ivar Stenberg – Ty Dellandrea – Tyler Toffoli

Barclay Goodrow – Zach Ostapchuk – Colin Graf

Goalies: Yaroslav Askarov and Alex Nedeljkovic

Potential scratches: Adam Gaudette, Nolan Allen

Injured Reserve: Igor Chernyshov and Logan Couture

Bringing on both Nurse and Trouba (for a combined $17.5 million cap hit this season and next) was a curious move when taken together. Grabbing one veteran in that mold was seen in many places as enough (or even one too many) getting them both in an effort to level up and

Wennberg recently returned to the lineup, he's quietly a big piece of the team (55 points last season) and has missed half the games this season so far, which doesn't help matters.

The second line has some tough customers, Sherwood leads the NHL in his this season with 106. Marchment just picked up a $5,000 fine for sticking up for an Islander who boarded Sherwood last game.

Lots of youth for the Sharks, which has led to some uneven offensive development. Giving up chances and more goals than they've been able to score has been a big issue. Some have risen, like Misa in his second year, some have faded away at the moment – like Graf who scored 21 goals and 46 points riding shotgun with Celebrini last year and has barely been on the scoresheet this season.

Taking the step from tearing down and acquiring assets has gone well, now getting up the next hurdle to become a competitive team is something SJ is trying to figure out on the fly. Toffoli has been great in support, others like Sherwood and Marchment will need to step up as the veteran help the young core needs.

Key to the game: Start fast and don't get burned by the young talent

After taking a step forward in 2025-26, San Jose is down across the board on stats so far in 2026-27. Their offense is way down and the defensive process looks as broken as ever.

Shayna Goldman at The Athletic wrote an interesting bit about the Sharks yesterday:

High-flying rebuilding teams that play a run-and-gun style (think the 2022-23 Sabres and 2021-22 Ducks) often start stressing defensive structure above all else. But sometimes that shift can suppress what makes a team so special offensively, and doesn't actually move the needle defensively.

That has been the case so far in San Jose, where the hockey and overall team progress have been uninspiring. Now, despite an attempted shift to play more defensive hockey, the Sharks are still bleeding chances against. The team is allowing a higher rate of chances off the rush compared to last season, as well as more passes to the slot, and is failing to limit their opponents' offensive-zone time. And unlike last year, there isn't that same offensive punch to make up for it. The Sharks' young guns aren't creating nearly as many rush chances or moving the puck as well, and are overall looking disjointed after last season's progress.

And yet, with Celebrini and Smith and Stenberg, there's still plenty of dynamic high-end talent that can burn an opponent at any given moment, which will have to be a priority to be mindful of for the Penguins. The Sharks season, and maybe rebuild as whole, seems like it's in a precarious and unsteady spot at the moment. That could be good timing to meet a team now in disarray, it could also make them dangerous as they look to get on track.

The start of any game is crucial – and that will hold in this. The Sharks have only scored the first goal in 5 of their 20 games this season. They have only been leading after 20 minutes on three occasions, compared to being behind at the first intermission ten times.

For the Pens, don't give them a reason to believe and that will trap SJ in the familiar position of chasing the game from behind and likely not being able to get a result. To avoid that, shut down the first line and the Stenberg+Toffoli combo and the Sharks don't have a lot of other pieces that have been stepping up. (All of this is easier thought out than done, especially with a defense like Pittsburgh employs..)

Evgeni Malkin – Sidney Crosby – Rickard Rakell

Egor Chinakhov – Ben Kindel – Nick Robertson

Ville Koivunen – Tommy Novak – Justin Brazeau

Connor Dewar – Blake Lizotte – Rutger McGroarty

Goalies: Arturs Silovs and Sergei Murashov

Potential Scratches: Hendrix Lapierre, Andrei Kuzmenko, Ilya Solovyov

IR: Ryan Graves, Trevor van Riemsdyk, Elmer Soderblom, Bryan Rust

Could be three new forward lines, based on practice yesterday. The first line remained the same as it has been these last few games, and then FINALLY Nick Robertson gets elevated into a bigger role after scoring as many goals as anyone for the team this year in mostly a limited and defensive line. Tommy Novak, one of the team's best players in the last handful of games, gets a new challenge and moves back to center.

Sam Girard missed practice yesterday with what was termed a 'maintenance day' and usually indicative that the team is thinking the player will still play the next game.

Trevor van Riemsdyk, who said said to have a day-to-day injury on October 10th and hasn't been around much ever since, has been cleared for contact and was a full participant in practice. van Riemsdyk has been limited to playing in only five games.

There is something positive to be said about being used in the key defensive role with Connor Dewar and Blake Lizotte, as Robertson has for much of the season. That is an important line for the Penguins and one the coaches and team counts on in plenty of big situations, and not the completely typical or standard "fourth line afterthought" type of usage. The Pens have given Robertson a look on the PK and a real chance to pitch in there and grow his game and reputation as more of a two-way contributor.

That said, Robertson can score goals but has lacked the opportunity to get a lot of ice time and play with talented offensive players for much of his career, so it's been frustrating to see him not get much of a chance to make a bigger impact so far this season. That makes it heartening to see him used with Chinakhov and Kindel today, two young and offensive-minded forwards. Robertson's sure earned it through his play and production (tied for team-high seven goals).

#2770. George leads Celtics to 123-101 win over 76ers in first battle between Jays

The battle of the Jays made the headlines, but Paul George seized the spotlight in his return to Philly.

The Boston Celtics handily beat the Philadelphia 76ers 123-101 behind George's 36 points, as he rattled off shot after shot against his former team. Boston's depth also put on a show against the Sixers, as 8 players hit at least 1 three-pointer and 3 players (George, Payton Pritchard, and Sam Hauser) hit at least 4.

It was the first of four regular season games between Boston and Philly this year and, other than the 2023 NBA All-Star Game, the first time the Jays have faced each other as opponents. The teams' next matchup won't be until Jan. 21, when they will square off in TD Garden.

Boston's starting squad included Derrick White, Jordan Walsh, Paul George, Jayson Tatum, and Neemias Queta. The team's injury report was clear.

Philly's starters included Tyrese Maxey, VJ Edgecombe, Jaylen Brown, LeBron James, and Joel Embiid. Adem Bona and Dominick Barlow were out with injuries.

George opened up the action for Boston with the team's first 4 points, as he capitalized early on his advantageous matchup against Edgecombe. Less than 3 minutes into the game, we got our first glimpse of the head-to-head matchup between the Jays. Tatum was guarding Brown and forced a turnover with some fast hands, then got an easy dunk and a cutting layup on back-to-back plays.

Brown got his first points of the game on a pair of free throws about 4 minutes in, but Maxey led the way early for the Sixers, with 8 of the team's first 12 points. Nevertheless, the Celtics had an 18-12 lead after 5 minutes and started off shooting a scalding 8-10 from the floor.

White had a nice redemption play about halfway through the quarter, where he got back in position after losing a turnover and drew a charge on Brown, who took the ball hard to the paint. The Jays starred on the next two plays, as Tatum hit a slick step back three-pointer that was followed up with a ferocious dunk by Brown.

Mitchell Robinson also put in some good work early on, battling with Embiid down low and grabbing 3 rebounds (one of which resulted in a scrappy putback) in less than 5 minutes of play time. However, he fouled Embiid on a three-pointer with less than 3 minutes to go in the quarter, which led Head Coach Joe Mazzulla to sub him out for Queta.

Luckily, Embiid hit only 1-3 free throws, and Boston rattled off a pair of layups to go up 30-21 with 26 seconds to go in the quarter, which ended with a missed Payton Pritchard three-pointer at the buzzer. The frame ended with the C's up 30-23.

Both teams came out firing in the second quarter. Almost five minutes into the frame, the Celtics had scored 15 points and the Sixers tallied 11 of their own. Other than a lone Luka Garza bucket, all of Boston's offense came from Pritchard and George, who were red hot to open the quarter. With 7:21 to go, the C's had taken a 45-34 lead.

Both sides cooled off a bit about halfway through the quarter. Maxey kept Philly's offense chugging along, but the Celtics took a 54-40 lead with the help of a few three-pointers (2 from Sam Hauser and 1 from Hugo Gonzalez). George's hot streak continued, as he came out of a timeout, rebounded his own miss for a bucket, then knocked down a free throw to complete the and-1 play. He also hit a three-pointer about a minute later to put the C's up 62-47.

The Sixers scored the last 4 points of the half, leaving the Celtics with a 62-51 lead after two quarters.

At the half, George led the C's in scoring with 17 points on 63.6% shooting from the field. He also had 4 rebounds and 1 assist.

Tatum was Boston's second leading scorer, with 13 points, 4 rebounds and a block.

For the Sixers, Maxey led the way with 12 points, while Embiid had 9 points (entirely from free throws, as he was 0-6 from the field).

Brown had 8 points, 2 rebounds, 2 assists, 2 steals, and 3 turnovers at the half.

Embiid hit his fourth three-pointer of the season (and his first in 7 games) to open the second half, but Tatum came back and hit a three-pointer of his own soon after. Brown also tallied his fourth foul of the game early in the quarter, putting him in foul trouble early. However, it was the Sixers who came out of the half with more of a spark. With the help of a LeBron three-pointer, a ridiculous circus shot by Edgecombe to score over Queta, and a Maxey layup, Philly went on a 7-0 run to cut Boston's lead to 69-63.

Following a Celtics timeout, Queta cut to the rim for an easy bucket on a dime from Tatum. It was Tatum's first assist of the game. Tatum also had what might have been the play of the game soon after, as he blocked an Edgecombe layup and flew down the court for a thunderous poster dunk on LeBron. Nevertheless, the Sixers kept chipping away, and underrated Celtics killer Dean Wade hit a 26-footer to tie the game up at 76 apiece with about 4 minutes left in the quarter.

Following a timeout, the momentum changed hands again. Pritchard and Maxey went back-to-back-to-back in a three-point shooting exchange that Boston got the best of. Hauser hit another from behind the arc soon after to put the C's up 85-79. That wasn't the end of the three-point shooting display, though. After the Celtics forced a shot clock violation, Tatum, Maxey, and Scheierman hit 3 three-pointers in a row.

By the end of the third, the C's had taken a 91-82 lead.

The Celtics' shooting stayed hot as the final frame began. Pritchard started the quarter with a deep step-back three-pointer, then hit on another a couple minutes later to increase Boston's lead to 15 points while both Maxey and Embiid were resting. George joined in on the fun and hit a pullup three-pointer of his own to give the C's a 100-82 lead, the largest of the night.

Philly called a timeout and subbed Maxey and Embiid back into the game, but they still had a hard time breaking through the Celtics' stifling defense. On the other hand, nothing could stop Paul George. He knocked down a sweet turnaround mid-ranger, then cooked his defender for an easy layup to put Boston up 105-82 with about 8 minutes left to go.

Brown hit his first three-pointer of the night following a Boston timeout, but George hit another 2 three-pointers soon after to give the C's a dominant 111-87 lead with less than 6 minutes to go in the game. The Sixers subsequently emptied the bench, all but conceding the loss to Boston. The Celtics depth then finished the job and never let Philly even whiff a potential comeback.

George racked up 36 points on 63.6% shooting, including 6-11 from beyond the arc, 5 rebounds, and 1 assist.

Tatum finished the game with 21 points on 47.1% shooting, 6 rebounds, 4 assists, and 2 blocks.

Pritchard, Hauser, and Hugo Gonzalez each finished in the double-digits scoring-wise, with 18, 12, and 10 points, respectively.

The team finished the game shooting 22-49 from three-point range.

Brown had only 13 points on 44.4% shooting, 5 rebounds, 2 assists, and 3 stocks. He also had 4 turnovers and finished with a +/- of -27 for the night.

Maxey, James, and Embiid had 24, 11, and 16 points, respectively.

The Celtics will play the Toronto Raptors tomorrow at 7 p.m. in Scotiabank Arena. It will be the last game of Boston's four-game road trip.

#2769. John Spytek: First "real" call on Kirk Cousins came this morning

As NFL trades slip into hibernation until March, it’s important to remember something the next time players can be sent from one team to another.

Teams push plenty of BS to the media — and the media often passes it along without scrutiny.

Case in point: The internally inconsistent claim made by ESPN on Saturday, undoubtedly based on information straight from the Raiders.

“As of this weekend,” Adam Schefter of ESPN tweeted, “the Raiders had not received any trade inquiries regarding their starting quarterback Kirk Cousins, nor are they interested in dealing him, per league sources. They plan to keep sticking with him until they believe their No. 1 overall pick Fernando Mendoza is ready.”

So the Raiders hadn’t received any trade inquiries, but they weren’t interested in the trade inquiries they hadn’t received? Right.

In a press conference with reporters on Tuesday, Raiders G.M. John Spytek addressed how it all came to be.

“I never made one call on Kirk Cousins,” Spytek said. “And I got a few phone calls. But one real one this morning.”

The “real one” ultimately entailed getting a third-round pick for Cousins. Which further highlights how silly it is for a team to claim — and for the media to share — the idea that “WE’RE NOT INTERESTED.”

Everyone is interested in a trade offer for all but a small handful of players in the entire league. Anything else is posturing. And, as is often the case when it comes to NFL reporting, the insiders allow themselves to become extensions of the team’s P.R. department in an effort to send a given message.

The Raiders weren’t interested, until they were. And it didn’t take all that much to make them interested in giving up their starting quarterback.

It was easier to make the decision because they were surely thinking about when to bench him for rookie Fernando Mendoza. And it surely was easier for Cousins to embrace the trade, given that he’s now in a position to keep playing for a team that has a chance to get to the postseason and to make some noise in January.

#2767. Position grades from the Patriots’ loss to the Packers

The New England Patriots got their proverbial butts handed to them on Sunday afternoon, losing to the Green Bay Packers in a game that very much was a 60-minute struggle for the home team on both sides of the ball. The offense looked like its early-season version by repeatedly shooting itself in the foot and letting opportunities to get back into the game slip through its grasp, while the defense failed to offer much resistance against one of the most explosive offenses in football.

The end result was a 45-27 shellacking that raises significant concerns for the team — in large part because its two best players, quarterback Drake Maye and cornerback Christian Gonzalez, both had forgettable days. The Patriots in their current state are simply not good enough to overcome off days from one let alone both of them.

Naturally, they will have to lead the way when it comes to bouncing back from this one. However, they are not the only ones who need to take a step forward.

Let's take a look at the film and hand out some grades.

Quarterback: Drake Maye is as talented a thrower of the football as there is in the NFL, and this was on display multiple times against the Packers. Not all of them were completed — we will get to that — but Maye looked like an MVP-caliber quarterback on multiple occasions. Unfortunately for him, he also looked like the error-prone player from earlier in the season as well, and it cost the Patriots. His three interceptions were reminiscent of those previous struggles: his first and third picks were the result of bad decisions and improper eye discipline, while his second was the result of an inaccurate throw that was tipped for another turnover. For as good as Maye was at times, those plays overshadow everything else and put New England on the road to defeat. | Grade: D+

Running back: Rhamondre Stevenson once again did what he could and continues to be the Patriots' most reliable player on the offensive side of the ball. Against Green Bay, he had three explosive plays, including a 30-yard touchdown catch on a well-executed wheel route. Unfortunately, as with Drake Maye, his 78-yard performance and 5.3-yard rushing average are partially overshadowed by a turnover as well as some insufficient pass protection. On the whole, however, he had a solid day. Corey Kiner did too, but most of his production came in garbage time. Lan Larison was quiet. | Grade: B-

Wide receiver: Mike Vrabel was complementary of Kyle Williams in training camp, but his impact continues to be limited even when given a prominent role. On Sunday, he continued to be mostly used as a sacrificial X-receiver that teams are not fooled by, and his plays included a drop on what would have been a significant gain, an interception, and two targets with Tommy DeVito at quarterback that resulted in him getting banged up. His stock is trending down, something that cannot be said for DeMario Douglas: the fourth-year man is New England's most consistent pass catcher and his five-catch, 102-yard performance proves that once again. He continues to perform well in space and even though he would have contributed to a fourth interception by stopping too early on one of his routes — that pick was dropped — he had a good day. Mack Hollins and Efton Chism also had some positive moments, even though Hollins and Maye were not on the same page on the first interception. | Grade: C

Tight end: Hunter Henry was on a snap count after practicing only once leading up to the game, and he was used primarily in the passing game. His impact was not profound, but he did make some positive plays — something that also is true for rookie Eli Raridon. The youngster has shown a good rapport with Drake Maye, even though he was the target on the third interception (a play that still falls on the QB for being baited into a throw). Tanner Arkin, on the other hand, had some noticeable struggles including when he picked up the wrong player on a 6-yard loss. The undrafted rookie was waived on Monday. | Grade: C

Offensive line: Will Campbell is the Patriots' best offensive lineman, and it isn't particularly close. He was very good against the Packers, even though he and Ben Brown failed to properly pick up a stunt resulting in a first-quarter sack on a 3rd-and-7. Still, he was the least of New England's problems. The rest of the line was uneven, with Jared Wilson and the replacement guards — Walter Rouse and Matt Pryor — all at the scene for sacks. Obviously, some hiccups are expected from Rouse and Pryor; the former has had his issues whenever on the field this year, while the latter is a solid player but nonetheless a replacement-level option. Morgan Moses was solid, as was Caleb Lomu after he entered the game in place of an injured Campbell. | Grade: C-

Defensive line: The Patriots defense had a bad game, but there were some positive moments up front. Milton Williams was at the point of attack on most of them, and had a solid game that included three quarterback pressures. Cory Durden and Christian Barmore stuffed three runs each, with the latter also picking up a sack. However, Durden opened the hole on Jordan Love's 13-yard touchdown scramble in the first quarter, while Barmore was washed out of his gap quite easily on Green Bay's 2-yard score in the second quarter. The edge players — Dre'Mont Jones, Elijah Ponder, Gabe Jacas — continued to showcase their high motors, but they also were undisciplined at times with Jones and Jacas both penalized for pre-snap infractions on third downs. For a team with a limited margin of error, unforced mistakes like these are back-breakers. | Grade: C+

Linebacker: Much like the defensive line, the Patriots' off-ball linebackers had some good plays, including one pressure and run stuff each from Robert Spillane and Christian Elliss. On the whole, however, their impact was marginal and they failed to help with the team's biggest issues while aligning in stacked boxes on early downs. Elliss also took a bad angle from the second level on Love's touchdown run in the early first quarter, while both he and Spillane fell victim to play-action fakes. | Grade: C

Cornerback: Carlton Davis gave up a 43-yard pass before leaving with an injury, Karton Prunty surrendered a 10-yard touchdown, and Marcus Jones was responsible for a 28-yarder; he also seemed to be at fault for the miscommunication on Matthew Golden's 5-yard touchdown. Their issues, however, paled in comparison to Christian Gonzalez's. Typically New England's best and most reliable defender, he had an uncharacteristically bad performance and saw nine passes for 188 yards and a touchdown completed into his coverage area — including five catches for 106 yards in traditional man coverage. So, what went wrong? A combination of things. The Packers performing at a very high level; some of the defensive calls and structures; insufficient safety positioning; bad luck (i.e. tripping on a 43-yard man-to-man catch); and possibly most worryingly an apparent lack of reactionary and closing speed. The Patriots are asking a lot of Gonzalez and trust him with diverse coverage assignments, but one has to wonder whether or not this slows him down and puts him out of his comfort zone. That doesn't excuse what looked like a lack of urgency at times, including on a missed tackle on a 34-yard run, but his performance a) started snowballing at some point, and b) requires some context the raw numbers simply cannot provide. | Grade: F

Safety: A defense giving up seven explosive passes is reflective of a breakdown that goes beyond just one position group; the entire secondary struggled top to bottom — including the safeties. Kevin Byard was slow to move into his zone on Matthew Golden's 49-yard catch in the first quarter, and Craig Woodson did not provide the necessary inside help when Christian Watson got inside leverage against Christian Gonzalez to beat New England's Cover 4 for a 39-yard touchdown. Woodson's run defense was solid, but pointing that out feels like rearranging the deck chairs on the Titanic. The ship went down nonetheless. | Grade: D–

Special teams: Kick coverage continues to be a problem for the Patriots, including on a 48-yard Bo Melton runback in the second quarter and a 13-yard Coleman Owen punt return in the third. That said, there also was a lot to like, including Andy Borregales making all three of his extra points and Mitch Wishnowsky teaming up with Erick Hunter to pin the Packers at the 2-yard line on a 50-yard punt. | Grade: C

How would you grade the Patriots' performance against the Packers? Do you agree with our assessment? Please head down to the comment section to discuss with the rest of the community.

#2765. Vasseur reveals why Ferrari accepted Hamilton's grid penalty in Brazil

Ferrari team principal Fred Vasseur has explained why Lewis Hamilton was given a completely new power unit at the Sao Paulo Grand Prix, the change that left him with a 65-place grid penalty. He explained that the change effectively cost Ferrari nothing in Brazil, and that the team wanted to protect Las Vegas instead.

Hamilton had already faced a penalty before the problems began. Ferrari had chosen to give both him and Charles Leclerc a fifth internal combustion engine of the season, resulting in a 10-place grid penalty for each driver. Things then went wrong in FP3. Hamilton first reported vibrations from the engine before telling his team that there was smoke in the cockpit.

He came back to the pits with smoke pouring from the car and played no further part in the session, with more than 20 minutes still left.

After FP3, Ferrari took the power unit out of the car for checks. The team then said it had decided to replace the entire power unit, which meant Hamilton would qualify but start from the back. Vasseur said the uncertainty over the old unit was what forced the decision.

"We had a doubt when we were not sure to be able to reuse the engine. I didn't want to take a risk and have another issue later on during the weekend and take a penalty for Vegas. As we were between FP3 and qualifying, the change of engine was for free."

After starting in 20th place, the seven-time world champion finished ninth and scored two points for Ferrari.

On social media, he also shared a heartfelt message after Sunday. He wrote: "Devastated by yesterday's race, especially with how it ended. It started so well, but we struggled with the tyres and massive oversteer. In those conditions, it made things incredibly difficult. I pushed as hard as I could, but we just didn't have the pace this weekend. We'll work to understand why and come back fighting at the next race."

The Briton also added: "To everyone supporting us, thank you for sticking with us through the difficult days as well as the good ones. I feel that support, and I don't take it for granted."

#2764. Jaguars-Ravens averages 13.96 million on Prime Video

When it comes to interpreting press releases regarding the audiences for sporting events, there’s a rule of thumb.

The higher the number appears in the release, the better the company thinks the audience is. The lower the number appears in the release, the less impactful the figure is.

And if the number is really bad, there’s no release at all.

For the Week 9 Thursday night game between the Jaguars and Ravens— which was destined to have a non-stellar audience thanks to the Ravens being down to their third-string quarterback — Prime Video led with the fact that the eight-game season-to-date average has outperformed last year’s numbers.

The 33-10 win by the Jaguars, which Prime Video accurately called “lopsided” in the release, generated an average of 13.96 million viewers.

It nevertheless was, as Prime Video notes, a 13-percent bump over last year’s Week 9 Thursday night game. And for good reason. The Week 9 Thursday night game in 2025 featured the Ravens at the Dolphins, a 28-6 Baltimore win.

Even with an audience of less than 14 million in the eighth TNF game of the season, the package is offering 17.15 million per week for 2026.

This week’s game — Commanders at Giants — should do well, given that the Giants are both doing well and occupy the nation’s top market. In Week 11, it’s Colts at Texans. Which won’t be great.

The following week, Prime Video has a potentially massive game on Black Friday between the currently 7-2 Broncos and 6-2 Steelers.

After that, it’s Chiefs-Rams, Vikings-Patriots, 49ers-Chargers, Texans-Eagles (on Christmas Eve), and Ravens-Bengals.

#2763. Rapid Recap: Knicks 117, Bucks 85

The Milwaukee Bucks just experienced arguably their ugliest loss of the season, losing to the New York Knicks 117-85 after awful second and fourth quarters. Jaime Jaquez Jr. led all Bucks starters with 16 points, while Kasparas Jakucionis led the bench scoring with 11 points and four assists. Meanwhile, Jalen Brunson led the Knicks with 23 points, while Marquette's own (and newest enemy of the Swifties) Tyler Kolek led New York's bench with 12.

With Tyler Herro sitting out, Ryan Rollins got his first start since Halloween against Cleveland. The Bucks hit the first field goal of the game—a Turner triple from the top of the key—and hung tough in the first half of the quarter, tying it at 13 on the heels of five quick points and two assists from Rollins. The Knicks defense, though, proved stout, with Mikal Bridges rejecting Nate Ament's first attempt on the fast break. After a quick five points put the home side ahead, Jenkins called a timeout. Some positives for the Bucks followed out of the break, with Ament spinning through double coverage for the fancy and-one finish for his first points of the night, ending an 8-0 Knicks run. Kasparas Jakucionis kept the scoreboard ticking over as the Bucks exited the first quarter down 26-21.

The Bucks got off to a slow start in the second quarter, with Kel'el Ware scoring the lone field goal nearly four minutes in. Notably, AJ Green and Ousmane Dieng started alongside Ware and Jaquez Jr., and while it was an interesting experiment, the Bucks simply didn't have the speed to keep up with the Knicks on either end. Unfortunately, the Bucks went on another cold stretch, with a Dieng three being the only made bucket in a long stretch. Finally, Ament finally broke the seal after subbing back in and immediately picking off an Andre Drummond pass to finish in transition with balance and poise, looking more like a seasoned veteran than a rookie. Ament proved to be the lone silver lining during their regularly scheduled dumpster-fire quarter, finishing the half with a team-high seven points and two steals. Bucks enter halftime down 58-34.

Thankfully, Milwaukee got out to a faster start in the third, scoring nine quick points, a run capped off by a Jaquez steal and layup plus the harm. After turning it over on the next few possessions, the Bucks got back on track and went on an electric 15-3 run, forcing a New York timeout with the deficit down to 14. For the rest of the quarter, it seemed like almost everyone chipped in: Rollins, Jaquez, Ament, and Jakucionis all finished in double figures as the Bucks outscored the Knicks 38-27 and cut the deficit to 13, 85-72. This was largely because Milwaukee shot 64% from deep in the third and played a more physical brand of defense.

The visitors kept applying pressure to open the final frame with a quick bucket from Ware off a lob from Jaquez. Unfortunately, that was as close as they got, as the home side kept wearing them down, especially on the glass. Milwaukee scored just five points over four minutes, with the Knicks dominating the Bucks' frontcourt. On the night, Kuzma and Turner combined for eight points, eight rebounds, five assists, two blocks, and three turnovers on 2/11 shooting. At least there was the rare Bogoljub Markovic sighting, and Bogo made a smooth pass to Dieng in transition for an easy lay-up. That was about the only real garbage-time highlight, though, as the Knicks kept pouring it in. After mounting a comeback of sorts, the Bucks went out with a whimper.

59: The number of rebounds the Knicks got, and yes, of course, they won the rebound battle 59-32.

Three Bucks starters combined for just 11 points. One of those starters was Burries, a rookie who will likely take steps forward and backward all season. The other two are Kuzma and Turner, and if the first 10 games were not enough evidence that they need to be benched, then this game should be. The Bucks are starting to lose the identity they built over the first eight games, when they ranked top five in rebounding and second-chance points. Ware played more effectively and put in better effort, so start him and Ament. If the Bucks are going to lose, they may as well do it while developing young players.

#2759. As Jaguars go all-in for Super Bowl, it's time to praise them – and bury them | Opinion

I come to bury James Gladstone but also to praise him. For now.

The Jacksonville Jaguars' second-year general manager indulged his hyper-aggressive tendencies on Nov. 9, acquiring safety Jessie Bates III and defensive tackles Jordan Davis and Davon Godchaux in an obvious bid to further fuel his team's championship aspirations. And why not? The Jags are one of four NFL franchises to never appear in a Super Bowl – and if they fail to play on Valentine's Day this season, it won't be for lack of trying.

"We don't give enough credit or enough discussion about the Jags," former NFL head coach and current NFL Network analyst Steve Mariucci said Monday on "NFL GameDay Final." "Rodney Dangerfield, get no respect. Nobody talks about those guys.

"What did they do? They said, 'This is a window for us to win the darned Super Bowl. Let's load up our defense, because in the playoffs we're gonna be playing against some great quarterbacks, some MVP, great Hall of Fame-type quarterbacks.'"

NATE DAVIS: Vikings' Kirk Cousins deal might doom NFC West: NFL trade deadline winners, losers

Likely true. The Jaguars, who went 13-4 while winning the AFC South last year, couldn't escape their wild-card round matchup in Jacksonville against Josh Allen and the Buffalo Bills, who are currently locked in a race with the Jags in a bid for this year's No. 1 playoff seed in the AFC.

And yet as focused as Gladstone, 36, is on reaching for the brass ring, he's also drawn a clear line between himself and Philadelphia Eagles personnel czar Howie Roseman, with whom he brokered his biggest deal Monday. Moving forward, Jacksonville's title opportunity is quite likely akin to a fleeting aperture, while Roseman's Lombardi bay window could look out on the league for another decade or so … after this year's remodeling is done of course.

Should we fault Gladstone for trying to shed glory on a franchise that's rarely won, has long had one foot in Europe and – next year – will have both feet in Orlando while EverBank Stadium's $1.4 billion renovation is presumably completed? Not at all, even if only 42,000 fans can currently occupy the venue for what Gladstone and Co. hope are five more home dates this season, which presumes the Jags secure that top seed and win their playoff opener. After 31 mostly fruitless seasons, is this the time to strike with Trevor Lawrence belatedly justifying expectations that he could become a generational quarterback under the stewardship of second-year head coach Liam Coen? Yeah, probably.

NFL POWER RANKINGS: How does trade deadline affect pecking order, Jags' standing?

But as far as what the people of Duval County should expect in 2028, when their stadium reopens in hopes of filling its 65,000 or so seats?

▶ They should expect that CB/WR Travis Hunter is an impact player and performing at a level commensurate with the contract extension he'd be positioning himself for by then. Whether that actually happens is anyone's guess. Right now, the guy who was a two-way star for the University of Colorado and won the 2024 Heisman Trophy has decidedly not lived up to expectations after Gladstone surrendered a package to the Cleveland Browns that included two first-round picks and one in Round 2 in order to get Hunter with the No. 2 pick of the 2025 draft. Hunter has been better in Year 2 after an injury-curtailed rookie season, but that's hardly an achievement. He's not Darrelle Revis or Jalen Ramsey yet − not even close − but is starting for a foreboding defense. Offensively, he has seven catches this year. Gladstone needs him to truly flourish to justify the buy-in.

▶ They shouldn't expect to still have coordinators Grant Udinski (offense) and Anthony Campanile (defense), who both interviewed for head jobs earlier this year, and will almost certainly land ones in the next year or two. How effectively Gladstone and Coen, who's emerging into a superstar in his own right, are able to reload the staff remains an unknown that's likely to be tested in short order.

▶ They should expect WR Parker Washington to remain their primary offensive weapon … after Gladstone is obligated to sign him to a massive extension next year after Washington – wisely – turned down a less lucrative offer a few months ago. And don't forget, Gladstone acquired WR Jakobi Meyers at last year's trade deadline for fourth- and sixth-round picks before signing him to a three-year, $60 million extension. The team's approach to the receiver position is all the more befuddling given the investment in Hunter and Jacksonville's apparent unwillingness to trade Brian Thomas Jr., who's regressed from blossoming star as a rookie in 2024 to almost completely faded from the game plan nowadays.

▶ They should not expect this team to have a deeply set foundation. The Hunter trade has already limited the Jags' ability to import quantity from the past two drafts, though getting RB Bhayshul Tuten in the fourth round last year was a heist. But Gladstone has no first- or second-round pick next year, Bates costing him the latter selection at extreme cost given the 29-year-old will be a free agent next year, same as Godchaux.

▶ They should not expect Davis to be the second coming of John Henderson or Marcus Stroud. Yet Roseman extracted a 2027 first-rounder and 2029 second-rounder from Gladstone for Davis, a good player, though hardly a dominant one and with nary a Pro Bowl nod on his résumé.

▶ Barring a Super Bowl MVP or some such, they should not expect the Bates trade to age well. Make no mistake, he's a cagey player and first-rate leader. But giving up Round 2 (2027) and Round 5 (2028) selections for what might be a rental of a dozen games is unlikely to look wise in hindsight (if not foresight). Perhaps worse, the Buffalo Bills basically paid the same price Tuesday for another high-end safety, Amani Hooker (formerly of the Tennessee Titans) ... who also happens to be under contract through the 2028 season. Woof.

Jacksonville's approach seems almost diametrically opposed to that of Roseman, who tends to stockpile draft picks, nails a good percentage of the selections he makes and locks up his home-grown players with early extensions, all while maintaining the flexibility to target players like A.J. Brown in a trade or Saquon Barkley in free agency without seemingly ever crippling the roster.

And, yes, the Eagles' 2026 season has gone south for a variety of reasons. But Roseman is now in the process of laying the groundwork for the next iteration of the team. After spinning off Brown, Davis and offensive lineman Cam Jurgens over the past five months, Roseman has 10 total picks in the first two rounds of the next three NFL drafts. The ability to maximize and replenish his assets is why Roseman has positioned the Eagles, who have reached the Super Bowl three times in the past nine seasons and won it twice, alongside John Schneider's Seattle Seahawks as the NFC's most dominant organizations of the 21st century.

Based on the course they've charted, it's hard to envision the Jaguars achieving such consistent longevity. Gladstone, who worked in the Los Angeles Rams' front office for nine years before coming to Jacksonville and was part of the 2021 Super Bowl winners, has taken former boss Les Snead's "F--- them picks" to a new level. While the Jaguars are almost certainly better now than they were 10 days ago – when they lost starting safety Eric Murray and highly regarded defensive tackle DaVon Hamilton to season-ending injuries – Gladstone is also paying (overpaying?) for players without the pedigree to have nearly the same impact of stars like Ramsey, Von Miller or, certainly, Matthew Stafford, major difference-makers Snead once successfully imported at adjacent price points.

It's a major – and quite possibly myopic – gamble for an organization that's won one playoff game since the start of the 2018 season. And potentially a very costly one that will reverberate well into the future if Gladstone and the Jags have miscalculated.

#2754. CBA allows 49ers to not pay Brandon Aiyuk during two-week roster exemption

When unusual situations emerge in the NFL, it becomes a piece-by-piece exercise in figuring out the specific rules that apply. And few situations have been more unusual than 49ers receiver Brandon Aiyuk’s odyssey of the past year.

He’s back on the 49ers, at a salary of $13.75 million for the rest of the season. That fact pointed to the 49ers releasing him by 4:00 p.m. ET on Tuesday, in order to avoid owing him one-ninth of the total amount ($1.52 million) for Week 10.

But here’s where yet another obscure wrinkle applies. Under Article 20, Section 4 of the Collective Bargaining Agreement, the 49ers owe Aiyuk nothing during his two-week roster exemption.

From the relevant provision: “If a Club obtains a roster exemption for a player under contract who does not report to his Club at least five days before the final day of Preseason Training Camp as defined in Article 23, Section 10, the player will not be entitled to preseason or regular season compensation until such exemption is removed, provided the player is given written notice of such fact upon reporting to the Club. If such notice is not given to the player, the player must be paid his Paragraph 5 Salary during his exemption.”

So if the 49ers gave Aiyuk written notice that he won’t be paid during the two-week roster exemption (and they surely did), they don’t have to pay him. Which pushes their deadline for avoiding owing him a game check until Tuesday, November 24 — one day after the expiration of the exemption.

Why not just cut him? The 49ers are delaying the move because they can, postponing by up to two weeks his passage through waivers and, given his salary, inevitable free agency.

In the interim, he’s on the team. But Aiyuk won’t be reporting for work on Wednesday. He has been excused, we’re told, from team activities and he’s working out on his own.

The 49ers could release him at any moment. There’s no reason not to do so, other than to apply the brakes to his ability to join another team.

The circumstances counter the notion that he was reinstated by the league subject to any type of agreement with the 49ers. If that had happened, the agreement surely would have included a requirement that the 49ers promptly cut him.

Which means that the NFL, after apparently working with the 49ers to delay Aiyuk’s reinstatement in order to help the 49ers recover bonus money from Aiyuk, finally decided that reinstatement from the reserve/left squad list can’t be delayed in order to advance a team’s strategic objectives.

So, yes, Aiyuk eventually will be released. He wasn’t released today because the 49ers don’t owe him a game check for Week 10, or for Week 11. Eventually, when the roster exemption expires, they’ll cut him.

For now, the team’s delay in doing the inevitable points to a desire to keep another team from getting him, sticking it to Aiyuk, or some of both. It’s petty, but the 49ers have the power to do it.

#2751. Game Recap: Suns bench pours in 81 points in blowout win over Clippers, 133-110

Do you see what happens when you go from Victor Wembanyama to *checks notes* Brook Lopez? (with all due respect to the vet)

The Suns' second unit took this one over early and never gave it back. Phoenix beat the Clippers 133-110 Tuesday night, improving to 4-6. The bench poured in 81 points, Phoenix hit 22 threes to LA's 15, and the Suns led for 44 of the 48 minutes. Seven Suns finished in double figures.

It was a much-needed bounceback win for the Suns. We are now 10 games deep into the NBA season, and Phoenix sits at 4-6 after a brutal schedule to open up. All things considered, it could be worse.

Jordan Goodwin led Phoenix with 18 points in under 14 minutes, going 6-of-7 from the field with all six makes from three. Devin Booker added 17 points on 6-of-14 shooting with 5 assists. Luke Kennard scored 14 on 5-of-7 shooting, and Jalen Green had 13 on 5-of-7, including 3-of-4 from deep, with 5 rebounds. Collin Gillespie scored 12 points, all on threes (4-of-9), and dished out a game-high 8 assists. Man Man finished with 11 points on 4-of-5 shooting, 7 rebounds, and 3 assists. Ryan Dunn added 10 points on 4-of-5 shooting and 8 rebounds, and Oso Ighodaro grabbed 8 rebounds and finished +18.

Darius Garland and Rui Hachimura each scored 13 for Los Angeles. Garland shot 5-of-12 with 6 assists, and Hachimura went 4-of-10 with 3 threes and 5 rebounds. Baba Miller also had 13, all in the fourth quarter, on 4-of-4 shooting. Max Strus added 12 points, and Derrick Jones Jr. and Keaton Wagler each scored 11.

The Suns jumped out to an early 6-2 lead, led by 4 points from Devin Booker.

This quarter was tight for most of the first quarter. Los Angeles took an 18-16 lead behind 8 points from Rui Hachimura, who hit two of his three attempts from deep. Then the Phoenix bench took over.

The Suns closed the period on a 13-0 run. Collin Gillespie went 2-for-2 from three, Ryan Dunn was perfect at the rim, and Jordan Goodwin added a triple.

The Phoenix bench outscored LA's reserves 13-0, and the Clippers' second unit went 0-for-4 from the field.

Man Man didn't attempt a shot, but he still had 3 rebounds and 3 assists in under five minutes. Phoenix won the glass 17-8 and the paint 12-4. Devin Booker led all scorers with 8, though he turned it over three times.

Phoenix led after the first quarter, 29-18.

Jordan Goodwin turned the second quarter into his own shootaround. He went 4-for-4 from three for 12 points in just over six minutes, and Luke Kennard added two more triples off the bench. Phoenix shot 8-of-14 from deep in the quarter.

The Clippers found more offense this time, shooting 50 percent with eight different players scoring. Isaiah Jackson and Max Strus gave LA's second unit some life after it went scoreless in the first. Phoenix still stretched the lead to 17 at 48-31, its biggest of the half.

Devin Booker went 0-for-4 from the field in the quarter, and his only point came at the line. Ryan Dunn did not play in the second half after his strong first quarter. Collin Gillespie drilled a deep three at the buzzer to close out the half.

The Suns opened the second half with a bang.

Miles Bridges finally got going after a scoreless first half. He scored 8 points in the third on 3-of-4 shooting, including 2-of-3 from deep.

Devin Booker played all 12 minutes and found his rhythm with 8 points on 2-of-4 from three. Phoenix hit 7 threes in the quarter, while LA went 4-for-15 from deep.

The Suns did damage on the offensive glass. They scored 16 second-chance points in the quarter, compared to 7 for the Clippers, and the lead hit 32 at 91-59.

Man Man added 7 points on 2-of-2 shooting and a perfect 3-of-3 at the line.

With a 27-point cushion, both benches took over. No Phoenix starter played in the fourth, and the Suns closed with an all-reserve group.

Luke Kennard led the way with 8 points. Jamaree Bouyea made all five of his shots, going 2-of-2 from the field and 3-of-3 at the line for 7 points, and added 3 assists. Koa Peat chipped in 5 points, and Rasheer Fleming knocked down his only three. Phoenix shot 12-of-16 in the quarter.

Baba Miller made the most of his minutes for Los Angeles, scoring 13 points in the fourth on 4-of-4 shooting and 4-of-6 at the line. The Clippers took the quarter 38-34, helped by six Phoenix turnovers.

The Suns' never-ending homestand continues as they take on the Hornets on Thursday night.

#2748. Panthers vs Broncos game review: The other stuff

This was the worst loss against the Denver Broncos since, well, you know. At least this one was different, I suppose. Could you imagine if the game on Sunday was surrounded in controversy due to some highly questionable refereeing that seemed to heavily favor one side and for all intents and purposes ended on a sack-fumble? That would have been traumatic.

The obvious route to take this game review would be to list out and dwell on the many aspects of the game that boiled my blood. I will even encourage you to do so yourselves in the comments and I'll join in, as there's probably something cathartic about listing out the laundry list of frustrations stemming from Sunday. That said, rather than add on to that vitriol here, I'm going to take a different direction for the sake of our collective sanity.

Let's take a moment to look back and acknowledge the encouraging moments from Sunday that would have received some praise and fanfare had there note been all the rest of the other nonsense taking up the conversation.

Young had had back-to-back games with less than encouraging performances. While far from being the central issue or reason for the disappointing performances given the state of the offensive line and the quality of football being played by the defense, the downward tick in performance coupled with rumors of a contract extension led to some negative, even if somewhat warranted, takes being spread on social media.

Despite Facing a defense that's near the top the league at creating pressure and producing takeaways, Young found a way to be productive and find ways to move the ball. 276 yards, 3 touchdowns on 71.8% completed passes would get the job done on most NFL Sundays.

After Sunday's 8 reception, 90 yard performance Darren Waller is up to 299 receiving yards this season. For comparison's sake, that already surpasses Tommy Trembles 249 yards in 2025 which lead the position in receiving yards. Speaking of Tremble, those 249 yards were his career high to date and he currently stands about 80 yards short of that total in in 2026.

There were a handful of splash plays intertwined with the baker's dozen of penalties and other mid-play meltdowns. Tetairoa McMillan continues to improve and produce when needed, including a critical first down as well as a touchdown while lined up against Patrick Surtain. Lee Hunter flashed on multiple plays including an outstanding tackle for loss early in the contest that will surely earn him more than the 13 snaps he played Sunday. Chau Smith-Wade had multiple touchdown-saving pass break-ups while Corey Thornton baited Bo Nix to throw him his first interception of his career.

The Panthers rush defense has some Dr. Jekyll and Mr Hyde thing going on, but overall rank as the 28th rush defense in the NFL. Holding the Broncos to 82 yards and 3 yards per carry is certainly an improvement for the newish-look defense that Todd Wash is trying to implement. Let's hope they can make a trend out of keeping the opponents to less than 100 yards rushing a game.

It wouldn't be an article on the Panthers if there isn't mention of the injuries currently plaguing the roster. Dave Canales spoke on Monday and mentioned that the practice window for Xavier Legette will be opened this week and that Jaycee Horn, Mike Jackson and Jonathon Brooks are close. Brady Christensen is likely to return in the next couple weeks as well to boast the offensive line one way or another. Fingers firmly crossed for the returns of Damien Lewis, Bobby Okereke, and Jaelan Philips who all remain on the active roster.

There's a lot to be mad about right now. But there's also a lot of positive aspects and improvements lying underneath.

We'll meet back here next week after the Panthers take on the New Orleans Saints for the first time this season. Until then, keep pounding.

#2744. Jonah Jackson on Luke Goedeke's grievances: "This is football, man"

After Sunday night’s game between the Buccaneers and Bears, Tampa Bay tackle Luke Goedeke had some grievances to air about Chicago defensive tackle Jeffery Simmons. Bears guard Jonah Jackson was unpersuaded by Goedeke’s complaints about Simmons launching himself at and/or holding Bucs linemen.

This is football, man. Especially in the trenches. It gets rough and rowdy. . . . Did you see that big guy, number 50 [Vita Vea], launching at us? . . . It is what it is. We signed up for this.”

As to Simmons holding Goedeke, Jackson was equally blunt.

“They all do it. It is what it is. You’ve got find ways to combat it,” he said.

It really is anything goes when it comes to line play, subject to what the officials see and are willing to call. Especially when there are so many uncalled holding penalties on offensive linemen, arguably since defensive ends are so good and the powers-that-be prefer to keep quarterbacks in one piece.

The best, most recent example of that came in Carolina on Sunday, on the play when Broncos linebacker Nik Bonitto forced a fumble by Panthers quarterback Bryce Young to seal the game. Bonitto was being held the entire play. And he still got it done.

That’s the message for all offensive and defensive linemen. Do whatever you have to do to get it done. It’s only a foul if a flag is thrown.
