#2675. Damian Lillard is back and Ja Morant is here. How exactly is this going to work? | Bill Oram

In the history of basketball, we have certainly seen some why-would-they-do-that? pairings.

Jerseys and sleeves. Kawhi Leonard and a tree sponsorship. Utah and "the Jazz."

Once, there was even Detlef Schrempf and a headband, if you can believe that.

We're about to find out if they belong on such a list.

Because of all the things you might have said the Trail Blazers needed as they prepared to welcome Lillard back after making a playoff run without him, a slight-of-stature ball-dominant guard with a questionable jump shot would not have topped anyone's list.

Depth on the wing? Yes. Shooting? Definitely. Defense? Always.

Morant doesn't particularly address any of those, and yet, he's here, a dynamic two-time All-Star in need of a second act, being paid a team-high $42.1 million to play the same position as not just Lillard, but Jrue Holiday and Scoot Henderson.

Heck, the Blazers' most valuable point guard last season was forward Deni Avdija.

"I'm sure there will be questions about fit," General Manager Joe Cronin said Monday.

The Blazers have little more than three weeks before the regular season begins in which to figure that out. At the team's annual media day on Monday, Morant appeared in a fresh white No. 1 Trail Blazers jersey. It's happening.

"It's easy for people to be like, 'Man how is this going to work,'" Lillard offered. "'They can't do this, they can't do that.' But being on the floor with them … we can be a dangerous team and I really believe that."

The onus is on the Trail Blazers starting this month to prove that they bet right in acquiring Morant. And that pairing him with Lillard isn't the boondoggle conventional wisdom suggests it will be.

Lillard noted how many teams that succeeded in the playoffs last year, think San Antonio with its four point guards, relied on numerous playmakers. To his credit, Morant said he would be comfortable coming off the bench, if necessary.

But they would not be the first NBA team to fall into the trap of believing they are capable of adjusting or that they will be comfortable sacrificing. It isn't uncommon to see players in those situations default to familiar habits and sensibilities once the season is underway or struggles come.

That's what made a lot of the positive energy around what sure seems like an awkward roster ring so hollow. We're going to need to see it to believe it.

Morant tried to lay out a vision for how it could look. If he drives to the paint and is double-teamed, someone else is inevitably open. That's how basketball works.

"That allows me to have more space to be the best Ja I can be," Morant said.

The 36-year-old Holiday, who would be a more natural complement next to Lillard or Morant than they are to each other, made his own case for why the point guard rotation makes sense.

"It's about being a complete basketball player for myself," he said, "and I think we have a lot of guys like that."

There is a long history of teams talking themselves into superstar additions that make little sense. The Los Angeles Lakers once made a conscious decision to acquire Russell Westbrook and pair him with LeBron James. Nobody made them do that!

The talent and star power of a Lillard-Morant backcourt is undeniable. Still, I remain unconvinced that Cronin, with a very hands-on new owner in his ear, made the deal with winning basketball games at the front of mind.

Although, admittedly, Cronin's biggest wins as a GM have been in the trade market.

The haul of assets he collected for Lillard, only to get him back two years later, will go down as an all-time great swindle. So, too, will the oft-questioned Avdija trade a year later.

Maybe he sees something in a Lillard-Morant pairing that many of us can't.

Morant could return to the All-Star form he had achieved before injuries and off-court issues derailed his ascent. And if he does, the Blazers can either trade him for pieces that fit better or clear out the logjam and build around him.

But to sell the current roster as a basketball strategy doesn't quite pass the smell test.

Neither Lillard nor Morant has achieved stardom due to his defensive acumen. Each player needs the ball in his hands to thrive. If the duo is on the floor together, Avdija is no longer the secondary playmaker, he becomes tertiary.

So, you are left to wonder whether the Blazers sold themselves on Morant because of how he can help the current collection of talent or if they simply saw the opportunity to land a 27-year-old All-NBA talent for cheap, regardless of what it meant for the existing roster construction.

And if you're being honest, you probably don't need to wonder which of the two it is.

"We were very focused and we'll continue to be on … adding to our talent base as much as we can," Cronin said.

That thinking right there may tell you just how far ahead of everyone else the San Antonio Spurs and Oklahoma City Thunder are in the Western Conference. They are positioned to dominate for the next half-decade, if not longer. The only chance any other team has of disrupting that is taking bold risks.

But I thought the goal was to go all in on the twilight years of Lillard's career?

"Dame literally just wants to win," said first-year head coach Micah Nori, whose charge is to sort out arguably the most talented glut of point guard talent in NBA history. "I think that's the only thing left he really has to (do). He's already proven he's a winner, but at the highest level."

Does adding Morant move Lillard closer to a title? Or simply give Portland a potential off-ramp if Lillard is no longer the same player after tearing his Achilles tendon?

Morant was without question a low-risk, high-reward addition. He came at the reasonable price of Jerami Grant and Kris Murray. If it becomes clear that Morant is one point guard too many, or that he's just not the player he once was, some will argue that it didn't cost the Blazers much to try.

However, there is an opportunity cost to messing with Lillard's swan song. If you don't get it right, you risk wasting the gift of his voluntary return last summer. And, not for nothing, Lillard has the option to become a free agent again after this season.

The franchise icon certainly hasn't said anything that would suggest he is unhappy about Morant's presence, although he stopped short on Monday of a full-throated endorsement. He said he knew about the trade before it went through.

When I asked if he thought it was a good idea right away or if he needed time to get on board with the plan, Lillard said, "My position on it was, I'm prepared for whatever."

It's good that he's already thinking about other positions. Because his old one is getting awfully crowded.

#2674. Week 9, 3 up and 3 down: A disappointing result triggers a sell-off

The Atlanta Falcons Spanish expedition was fruitless, and the team returned to the States with another L to their name. The front office responded by doing something we haven't seen in years: sell off assets. There were role players with good contributions to highlight, but a handful of starters let the team down.

The Falcons are 3-6, and while they are technically in play for the NFC South title, that's not good enough for Cunningham, and that's a refreshing mentality. It's never easy losing a player like Jessie Bates, but with free agency looming and the team being far from a Super Bowl-caliber roster, Cunningham made the trade with an eye toward the future, collecting a 2nd and 5th-round pick.

He also made a buzzer-beater trade that shipped Ryan Neuzil to the Ravens and netted the team a 2028 6th-round pick and Andrew Vorhees. Neuzil doesn't fit this new scheme, and instead of getting nothing for him and knowing the comp formula wouldn't go their way with future spending, the GM took a proactive approach.

Woerner has been pretty steady after a slow start and had himself a respectable game. While the Falcons run game has been in a slump, it's not due to him. On the Falcons best runs you'll almost always find Woerner in the mix. He wins most of his battles against opposing linebackers and can be quite stout on the edge. It was nice to see the team reward him early with a touchdown.

He still needs to work on that Tush Push, but that's gonna be hard to do behind the centers on the roster, especially when Dexter Lawrence is across from you.

London is a bargain for what he provides. His presence was felt against the Bengals; he had two pressures, a sack, and a tough run stop on the goal line. Year after year, he's proven he can handle double teams and make plays off pure effort.

He's a glue guy that plays with an edge, and every roster needs guys like these. London is playing on a one-year deal and looks like a no-brainer for a new contract in 2027.

Terrell got worked early and often in this matchup. Ja'Marr Chase picked up where he left off in the 2019 National Championship, and had his way with Terrell. Tee Higgins was also able to haul in a touchdown on the corner. Man, press, zone—it didn't matter what the coverage was; Terrell got scorched. It has been somewhat of a down year for the corner, who spent time on IR, but this game has fans irate.

I understand where they're coming from, but this did happen against the best QB-WR pair in the league, and it's not like the Falcons are better off without Terrell, for now. Still, his days as a top-flight corner in this league are fading.

It was another rough performance for the linebacker, who has taken a massive step back during his second year in Atlanta. I respect his willingness to play through injury, but it's hurting the team, and his odds of getting anything more than a cheap one-year deal somewhere in 2027. He can't even perform a form tackle right now.

If it was just his body breaking down, that'd be one thing, but his coverage drops have been sloppy, and he isn't diagnosing plays close to the speed he was last year. He may have been an X-factor in 2025, but he is one of the weak links in 2026.

I begged for Folk to be cut and Cunningham delivered. It was one thing when the missed kicks happened from the 50s, but from 38?! Folk will still be remembered as one of the best to do it over the past decade, but unfortunately he ran out of gas when he got to Atlanta.

The Falcons are 3-6 and without some familiar names heading into Week 10. The team is in full evaluation mode, and while it's hard to get excited about that in-season, it's the right call.

#2673. "We know him and his talent" – Martínez explains decision to bring Tillman into Leverkusen's starting XI

After starting on the bench in two consecutive games, Malik Tillman was restored to Bayer Leverkusen's starting line-up for Sunday's 2-1 Bundesliga win over 1. FC Köln.

Having been criticised for failing to live up to expectations since his €35 million move from PSV in the summer of 2025, the 24-year-old United States international was handed a rare start and impressed head coach Carles Martínez.

"It wasn't easy for Malik. I know he had to deal with a lot of criticism, but we know him and his talent," Martínez explained at the press conference after the game.

"I thought today was the right day, in this atmosphere and setting. Tactically, too, I felt Malik could create something alongside Ibo," the Leverkusen coach continued, referring to his partnership with Ibrahim Maza.

“We were sure he was the right player, and he responded with a very good performance.”

Tillman will now link up with the United States national team for their Concacaf Nations League quarter-final matches against Haiti.

"Over the years, obviously, I've developed a friendship with him and have a ton of respect for him," Crosby said to the media Monday with the Ovechkin news. "It's tough, you come into the league at 18 years old, and before we even met, we were built up against each other."

It should be Logan Thompson in net for Washington, and he was excellent in his season debut in allowing two goals in a win at defending Stanley Cup champion Carolina last Friday. Last season at home, he was 19-9-5 with a 2.18 GAA and three shutouts. Thompson made two starts vs. Pittsburgh overall last campaign and won both with a 1.50 GAA.

The Penguins and Capitals have three meetings left, including Washington's home finale on April 4. That should be quite the Sunday night if both Crosby and Ovechkin are healthy then. Tickets on the secondary market are north of $800 to get in.

#2670. Rangers lose star goaltender Igor Shesterkin for season with lower-body injury; what's next for New York?

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

New York Rangers goaltender Igor Shesterkin will miss the remainder of the season with a lower-body injury, the team announced on Saturday.

Shesterkin suffered an apparent leg injury in the Rangers' loss to the Washington Capitals on Friday night as his right leg slid awkwardly into the post while scrambling to get back in position. Shesterkin fell to the ice immediately, and he needed assistance to get down the tunnel.

Prior to that loss, the Rangers were off to a terrific 4-1-0 start, and Shesterkin was a driving force behind that success. In just five appearances, Shesterkin posted 3.90 goals saved above average with a .900 high-danger save percentage, according to Natural Stat Trick.

The 2022 Vezina Trophy winner, Shesterkin has put up sparkling numbers since he entered the NHL in 2019-20. In 330 games, Shesterkin boasts a .917 save percentage, a 2.51 GAA and 22 shutouts. Over the last three full seasons from 2023-26, Shesterkin ranked third in goals saved above average with 45.4. Only Connor Hellebuyck and Andrei Vasilevskiy were better in that category.

Shesterkin was a big reason why the Rangers felt they could bounce back from a disappointing 2025-26 season, and losing the star goaltender puts a huge dent in the team's playoff hopes. It doesn't help that backup goalie Joonas Korpisalo is also hurt.

Dylan Garand replaced Shesterkin on Friday night, and Spencer Martin will be recalled from the AHL after recovering from his own injury. With the Rangers playing well early, it wouldn't be a shock to see them explore better replacement options for Shesterkin.

New York won't be able to replace Shesterkin's impact because he's one of the five best goalies in the world. However, the team should be able to upgrade its current goaltending situation, which is a fairly low bar to clear.

First, there are unsigned veterans still on the open market in Petr Mrazek and James Reimer. Neither one was great last season -- hence their availability at the moment -- Reimer and Mrazek could provide a level of stability in the crease that the Rangers simply don't have right now.

New York could also explore trade possibilities, and Minnesota Wild netminder Filip Gustavsson could be a solution there. Jesper Wallstedt is the future of the crease in Minnesota, making Gustavsson more of a luxury. Would the Wild send Gustavsson to New York in exchange for some draft capital it could use to acquire a center?

The one snag in a potential Gustavsson deal is his contract. Gustavsson is in the first year of a deal that pays him $6.8 million over the next five seasons. That's a big commitment for a player who will become a backup when Shesterkin returns.

Obviously, Connor Hellebuyck has been on the trade market for months now, but that trade wouldn't make sense for the Rangers. Hellebuyck is on an expensive long-term deal, and New York would have $20 million tied up in goalies if they made that move, not to mention the astronomical acquisition cost.

However, if you'll allow me to get creative here, it's no secret that the Florida Panthers have pursed Hellebuyck. What if the Panthers traded Jacob Markstrom -- just acquired in the offseason -- to the Rangers in order to make room for Hellebuyck?

Markstrom does have a 20-team no-trade list, so the question is whether New York would be one of his 11 approved teams. Florida flipping Markstrom so quickly seems like a long shot, but the team has taken plenty of big swings in recent history.

#2668. Oregon star edge rusher Teitum Tuioti out for the season

EUGENE — One of Oregon football's most important defensive players is done for the season.

Ducks senior defensive end Teitum Tuioti suffered a season-ending knee injury in Oregon's 41-28 win over Ohio State, Dan Lanning announced on Monday.

"Teitum has been unbelievable for us this year, and every year he's been here," Lanning said. "Just watching him grow as a player and person has been a lot of fun for us. But unfortunately Teitum's done for the year, he had a knee injury, he'll end up having surgery."

Tuioti was among the Ducks' leaders in tackles with 44, and ranked second on the team in sacks with 5.5 on the season. The former Sheldon High School star sits at No. 8 all-time for Oregon with 22.5 sacks across his four seasons, providing steady leadership on a talented and experienced defensive front.

In the win over the Buckeyes, he also showed off his arm: Tuioti completed a pass to fellow defensive end Matayo Uiagalelei on a memorable fake punt which shifted momentum in the game.

"I hate it for him, because (the injury) was a routine, weird play that it happened on," Lanning said. "He left it on the line there on the field, and I don't know if he'll get another chance to play as an Oregon football player, but whoever gets to have that guy on their team in the future is gonna be really, really lucky."

Should Tuioti forgo his fifth year of eligibility and enter the NFL Draft, he is a projected second- or third-round pick according to some mock drafts.

#2666. 7 great NFL rookies are who already changing their teams’ future

The consensus entering the 2026 NFL Draft was that the class was light on top-end, elite talent — but incredibly deep when it came to finding reliable starters. Now we're at the midpoint of the season it's time to check in and see how the rooks are progressing.

Broadly speaking, we've seen an incredible depth of defensive talent come out from the 2026 class, but the offensive side is a lot trickier to pin down. The Raiders are taking a slow, measured approach to elevating Fernando Mendoza to starter at quarterback; the season has been objectively horrible for Jeremiyah Love in Arizona, and the top receivers are struggling inside mediocre offenses to really drive the point home.

Today we look at the best rookies from the season so far, and who has the inside track for the end of season awards.

The race for offensive rookie of the year has come down to three receivers, and Denzel Boston is in the driver's seat. The 39th pick has been incredible for the Browns in spite of having horrible quarterbacks feeding him the ball, and he's within earshot of the same numbers that 2025 OROY Tetairoa McMillan put up a year ago. Here are their comparative stats over the first nine games of their career:

Tetairoa McMillan (2025): 41 receptions, 558 yards (13.6 YPC), 2 TDDenzel Boston (2026): 32 receptions, 507 yards (15.8 YPC), 3 TD

It's wild that this might be the second straight year we have seen an Offensive Rookie of the Year receiver who was underrated in the draft process. Boston does a phenomenal job using his frame to high-point the ball and fight through contact, but like McMillan, his route running and separation were vastly underrated during the pre-draft process. Right now he's the offensive steal of the draft, and should win the OROY unless something dramatic happens.

The Titans are still a work in progress, and it's unclear if Cam Ward will ever become "the guy" at quarterback — but at least Tate is looking like the correct pick. Tate has 413 receiving yards, including 18 receptions for a first down through seven games and five starts. That's fairly astonishing when you consider that Ward only has 1,483 passing yards on the season — meaning that Tate has accounted for over a quarter of all air yards, despite missing two games.

While the skills are definitely there, ball security is something the rookie needs to work on. Tate has fumbled three times this season after the catch, and while they haven't been back-breaking plays, this is an area where he could improve. That won't affect his rookie of the year chances, but there is some ground to be made up in order to pass Boston, and the Titans' passing game isn't doing him any favors.

It's a testament to how bad the Browns' QB room is that they have two of the top offensive rookies, and yet Cleveland ranks 29th in scoring and 20th in passing yards.

Concepcion is a receiver made for a good quarterback to leverage. That's been the biggest knock against him so far. Right now he has 437 receiving yards and 1 TD — but it should be so much more based on how open he's getting, as well as his unreal ability to carve up zone coverage.

The numbers are very good, and Concepcion is picking up steam this season, but as less of a big-play receiver it's trickier to get noticed in comparison to his teammate. Mark my words though: When the Browns find a real QB he will elevate to become their best offensive weapon.

Arvell Reese is exactly who we thought he was, and that's a very good thing for the New York Giants. A do-everything defensive Swiss army knife, Reese has been the biggest x-factor on a Giants defense that is extremely scary, albeit still a work in progress.

The rookie has stuffed the stat sheet in almost every area. He has 49 tackles, 4.5 sacks, 32 run stops, 1 forced fumble, and 1 interception. If you need anything on defense, Reese is going to give you it. It feels like we're not just witnessing the best rookie defender of 2026, but potentially the best defensive player to enter the league since Myles Garrett — that's how good Arvell Reese has been.

Home run pick, and he's going to run away with the DROY this year.

The Jets got clowned on a little when they took David Bailey with the No. 2 overall pick and left Reese on the board, but he's been phenomenal for them. Sure, he might not have the same all-around game as the Giants' linebacker, but with 7.5 sacks so far this season he's emerged as the primary pass rusher on the team.

Bailey has been great at both generating pressures and sealing the edge against runs. He's trending as a Top 20 EDGE in the NFL this season in both areas, which is phenomenal for a rookie to achieve. In any normal season he would be the runaway favorite to win the end of season award, but as it stands he might need to eclipse 15.0 sacks to get noticed or hope that Reese falls off at the top.

Despite recent headlines when Trey McBride tried to stunt on Caleb Downs, the Cowboys' rookie safety has been really, really good this season. He ranks highly among all NFL safeties in pressures and run stops, while also being one of the most reliable solo tacklers at the position.

There are some weaknesses to his game, most notably diagnosing and interrupting pass plays — but we knew that was an area he needed to work on during the draft process. Overall Dallas got a very good player who will anchor the defense for years to come, but it's a very hard sell on end of year awards when it comes to defensive backs — largely because they don't stuff the stat sheet in a way that attracts voters.

It's been incredibly easy to ignore the Dolphins this season. In fact, it's better for your health if you ignore this team — even if you're a die-hard fan. One bright spot has been 2nd round pick Jacob Rodriguez, who is proving to be every bit the tackling machine in the NFL that he was in college.

With 79 total tackles this season, Rodriguez is on pace for 168 combined when the dust settles. He's even shown glimpses of pass-rushing chops from the middle of the field, adding a handful of pressures for good measure — which wasn't really in his skill set.

The Dolphins have been desperate to get that Zach Taylor-esque leader in the middle of the field for some time now, and they've got their guy. He won't do a lot that's eye-popping, but that's also a good thing, because like a true old-school middle linebacker it's best if they do their job and get quiet stops, rather than hearing their name while making big plays, and giving them up in equal measure.

#2664. Giants-Commanders matchup: New York defense needs to stay on the attack

The 5-2-1 New York Giants host the 2-5-1 Washington Commanders on Thursday Night Football. The teams tied 27-27 in Week 5. New York is favored by just 1.5 points, and the Over/Under is set at 42.5 points.

Both the Giants and Commanders allowed victory to slip through thier fingers in Washington. Cam Skattebo's fumble led to a subsequent six-snap game the following week, and Washington's botched final ten seconds of overtime will be notorious in Commanders' lore for years to come.

Still, the Giants are now starting a different quarterback in J.J. McCarthy, and sitting comfortably at the top of the NFC East. This is an important home game on a short week for John Harbaugh and the Giants, who are looking to go on their first three-game winning streak of the season.

Washington ranks 20th in total offense, 22nd in passing offense, and 11th in rushing offense, largely due to Jaydeon Daniels' 252 yards on the ground, which leads the team. The Commanders average 21.5 points per game, which is 21st in the league. Despite the underwhelming numbers, the Commanders aren't a pushover team; they defeated Seattle in Week 3 and made their Week 6 loss in San Francisco kind of interesting in the second half. Still, the Commanders lack an identity on offense.

Washington lost star receiver Terry McLaurin three weeks ago, and the Washington rushing attack has struggled all year. Jacory Crosky-Merrit had an early 33-yard touchdown run against the Giants in Week 5, but he's still on I.R., and the rushing attack hasn't exactly taken off with Richaad White and Austin Ekeler.

Rookie wide receiver Antonio Williams has 26 catches for 284 yards on the season, but he hasn't exactly stepped up yet post-McLaurin injury; he has talent, and a big game could be coming for him soon. Williams has led the Commanders in snap share since the McLaurin injury.

Stefon Diggs plays 60-65% of the snaps, and he leads the Commanders in receiving yards. He has 30 catches on 49 targets for 303 yards with a team-high five touchdown receptions. Treylon Burks has been playing through injury, and Luke McCaffrey is a good special teams player who doesn't receive snaps on offense every week.

Van Jefferson played 58% of the snaps against the Rams in Week 9, catching five of seven targets for 58 yards with a touchdown. Jefferson seemed comfortable, and Washington looked for him in key situations; it's something to pay attention to on Thursday night.

Tight end Chig Okonkwo was used early and often against New York, and I expect more usage in Week 10. Ben Sinnott and John Bates are the two-and-three tight ends. Washington's offensive line consists of (from left to right) Brandon Coleman, Chris Paul, Lucas Patrick, Sam Cosmi, and Josh Conerly Jr.

ATTACK! Dennard Wilson dialed up pressure against Jayden Daniels and forced four three-and-outs in the game. Wilson blitzed on 62% of the Giants' dropbacks; 40.5% quick pressure rate, which is a 99th percentile performance. They blitzed on 23 dropbacks and got a quick pressure on 12 of those. Dru Phillips had 5 quick pressures on 7 pass-rush snaps as a blitzer.

New York used Cover-0 in critical moments toward the end of the game. Washington offensive coordinator David Blough is going to have better contingencies than he did in Week 5. New York out-coached a young coordinator, and the Giants should continue to show pressure, but be willing to change it if Blough's adjustments start to yield success.

The Giants surrendered a 33-yard touchdown to start the game against Washington, but the team has been much better with their run fits over the past two games. Disciplined football up front and better-angle discernment by the safeties in the alley can help mitigate an already struggling rushing offense; Jason Pinnock and Ar'Darius Washington have been solid so far, displaying those traits.

Blough's offense used simplified concepts against Wilson's heavy man defense. A lot of simple half-field curl/flat to slant/flat reads with stacks/BUNCH in third-and-short to create rubs/picks upon the release. New York must be dialed in spatially in man coverage and very communicative if they're passing routes off to one another; pick/wheel and post/wheel were used several times in Week 5.

When Blough uses condensed formations, New York should — and will — load the line of scrimmage and bring defensive backs on five-man pressure blitzes. Expect Fire-Zone blitzes and a lot of interior isolation for Arvell Reese and Micah McFadden against the interior offensive line. Reese vs. a running back in protection on third-and-longs will be a mismatch to exploit — as it was in Week 5.

The Giants must be cognizant of Jayden Daniels' legs. His ability to extend plays and evade defenders is difficult to handle, but Wilson incorporated these rush-spies that forced offensive linemen to commit to blocking but were tepid enough to watch Joe Milton as he tried to pick up yards with his legs. Arvell Reese's second sack was one of these rush-spies.

New York needs to continue to send six rushers at the snap, with two bailing into underneath coverage half a second after the sack. Wilson has used defensive linemen and linebackers in the rush this season; some of those underneath players and zones can help contain the quarterback. High-side rushes can't just abandon rush responsibilities with no spy if it is man coverage.

The Giants defense is playing like a top-10 unit, and the potential of these high picks is being actualized. Containing Daniels is difficult, but doable, and I expect the Giants to make Washington's offense uncomfortable. Giants win, 20-13.

#2663. Hoeneß' Musiala comments spark internal criticism at Bayern

Bayern Munich honorary president Uli Honess caused headlines on Sunday after questioning whether Jamal Musiala will ever rediscover his best form following his neurological diagnosis and recurring injury problems.

“Just imagine if FC Bayern were now to question his contract and say: ‘What he is capable of delivering now is no longer what was stipulated in the contract’,” Hoeneß remarked, among other things, during an appearance on the BR programme “Sonntags-Stammtisch”.

According to local outlet TZ, the 74-year-old's comments have sparked internal frustration at Bayern, with the general feeling being that while his concerns were understandable in terms of substance, the way he chose to express them was unnecessary.

The main source of frustration is that Hoeneß has once again shifted the focus towards Musiala's neurological condition, despite the fact that it has nothing to do with his current absence. Instead, the 23-year-old is recovering from a muscle fibre tear.

After collapsing twice earlier in the season, Musiala has not experienced any further absence seizures in the past two months following an adjustment to his medication. His condition is therefore considered to be well under control.

The report further states that Musiala remains the ultimate game-changer for Bayern coach Vincent Kompany, who has consistently supported and motivated the German international publicly.

If Hoeneß was also trying to motivate Musiala, he certainly went about it in a very different way.

#2662. NBA Panic Meter: Why Nuggets, Heat, Suns should be worried after just two weeks

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

We've now seen two weeks of the 2026-27 season. Is that enough time to draw conclusions? Almost certainly not. No team has even played 10% of its schedule yet, and outlier stretches are inevitable. Case in point: last year's champion, the New York Knicks, had a mostly healthy 2-9 stretch last January that included losses to the tanking Dallas Mavericks and Sacramento Kings. Weird things can happen for a few weeks.

But the first few weeks give us our first taste of who these teams are, and inevitably several will be worse than we expected. We may not have seen enough of a sample at this point to write anyone off completely, but alarm bells are starting to ring in a few notable markets. So let's go through a few of these struggling teams and figure out just how much reason there is to panic after two weeks.

It's easy to forget this now, but New York's championship season started relatively slowly. The Knicks won their first two games, but lost their next three. Mike Brown gave a lengthy and informative monologue about some of their process issues after one of those losses, a road defeat at the hands of the Milwaukee Bucks, and the Knicks righted the ship from there. And aside from that disastrous January stretch, they were mostly great.

It's hard not to look back on that stretch now, as the Knicks limp through a slow start to their title defense. Brown has echoed many of the same criticisms he made last October, most notably the offense's tendency to stand around rather than committing to the all-out motion machine that powered the greatest playoff offense of all time last spring. Perhaps that style wasn't fully replicable for this group across 82 games. That doesn't mean it can't be summoned again in April. All four Knicks losses have come by single digits. I'm going to need more than two weeks before I start worrying about Jalen Brunson's team in clutch settings. The Knicks were the fourth-most efficient late-clock shooting team in the NBA this season. They're 28th so far this season. That's going to change.

Brunson's offseason wrist surgery is a reasonable concern. His shooting is down from everywhere, even the foul line. Maybe he'll need a midseason break to get right. Mikal Bridges is (slowly) starting to make shots again. He needs to be more aggressive, and his on-ball defense has slipped. He was never going to match the intensity he played with in the postseason given his aversion to contact, but he'll have to improve on this front. Karl-Anthony Towns needs to stop fouling, but that's hardly new. Josh Hart is missing too much in the paint, but it's too early to draw conclusions there. OG Anunoby will start making 3s because he always does.

The October Knicks look like a team that spent July, August and September celebrating. If they still look like that in December, panic becomes reasonable. For now, the concerns are relatively light. They have a proven formula, and the big concern that did exist before the season -- the backup center situation -- has thus far been a relative strength. A championship earns you quite a bit more grace than the rest of these teams deserve.

If you shouldn't write off teams after two weeks, then you certainly shouldn't do so to rookies. Still, Darryn Peterson has certainly been the worst of the much-ballyhooed top four in June's draft. He's never getting to the basket or the line, not quite prerequisites for stardom at his size given his shooting, but enormously important traits for an aspiring star guard. Defense has been an adventure as well, though that's to be expected for a rookie guard, and the early returns on his fit with Keyonte George have been clunky. The Jazz ranking 29th in offense for any stretch in which they're actively trying to win is jarring. Will Hardy had the Jazz in the top five offensively in his debut 2022-23 season before the front office broke up the team at the trade deadline.

One of the motivating factors in selecting Peterson over Rookie of the Year favorite Cameron Boozer was February's acquisition of Jaren Jackson Jr., who is currently sidelined with a torn MCL. Considering his injury history in Memphis, his long-term reliability poses real concerns, yet Utah banked most of its interior defense on him, at least in the short term, when it traded Walker Kessler to the Lakers. It's hard not to wonder about an alternate timeline in which the Jazz chose Boozer and kept Kessler instead of trading for Jackson.

If we were purely talking about the 2026-27 season, the panic meter would be higher here. We're not. The Jazz wanted to be competitive this season. There's still plenty of time for that to happen, and the eventual return of Jusuf Nurkić should help on that front for a Utah team that has gotten very little out of the center position. The real championship window, even under the most optimistic projections, was always a few years down the line. The Jazz are still young and asset-rich. There's plenty of time to right the ship. Teams with more invested in this season specifically can't say the same.

The defense is bad, but the defense is always bad. They're at the bottom of the league in 3-point volume, but they're always at the bottom of the league in 3-point volume. Aaron Gordon is no longer finding easy looks at the rim nor finishing remotely effectively, but he's spent most of the last two seasons hurt, so he might simply need time to work himself back into a groove. These were predictable concerns. Nikola Jokić was supposed to paper over them like he always does.

So far this year, he hasn't. The best player of the 2020s is suddenly human, and the Nuggets are not built to win with Jokić as anything less than divine. His own defense has been perpetually shaky, but he's always at least been an elite possession-finisher. Since becoming a full-time starter in his second season, he's never had a defensive rebounding rate below 26%. He's below 22% so far this season. He's currently tying his career-high in turnovers per game, and his assists are back to single digits for the first time since 2024.

The real issues, though, are with his scoring. Jokić's overall statistical decline after a midseason knee injury last season was well documented, but what flew under the radar at the time was the precipitous decline in his 3-point shooting following a wrist injury. This was a big driver of last season's playoff upset at the hands of the Minnesota Timberwolves. Rudy Gobert didn't have to defend him out to the 3-point line, and considering Denver's shooting deficiencies elsewhere, that allowed the Wolves to completely take away the rim. Jokić is 7-of-31 from 3 so far this season. More distressingly, his legendary intermediate finishing is slipping. After five straight years in the 95th percentile or better in terms of efficiency, his runner is down to the 86th percentile, according to Synergy Sports. His hook shot, similarly dominant, is in the 50th. His free-throw attempt rate has nearly been cut in half since last season.

There's no point in talking about the defense, the shooting, or the iffy DeMar DeRozan fit if this is the case. Either Jokić is one of the best two or three players in the world or the Nuggets are not to be taken seriously as a championship contender. Jokić has earned a lot more deference than a six-game judgment. Nobody should be surprised if he's the MVP frontrunner in a month. Those other concerns will merit closer looks if he is, because even the idealized version of this roster is pretty flawed. But there's no scenario in which these Nuggets meaningfully contend if Jokić doesn't improve. For now, that's really all that matters here.

The Suns earn the dubious distinction of becoming the first team of the 2026-27 season to have their dysfunction leaked to the press. Ironically, the thing they're reportedly upset about isn't even really the problem. Chris Haynes has reported that the Suns locker room is frustrated by the roster's lack of a point guard. But Phoenix does have a point guard; it just isn't starting him. Let's compare Phoenix's offense with Collin Gillespie on the floor to how it plays without him, using stats from Cleaning the Glass.

This isn't rocket science. The Suns assist on almost 74% of their made field goals when Gillespie plays and below 60% when he doesn't. Both Devin Booker and Miles Bridges see their true shooting improve by at least eight percentage points with Gillespie on the floor. Starting Jalen Green isn't working. Whether it's in deference to his status as a No. 2 overall pick, his contract or an unfounded belief in his value, this experiment has failed. It's time to start Gillespie and add a more traditional point guard behind him.

So the point guard issues are solvable. You know what the bigger problem is? The Suns have completely lost the high-effort identity they built last season. Let's compare where the Suns ranked last year and this year in some notable areas.

Some of this comes down to bad opponents' shooting luck. Some of it is the absence of Mark Williams, because it has forced Khaman Maluach into a role he simply is not ready for (center has been perhaps Phoenix's biggest problem area). Most of it is rotational. Green isn't exactly known for playing hard or defending. Neither is Miles Bridges. Key players from last year like Jordan Goodwin, Ryan Dunn and Rasheer Fleming are playing less. The Suns simply aren't talented enough to win at the rate they did last year if they aren't playing as hard as they did then.

The Suns don't exactly have a pivot here. They don't control any of their own first-round picks in the seven-year trade window except for a 2032 selection that is currently frozen. They're not going to be able to trade Booker for a haul and reboot this thing, either. He's 30, never gets to the rim and is a declining 3-point shooter who seemingly needs to play next to the right type of playmaking point guard. His supermax contract has albatross potential. After giving up their 2033 first-round pick for Bridges, the Suns largely locked themselves into this core for the foreseeable future. There was never championship upside here, but for a team this heavily leveraged, this level of performance is simply unacceptable.

The following clip sums up one of Miami's biggest ongoing challenges:

Look at Tim Hardway here.. and then look at davion pic.twitter.com/qPTTtlY0Oq

The Heat have a reputation, and one of its pillars is defensive tenacity. Davion Mitchell obviously has that in spades. But given the unorthodox roster-building challenges of using two big men as your primary shot creators, the Heat have had to embrace players that don't. Tim Hardaway Jr. is on this roster because the Heat so badly need shooting around Giannis Antetokounmpo and Bam Adebayo. He is not yet making shots. He is also doing, well, this, defensively. Klay Thompson is getting hunted more mercilessly than almost any player in the NBA. The Heat have shooting. They have defense. They have alarmingly few players who offer both.

They have even fewer who can create their own shots. Antetokounmpo, Adebayo and Mitchell are the only members of the Heat who generated at least 30% of their made field goals without an assist. Toss Andrew Wiggins onto the pile, and everyone else who averages at least 10 minutes a game is assisted on 80% or more of their made shots.

Wiggins is averaging career-lows in everything. Miami's relatively egalitarian, pick-and-roll-less offense of a season ago suited him. Adjusting to the Antetokounmpo show thus far has been a struggle. Nikola Jović is veering dangerously close to dead money on their cap for the next four years. None of the core players, not Mitchell, nor Antetokounmpo, nor even Adebayo, is defending at the level expected. This was supposed to be a top-five defense. It's been in the bottom five thus far, and while some opponent shooting regression is coming, Miami's defense is designed to allow the very 3-pointers that are killing it.

Aside from simply having one of the best players in the world, it's hard to point to a distinct strength for the Heat. They're not shooting, defending or rebounding especially well. They're not winning the possession game. They're running quite a bit, but their transition offense ranks 24th in efficiency, according to Synergy Sports.

This is a team very much still finding itself, but it's one without many of the tools that made Antetokounmpo's Milwaukee teams work or the distinct advantages Miami's vaunted culture typically created for it. This roster is at least a trade or two away, but with minimal draft capital, addressing the holes here will be difficult. It might take multiple transaction cycles to get this right.

Antetokounmpo is in his 30s now and has a growing history of lower-body injuries. He might not have that many more prime seasons to waste. He's playing at a superstar level right now, and it just isn't clear how equipped Miami is to take advantage of that after giving up practically everything of value it had besides Adebayo just to get him.

#2661. Commanders finally face true “must win” game to keep their season alive - Daily Slop

Editor's note: Each day, Hogs Haven compiles a collection of articles, podcasts & tweets from around the web to keep you in touch with the Commanders, the NFC East, the NFL and sports in general, with a sprinkling of other stuff. Enjoy!

Washington will face the New York Giants on Thursday night in East Rutherford, New Jersey. Given the state of the NFC East race, it's easily the Commanders' most important game of the season. Whether they come out on top will probably dictate their fate.

While a win won't ensure anything, it would at least give Washington a chance moving forward. A loss, however, would make the team's road to the playoffs [effectively impossible].

After the Giants lost star outside linebacker Brian Burns to a torn ACL in Week 3, defensive coordinator Dennard Wilson…turned up the heat. Since Week 4, New York's defense has blitzed opponents on 46.5 percent of their dropbacks (second-highest rate in the NFL). That has helped the unit generate a pressure rate of 36.4 percent (13th) and a sack rate of 9 percent (sixth).

Wilson hasn't blitzed anyone more than he did the Commanders in Week 5. They blitzed on 62.2 percent of Washington's dropbacks and sacked quarterback Jayden Daniels five times.

The Giants had a season-high seven sacks in their win over the Eagles. Although they have a talented defensive line, their most effective pass rusher has been inside linebacker Arvell Reese, who had three sacks against Philadelphia.

As the Commanders attempt to curb New York's aggression, they will have to do so with a backup at center. Starting center Lucas Patrick suffered a concussion against the Rams and won't be able to clear concussion protocol by Thursday. Veteran Nick Allegretti will start in his place against the Giants.

The Commanders are optimistic Burks (foot) will play Thursday after he sat out last week. They also believe cornerback Amik Robertson, who suffered an ankle injury late against the Rams, will be good to go.

With their season hanging in the balance in the form of a Thursday night game at the division-leading New York Giants, the Washington Commanders stood pat at the trade deadline Tuesday — a tacit acknowledgment that they're trying to salvage the tenure of coach Dan Quinn but aren't willing to part with draft picks to add to an injury-riddled group that has produced just two wins in the first half of the season.

The Commanders — at 2-5-1 — are within a victory at New York of pulling within two games of the 5-2-1 Giants. Given their tie against New York last month — a game the Commanders should have won if not for an egregious late-game management situation — it's not unreasonable that Washington [are] holding out hope to get back into a divisional race that has no surefire winner.

Now, the Commanders head into the final nine games of the season — a stretch that will determine whether Quinn gets a fourth year or not — with a roster that is thinned by injury and hasn't efficiently closed out games. The Thursday night game against the Giants provides the first test as to whether that was the right path forward.

Patrick was signed on September 16 and performed better than Allegretti, who was still nursing a calf strain early in the season, so Patrick earned the starting role. Unfortunately, Patrick left Sunday's game against the Los Angeles Rams with an apparent concussion. He has been ruled out for Thursday's game against the New York Giants, and Allegretti will replace him.

Rookie center Matt Gulbin replaced Patrick against the Rams on Sunday and struggled to fill the role effectively. So, it makes sense that veteran Allegretti is getting the nod. However, the issue here is why didn't the Commanders turn to Allegretti on Sunday? Quinn said after the game it was because Allegretti had been practicing at guard.

Stefon Diggs and Jer'Zhan Newton missed October's 27-27 tie; now five players from that game are on IR, leaving Washington to find answers across its offense and defensive front

The last time the Washington Commanders and New York Giants played, the game ended in a 27-27 tie after both teams missed chances to win in overtime. That day, Stefon Diggs was inactive, and Jer'Zhan (Johnny) Newton was on injured reserve. Terry McLaurin, Dyami Brown, Daron Payne, Jacory "Bill" Croskey-Merritt, and Javon Kinlaw played; all five are now on IR.

A month later, Washington has managed only one win since, and will enter the game at 2-5-1 after losing 20-13 to the Rams in Week 9.

Van Jefferson has a much bigger part in this offense now, too. He played just three offensive snaps against the Giants, compared with 36 against Los Angeles, where he caught five passes for 58 yards and a touchdown. Antonio Williams' workload has grown from 42 snaps in the tie to 52 against the Rams. Jefferson should stay involved even if Treylon Burks returns from the foot injury that kept him out Sunday. He gave Blough another weapon to work with.

The backfield has changed as well. Croskey-Merritt ran for 82 yards and a touchdown on 11 carries in the first meeting. Rachaad White and Austin Ekeler handled the running-back snaps against the Rams.

Daronte Jones has two substantial workloads to replace up front. Payne played 63 of Washington's 89 defensive snaps in the tie, while Kinlaw played 56. Payne also recorded a sack and a forced fumble. With both players now on IR, Washington will ask a different group to handle the interior work and create some disruption of their own.

Newton's return to the lineup helps, but his first game back also shows how much work falls on the rest of the rotation. He played 20 defensive snaps against the Rams, while Shy Tuttle played 43, Tim Settle 33, and Ricky Barber 15.

Mathematically the Commanders remain alive, but with nine games remaining, any realistic hope the team has for a strong finish likely begins and ends vs. the Giants on Thursday (8:15 p.m. ET, Prime Video). A win and they would be two games back with eight to play and own the tiebreaker — if that eventually mattered.

"We all know how badly we need this," Washington coach Dan Quinn said. "Everyone in this building understands that."

Another loss would drop them to 7-18-1 since the start of last season and likely intensify the speculation by analysts over Quinn's future. Owner Josh Harris has not publicly commented on Quinn's job. Quinn said he regularly meets with Harris before and after games and also on Mondays.

But in training camp, one team source said what has been repeated by others at various points: "It's a results business."

And the results need to improve. Washington has now played five one-score games; the Commanders are 1-3-1 in those games — and 3-7-1 since the start of 2025. In 2024, when they went 12-5, Washington was 8-4 in one-score games — but that included a four-game winning streak at season's end.

The Commanders were in another one Sunday before losing 20-13 to the Rams. They had the ball last, drove to the Rams' 32-yard line with eight seconds left, but two failed plays ended the threat.

They lost 23-17 in Week 6 at San Francisco, failing in the red zone — a touchdown was nullified by a face mask penalty — and again on the last series when they reached the 28 with 22 seconds to play.

"We get in those moments and we have to finish," Daniels said.

The Washington Commanders defense played relatively well in the loss to the LA Rams on Sunday. They held the Rams to below their season averages for total yards, passing yards, rushing yards and points, which tells you that ultimately it was a pretty solid performance. But the Rams are dealing with a lot of injuries on offense and only really had one receiving threat in this game, star receiver Puka Nacua. Nacua caught 14 passes for 150 yards and a touchdown, while no other receiver had more than two catches.

So it's fair to ask if the Rams only really had one receiving threat in this game, how did the Commanders allow Nacua to be so productive? Surely you just double up on Nacua and stop the ball going his way and make others beat you? Well, it's not quite that simple unfortunately. For starters, the Rams did a great job moving him around and forcing the ball to him. Four of his 14 catches were on receiver screens, for example.

There's not really any way to stop a team throwing receiver screens if that's the way they want to force the ball to their star receiver. You'll notice that on three of those four plays, the Commanders were in a blitz look with multiple extra defenders walked up on the line of scrimmage. Those quick screens to Nacua were clearly a game plan option for the Rams to try and help deal with the Commanders tendency to load the box and send aggressive blitzes.

Ultimately, the Commanders did a pretty good job on these. Nacua gained some yards, but the first screen came on third and eight, Nacua only got six so the Commanders forced a fourth down. The second screen saw K'Lavon Chaisson punch the ball out and Nick Cross recover the fumble. The third screen came on third and 10 and Chaisson chased down Nacua to keep the gain to seven yards, again forcing another fourth down. It was only really the final one that did damage and that was just eight yards on first and 10, so that's not the end of the world either.

But that's only four of Nacua's 10 catches, so what happened on the rest. Well, there was a good mix of plays where the Commanders actually had pretty solid coverage and Matthew Stafford made a great throw or Nacua made a great catch. There were also a few plays where I think the Commanders would like to have done a better job. So let's first look at the plays where the Rams deserve credit, because I think the Commanders were pretty good on a lot of these plays.

Commanders are better than their record says. No doubt high stress level close game.

I say it every week! When we rush too fast up field it leaves gaping lane for him to run. If we don't get sacks fine. We cannot let him out of the pocket. You guys think we keep rolling [on Thursday night]?

With the trade, 2026 No. 1 pick Fernando Mendoza will take over as the Raiders' starting quarterback, beginning this week at home against the Seattle Seahawks. Aidan O'Connell will be Mendoza's backup.

Cousins posted a goodbye to the Raiders on his Instagram story, writing, "Thank you Raiders Nation! Go get em @fernandomendoza."

Trade talks between the teams didn't materialize until Tuesday, according to Las Vegas general manager John Spytek, who said the team was not actively looking to trade Cousins. Spytek said he received a few phone calls about Cousins until the most important one came from Vikings GM Nolan Teasley. He and Teasley spoke on the phone for a while to hammer down the framework on a deal that made sense for both sides.

Spytek said he did not speak to Cousins before Tuesday about the possibility of him being traded.

Willis was placed on injured reserve Tuesday due to a groin injury. With Willis shelved, second-year quarterback Kyle McCord will fill in, beginning Sunday on the road against the Indianapolis Colts.

The 27-year-old Willis, regarded as one of the best running quarterbacks in the NFL, was noticeably hobbled in his team's Week 9 defeat to the Detroit Lions.

A free-agent signing after renewing his career and promise under the tutelage of Matt LaFleur with the Green Bay Packers, Willis has shepherded a rebuilding Fins squad to mixed results. The Dolphins are 1-7 and he's completed 58.2% of his passes for 174.5 yards per game, six touchdowns, six interceptions, and rushed for 232 yards and three scores.

Drew Rosenhaus told Pat McAfee the $13 million that Aiyuk "allegedly" owes is "separate and distinct" from his playing status

Wide receiver Brandon Aiyuk has not yet repaid the 49ers any of the $13 million in bonus forfeiture that he "allegedly" owes the team, his agent said Tuesday.Agent Drew Rosenhaus said during an appearance on The Pat McAfee Show on ESPN that he will attempt to reach an agreement on Aiyuk's behalf on that matter "separate and distinct" from resolving Aiyuk's playing status.Aiyuk was reinstated from the reserve/left squad list, and NFL commissioner Roger Goodell granted the 49ers a two-game roster exemption for him that expires Nov. 23, according to Monday's NFL daily personnel notice."Brandon will either play for the 49ers when the two weeks is up or they can decide to release him, by which he will be a free agent and I expect that there will be interest in him," Rosenhaus told McAfee. "I definitely expect him to play this season. Judging [by] the comments from coach [Kyle] Shanahan, it doesn't sound like they plan on bringing Brandon back."So when the two weeks is over, it's my job to potentially find a new team for him. And I'm confident, now that he's healthy, that he will play. As far as the money that's allegedly owed … the $13 million, whatever it is—he hasn't paid anything yet. That's something that we'll work out separate and distinct from the issue of him playing. Hopefully we'll work something out to the benefit of Brandon's and something that's fair. And that's also part of my job."Aiyuk passed his physical with the 49ers, according to Rosenhaus."I think that in all likelihood Brandon would probably sign with a team that knows him, [with] somebody that has somehow been affiliated with him, either in college or the 49ers," Rosenhaus said Tuesday. "That's just my guess 'cause, you know, there's a lot of that in the NFL. You see people connect the dots where they [have] history, where there's relationships."

[GM John] Lynch told the station that "we can talk a little more in detail about the process" this week because it is "kind of a fluid situation." He was asked whether the 49ers would listen to anything that Aiyuk and Rosenhaus might have to say about a possible reunion.

"I think everything's possible," Lynch said. "You know, I will say this: We've worked with Drew a lot. You know, Drew is a good guy to deal with. He's reasonable. He's got integrity. … That's all good. We'll see how this thing goes. I think I'll just leave it at that."

#2658. Tom Izzo Reveals What He Told Jeremy Fears Before Dominating Duke

Michigan State head coach Tom Izzo had a message for Jeremy Fears Jr. before Tuesday night's showdown against No. 2 Duke, and apparently, it got through loud and clear. The Spartans' star point guard responded by putting together a brilliant performance in a 79-73 victory at the Champions Classic in Chicago.

Fears finished with 18 points, 11 assists, and seven rebounds as No. 5 Michigan State improved to 3-0. But following the victory, Izzo revealed that he had challenged his point guard to start playing like the superstar everyone expected him to be.

According to ESPN's Jeff Borzello, Izzo made it clear that preseason accolades come with serious expectations.

"You're given a rank, you have a responsibility to live up to that ranking," Izzo said.

Michigan State's Jeremy Fears Jr., right, celebrates with Coen Carr after Carr scored and drew a Toledo foul during the first half on Thursday, Nov. 5, 2026, at the Breslin Center in East Lansing. Credit: USA TODAY Network via Reuters Connect (Reuters)

Despite Fears entering the season with national recognition, Izzo wasn't completely satisfied with his performance through Michigan State's first two games. The Hall of Fame coach explained that his point guard simply hadn't looked like himself.

"And I thought he was okay in the first couple games," Izzo continued. "I didn't think he was Jeremy-like. And tonight I thought he played hard."

That shouldn't surprise anyone who has followed Izzo's career. The veteran coach had already raised the expectations for Fears, making it clear that being merely good was no longer enough.

Tuesday night was exactly the response Izzo wanted. Fears controlled the tempo, created opportunities for his teammates, and helped Michigan State build a lead Duke never managed to erase.

Fears acknowledged that Izzo had been pushing him, particularly when it came to playing faster and being more aggressive.

"He's been big on me lately, especially about pushing the ball, pushing the tempo," Fears said.

The Spartans had already earned a measure of revenge against Duke, a team that held Fears to 0-for-10 shooting in their previous meeting. This time, Michigan State's floor general made sure things ended differently.

Perhaps the most impressive part of Fears' performance was his ability to take over without needing a huge shooting night. His 11 assists kept the offense moving, while 15 second-half points helped Michigan State withstand Duke's comeback attempts.

Izzo's message was simple: If you're going to receive national recognition, you'd better play like you deserve it. Against one of college basketball's premier programs, Fears did exactly that.

And if this is the version of Jeremy Fears Michigan State gets moving forward, the rest of the Big Ten should be paying attention.

The NBA probably has been my favorite professional sports league since Michael Jordan's Bulls started dominating. Long time, I know. But I've been pulling back that interest some in recent years because I am so tired of healthy guys sitting out for "rest management." These guys only work seven months a year and make lifetime money. If you are hurt, that's hugely different.

In my opinion, the Pacers embarrassed themselves and the NBA on Monday in a 108-104 home loss to Atlanta, Indiana's fifth straight loss. Yes, some guys were out injured for the team in that one but 11 guys were out -- representing about 93% of their payroll – with six total available.  All six guys — including the team's three two-way players — played 34 or more minutes and reached double figures. Second-round rookie guard Braden Smith, so good in college at Purdue, had a double-double with 19 points and 10 assists in 42 minutes of action.

Per NBA.com, it marked the first time in 22 years that the Pacers used so few players in a game. While it was the eighth instance of teams using only six guys over the past 15 seasons, almost all the others were in meaningless games at the end of the campaign when teams are tanking or resting for the playoffs. This season isn't even two weeks old.

The last time a team used only six players in a game even in the first month of season was on Nov. 24, 2009, when Golden State did and still beat Dallas. ESPN topped that stat by telling me that the last time a team used six or fewer players this early in a season was in 1948, when the Lakers used five in their third game of the season.

What really irked me was Indiana resting arguably its second-best player in Pascal Siakam in the second of a back-to-back when the roster was in such bad shape. Kelly Oubre Jr. was a late scratch because of a bruised knee and Larry Nance Jr. sat with an illness.

Now, some guys are truly hurt and also won't play tonight: Superstar Tyrese Haliburton and fellow guards TJ McConnell, Ben Sheppard and Johnny Furphy. But Oubre, fellow forward Obi Toppin and starting center Ivica Zubac are all questionable after also sitting. Zubac would be a help, as he has been limited to only three games and has not played since Oct. 25. So I expect a competitive team tonight but one that also might be looking ahead to its next game against Denver in Mexico City on Saturday.

#2652. Should the NBA shorten games to 40 minutes? Pros and cons of move as league battles early season injury crisis

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Opinions vary on the causes and potential solutions for the NBA's early-season injury crisis, and an idea commissioner Adam Silver once floated is back in the conversation. Sports Illustrated's Chris Mannix said on the Open Floor podcast that he has heard that Silver likes the idea of shortening NBA games to 40 minutes. This is an idea that Silver has previously supported publicly.

"As we get more involved in global basketball, the NBA is the only league that plays 48 minutes. And I would be -- I am -- a fan of four 10-minute quarters," Silver said on The Dan Patrick Show in 2025. "I'm not sure that many others are. Putting aside what it means for records and things like that, yeah, I think that a two-hour format for a game is more consistent with modern television habits."

Silver is not the only major supporter of the idea. Mark Cuban has vouched for it as well, and given the sheer number of notable injuries the NBA has endured so far this season, the league is suddenly in a position in which it probably needs to consider pretty drastic changes to keep its best players on the floor. Is the idea of a 40-minute NBA game feasible? What are the pros and cons here, and why do the negatives ultimately outweigh the positives? Let's dive in.

Some basic math: 82 48-minute games equals 3,936 minutes of regular-season basketball for every team, before overtime. Trim games to 40 minutes and teams instead play 3,280 regular-season minutes per year, or around 17% less total basketball. Fewer minutes means fewer opportunities for players to get hurt.

That much is essentially indisputable. Where things get more promising is in the theoretical, compounding effect of playing less. If players are likelier to get hurt when they're overworked, reducing their workloads could potentially limit those more vulnerable minutes late in games and seasons because they simply aren't accumulating the same degree of wear and tear.

Fresher players would hopefully be healthier players.

College basketball games are 40 minutes. WNBA games are 40 minutes. FIBA games are 40 minutes. The NBA is the outlier here. It is the only major basketball league in which games have those eight extra minutes, and standardizing games across the sport could make it easier to translate player production across leagues.

This isn't strictly a basketball phenomenon, either. Major League Baseball is in the middle of a renaissance sparked in part by game-shortening measures like the pitch clock. Silver acknowledged this in that Dan Patrick Show interview, calling a two-hour game "more consistent with modern television habits." It's simply easier to hold the attention span of a television audience for a 40-minute game than a 48-minute game.

This has certainly been less true in the "eight champions in eight years" era we are currently living through, but the NBA tends to be more predictable than other sports when it comes to playoff outcomes. The NFL's single-elimination format makes the best teams extremely vulnerable in the postseason, and baseball is so inherently volatile because pitcher performance makes upsets so common.

Over a seven-game sample, the better team usually wins out in an NBA playoff series. This isn't absolute, of course, especially with health and 3-point variance factored in, but Cinderella runs are relatively rare in basketball. Only two NBA champions were seeded lower than No. 3 in their conference, and neither came this century. Nearly twice as many No. 1 seeds (53) have won titles than all other seeds combined (27).

Smaller samples create more volatility. It's easier for an inferior team to overcome a superior one across 40 minutes than it is across 48. Every hot shooting stretch means more; every key player in foul trouble has to miss a larger portion of the game. If you view the NBA through a purely competitive lens, this is a negative. If you view the NBA primarily as an entertainment product, creating more upsets is a real benefit of shortening games.

NBA games may last 48 minutes, but nobody actually plays anywhere near that much anymore. In fact, nobody even averages 40 minutes per game anymore, with Jamal Murray leading the league at 38.4 minutes per game thus far this season. What this essentially means is that teams could largely maintain the workloads of their superstars in a 40-minute game and simply use their bench players less.

This is the immediate reason that a change like this isn't feasible. Why on Earth would the NBA Players Association go along with a change that trivializes the majority of its membership? Stars would suddenly be more valuable than ever because they'd be playing a greater proportion of the game, but everyone else becomes less valuable for the same reason.

This has enormous team-building implications as well. Suddenly, superteams would be back in vogue because tying all of your money and assets into two or three players would make more sense in a world where fewer players are needed to get through a game or season.

On this note, it's not even clear what sort of health benefits this change would actually create. Bench players would certainly stay healthier just for playing less... but would stars benefit from this at all? That's less clear, and the NBA is obviously far more invested in keeping the best players on the court than role players.

There are theoretical fixes here, but none are perfect. The NBA could put a minutes cap on individual players, but remember, stoppages aren't uniform. Say the league sets a 30-minute cap, and a player crosses that threshold because no timeout, foul or dead-ball turnover stops the game for him to leave. How does the league handle that? It could mandate that players sit one full quarter, but doing so would inevitably lead to star players essentially playing at least one full half.

There's no clean solution to this problem, and until someone finds one, it's hard to believe this sort of change is feasible.

The length of games is only a small component of what makes the NBA schedule so grueling. Shortening games to 40 minutes wouldn't eliminate the need to travel to 41 regular-season road games. It wouldn't remove back-to-backs from the slate either, and it wouldn't bake more time into the schedule for practice, conditioning or a longer training camp.

NBA basketball is simply more difficult to play today than it was in the past. Players are more skilled and athletic than they used to be, forcing them to cover more space, play faster and endure more punishment than they once did. Shortening the game wouldn't change how it is played.

That's the danger of any incremental solution. Shortening games would carry substantial costs to the NBA. Shorter games would mean fewer commercial breaks for the television product. If the league tries it and it doesn't work, it has sacrificed revenue for nothing and is therefore less likely to take bigger financial risks to reap more substantial rewards, such as cutting games from the schedule.

Even if records and statistics aren't that important in the grand scheme of things, they're treated as sacred components of league history by many fans. Even if every other major rule has been subject to change across eras, the length of the game has been stable. That makes comparing stats and records across history at least somewhat viable. That changes if you shorten the game. Modern records become nearly unbreakable.

If the league were willing to tamper with its history in this way, there are simply lower-risk changes it could make instead of shortening games. One concept: increasing the value of 3-pointers to four points and similarly pushing 2s up to three. Doing this would narrow the value gap between shots behind the arc and those inside it, thereby incentivizing players to take more mid-range shots and, theoretically, forcing defenders to cover less ground than they do currently. One reason a change like this is unlikely is that it would make comparing numbers across eras pointless.

The NBA may one day decide it's willing to break that glass, but it has given no indication that it is prepared to do so now.

This is an article version of the CBS Sports HQ AM Newsletter, the ultimate guide to every day in sports. You can sign up to get it in your inbox every weekday morning here.

One of the biggest benefits of the NIL era is that college basketball has more elite talent than ever, now that players are returning for bigger paychecks instead of bolting for NBA money at the first opportunity.

That made selecting our 2026-27 CBS Sports Preseason All-America teams especially difficult, but our experts nailed it. Each of the three teams features players who will be performing at the next level very soon, but the best of those might be Florida superstar Thomas Haugh.

As our own Isaac Trotter explains, if Haugh can improve his range shooting, he won't have to wait long to hear his name called in the 2027 NBA Draft.

When it comes to how the talent broke down by conference, it was a a pretty level playing field for the most part.

Not to spoil anyting, but Arizona freshman Caleb Holt did not make the cut. He did, however, turn some heads in the Wildcats' exhibition game.

Loyalty is an excellent quality to have in a friend or partner. It's also why we love dogs.

It should not be quite as prevalent among college football coaches, some of whom have been undone because they did what was comfortable, not what was necessarily best for the team.

Our own John Talty highlighted five high-profile coaches who have been loyal to a fault, making hires and personnel decisions that have come back to haunt them. One of those coaches is Mike Elko. After a shaky season from Marcel Reed in 2025, Texas A&M chose not to pursue an upgrade in the portal.

Instead, the Aggies gave Reed a major payday, and they'll miss the College Football Playoff because of it.

Look, it can happen to the best of us. Dan Lanning and Dabo Swinney wound up on the list, despite the success that those two have had throughout their careers.

Steve Sarkisian is another coach who has fallen into the trap of being too loyal, but he may have a huge decision on his hands in the offseason. Arch Manning has struggled enough that another year in college should be on the table. If that happens, would Sark welcome back Manning with open arms, despite his shortcomings?

Finally, one person for whom loyalty is no an issue is Missouri QB Austin Simmons. After Trinidad Chambliss won the starting job at Ole Miss last year, Simmons didn't feel the need to stick around, but there won't be bitterness when Simmons returns to Oxford this weekend.

#2649. Victor Wembanyama after historic 52-point, 24-rebound night: 'It should be more like this, more often'

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Victor Wembanyama came into the 2026-27 season with expectations of taking over the title of Best in the World, but a dismal performance on opening night in a loss to the Thunder raised questions about whether we might see the Spurs' star plateau in his fourth year.

Those concerns were short-lived, as the Spurs have ripped off six straight wins after their 0-2 start. Wembanyama did his part on Wednesday night when he put together a historic stat line in a win over the Mavs, scoring 52 points, pulling down 24 rebounds and blocking eight shots in a 112-111 win.

CAREER NIGHT FOR VICTOR WEMBANYAMA 🚨🤯 52 PTS (CAREER-HIGH)🤯 24 REB (CAREER-HIGH)🤯 8 BLKFIRST PLAYER WITH 50+ PTS, 20+ REB, 5+ BLK SINCE BOB MCADOO IN 1974. pic.twitter.com/lHzUhYYSTz

It was a career-best performance for Wembanyama, who spoke after the game about finally starting to feel like he had his legs under him again after beginning the year battling an illness.

"I haven't been feeling great lately," Wembanyama said, via the Associated Press. "I've been sick for a while and today I felt like I got my legs back. So it should be more like this, more often."

While he's not going to average 52/24/8, an otherworldly stat line is what we've come to expect from the Frenchman, and he's starting to post those kinds of sensational performances more often. It's his third game in the last four with at least 36 points and his fourth game this season with five or more blocks.

For as great as he was against Dallas, Wembanyama still sees plenty of room for improvement. He highlighted his struggles shooting the ball, noting that it forces him to play a style that's less sustainable over the long haul of the regular season.

"I can still do more," Wembanyama said. "I mean, my shots weren't falling tonight and that forces me into a style of play that is exhausting. I can do it. I mean, the proof is here. I can do it, but I can be much better if my shots fall. I know it's just a matter of time."

Wembanyama has been pretty awful shooting the ball this season, hitting 24% of his threes and is just 11 of 36 from the mid-range this year. Perhaps getting his legs under him better and feeling more like himself can unlock his perimeter game, which would make him all the more terrifying.

That said, there's something encouraging for the Spurs about Wembanyama struggling to shoot and just finding a way to dominate anyway. One of the frustrations of watching the gigantic Frenchman is how he sometimes seems to forget he can basically get free buckets when he gets himself near the rim. While it's understandable that he'd want to conserve some energy in the regular season, noting it's "exhausting" to fight through defenders to get to the rim, it's what makes the Spurs the best version of themselves and that's going to be the mindset he needs in the postseason.

If he does get the jumper working, it'll lighten that load some and make the Spurs even more dynamic, but Wembanyama can't forget that his most dominant performances come when he's relentless in attacking the basket. If he can find the right balance, perhaps his proclamation that "it should be more like this, more often" can come true, and he can ascend to that Best in the World title as expected.
