#2646. Darius Acuff Jr. isn't a perfect rookie, but he may be just what the Kings need right now

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The usage rate leaders list through the first two and a half weeks of the NBA season features some familiar and expected names: Luka Dončić, Anthony Edwards (four games), Victor Wembanyama, Shai Gilgeous-Alexander and Stephen Curry round out the top five, with Brandon Miller and Jayson Tatum not far behind.

However, the name below them might come as a surprise. Kings rookie guard Darius Acuff Jr., who has a 31.6% usage rate through the first eight games, is No. 8 on the list.

The only other rookie in the top 40 is Bulls forward Caleb Wilson (No. 38).

Here are the last five players to win NBA Rookie of the Year, along with their respective usage rates.

Even with a sample size that represents barely 10% of the season, what Acuff is doing will likely be sustainable, as he's being asked to do more than any rookie in his class on the offensive end of the floor. It's for that reason that his play has drawn eyeballs and why everybody seems to have an opinion — whether it's positive, negative, or maybe even somewhere in between — on him.

Is the 19-year-old guard a perfect rookie? Absolutely not. But he is just eight games into his NBA career and is posting numbers that get him in the same conversation as players like Dončić, LeBron James and Oscar Robertson.

After finishing with 22 points and 12 assists in a loss to the Lakers on Wednesday, Acuff became the fastest NBA player in NBA history to reach at least 200 points and 50 assists. It's hard to imagine he won't be writing his name into the record books across his rookie season.

As someone who watched Acuff throughout his entire college career at Arkansas, I'm not surprised to see the numbers he is putting up in the NBA. Acuff was just the second SEC player (and the first since Pete Maravich) to average at least 22 points and six assists per game in a season.

John Calipari has coached plenty of outstanding one-and-done guards during his time at Memphis, Kentucky and Arkansas, including Gilgeous-Alexander, Devin Booker, Derrick Rose, De'Aaron Fox, Jamal Murray, John Wall, and Tyrese Maxey. Simply put: if you're an elite high school guard prospect, you want to play for Coach Cal.

Acuff's season at Arkansas had him in the conversation for the best freshman guard Calipari has coached. Does that mean he's going to become a two-time NBA MVP like SGA or a multi-time NBA All-Star like the other names on that list? The jury is still out, but his college production — on both ends of the floor — is similar to what we are seeing play out in the NBA.

For starters, Arkansas didn't have a deep roster, which meant Acuff was on the floor a lot. He played just over 35 minutes per game, which is slightly less than he's playing with Sacramento right now. The same depth issues Acuff experienced at Arkansas are what he's dealing with in the NBA with his new team.

The Kings don't have a true backup point guard, which means Acuff is playing more than anybody else on the roster. When Acuff comes off the floor, Sacramento has been playing Malik Monk as the de facto point guard — a role he has filled in spot minutes throughout his time with the Kings.

Ben Simmons was also expected to be in Sacramento's starting lineup this season, where he could've taken on some of the ball-handling duties in the first and second units, but he suffered a torn Achilles days before the 2026-27 season began. That leaves Acuff, most nights, to play the entire fourth quarter and run the offense with a team full of players who can't create their own shot.

While Acuff's offensive game is as good as anybody in his class, the knock on him during the pre-draft process was his defense. It showed up throughout his time at Arkansas, but in Acuff's defense (no pun intended), he was asked to be the primary engine of the offense while staying on the floor for most of the game.

In Sacramento, it's been more of the same.

Acuff isn't a strong defender, and projecting him as a net-neutral defender over the course of his career would be a big win for his development. The offensive end is where Acuff is going to make his money. His processing skills for his age are elite and will only get better.

Acuff to Sacramento was one of the worst-kept secrets throughout the entire pre-draft cycle. The connections between his family and Kings general manager Scott Perry run deep: Perry coached Darius Acuff Sr. when he played at Eastern Kentucky in the 1990s.

After Sacramento fell in the draft lottery and landed pick No. 7, it became almost too obvious that Acuff would end up a King. The Clippers coveted Keaton Wagler early in the cycle, while Brooklyn liked the shooting upside of Mikel Brown Jr. Even though the Kings were said to be deciding between Acuff and Kingston Flemings, the former felt inevitable if Acuff was indeed available when Sacramento was on the board.

With that context, it's easy to understand why he is being handed the keys to the offense immediately, despite being on a roster that includes former NBA All-Stars Zach LaVine and Domantas Sabonis. LaVine has the second-highest usage rate on the team (25.6%), while Sabonis — who thrived as the hub of Sacramento's offense during the 2022-23 season— has a usage rate of just 15.7%.

Even with a roster that might not look 1-7 bad on paper, the Kings simply don't have enough shot creation and shot-making outside of Acuff and LaVine. The stat that stands out? Only 23 of Acuff's 189 shots have been catch-and-shoot attempts, per Synergy. At Arkansas, Acuff thrived in the catch-and-shoot department, shooting 50% (60 of 120) in that category.

Please don’t try to hate on Acuff’s shot attempts if you don’t watch the Kings 😭Directing traffic for his own teammates, & they end up needing him to create a quality shot. He’s literally his entire team’s system. James Harden type shit. pic.twitter.com/ag5MWTcWAE

Acuff is averaging 23.6 shot attempts per game, which ranks second in the NBA, behind only Gilgeous-Alexander. While that stat might pop, most of the looks Acuff is getting have been a massive improvement from his NBA debut, where he shot 5 of 24 against the Clippers.

For a smaller guard, Acuff has done a great job of getting to the paint; he's shooting 25 of 52 (48.1%) at the rim. Acuff is also getting a healthy number of 3-point attempts. He shot 44% from beyond the arc at Arkansas, but has connected on just 30.8% of his 3-point attempts so far. Rookie guards are historically inefficient, so it shouldn't be that much of a cause for concern.

Sacramento seems to be waiting on the 2027 offseason to take a step toward a proper rebuild, though the front office has reportedly been trying to move LaVine and Sabonis — the two highest-paid players on the team — since Perry took over as GM in 2024. LaVine and De'Andre come off the books this summer, while Sabonis and Malik Monk (player option) are free agents in 2028.

The blueprint for building a team around Acuff — a player who can score at will and be the offensive engine for a team — should be what the Knicks have done with Jalen Brunson. New York surrounded Brunson with 3-and-D wings, which takes the pressure off him on the defensive end of the floor. Sacramento has just one true 3-and-D wing on the roster: Keegan Murray, who is currently out with an ankle injury.

With several high-priced veterans on the roster, this will be Sacramento's short-term future. The No. 1 priority this season for Sacramento is developing Acuff so when the big names come off the books and the team has cap space, the franchise can properly build a team around him.

One popular comparison Acuff has drawn, dating back to the pre-draft cycle, is Cam Thomas. No disrespect at all to Thomas — who was one of the best pure shotmakers and scorers in the league when he played — but Acuff is by far a more advanced passer and facilitator for his age.

Acuff is averaging seven assists per game, which ranks 12th in the league. He is also averaging 12.4 potential assists per game, per the NBA's tracking data, which ranks 11th. Acuff at Arkansas was an elite facilitator despite being a high-volume scorer. Over the last few games, Acuff has been making an effort to get his teammates involved in the high pick-and-roll.

This clip from Wednesday's loss to the Lakers is exactly the kind of play Acuff is making that won't show up on the box score: he falls over while making a cross-court pass to a wide-open shooter (Monk) who missed a 3-pointer. Acuff finished with 12 assists against the Lakers, but had 17 potential assists, per the tracking data.

Darius Acuff ter 7 assistências nesse jogo é um crime federal.O garoto tá fazendo tudo pra achar visuais para os companheiros de time e nada cai.Olha isso irmão… revoltante uma parada dessas. pic.twitter.com/TIu2m3Gm1X

Let's go back to Thomas, who didn't have a game with more than four assists during his rookie season. Acuff has recorded at least five assists in six of his first eight games, including two with over 12 assists.

Acuff's passing was one of his strengths throughout his college career. He is a very good lob passer who routinely made tough cross-court or skip passes with multiple defenders in the area. While Acuff is known for scoring, his passing is underrated.

Acuff isn't a perfect rookie, but he isn't even 20 years old and Sacramento projects as one of the worst teams in the NBA. The Kings will happily trade the good for the bad if he continues to develop and post the numbers he's putting up.

#2644. Tarik Skubal landing spots: Predicting new home for two-time Cy Young winner, the offseason's best free agent

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Arguably the best pitcher in baseball is up for grabs this winter. Tarik Skubal is a free agent for the 2026-27 MLB offseason, easily the top available on the market, and every team should be trying to earn his services. But will they? Almost certainly not.

The 29-year-old southpaw spent the first six years of his major-league career with the Detroit Tigers before being traded to the Los Angeles Dodgers at the 2026 deadline. He won back-to-back Cy Young awards in 2024 and 2025 and earned MVP votes in both seasons. He's likely to become the highest-paid pitcher in MLB history both in total value and AAV.

Of course, the giant flashing sign floating above all of this is the expiring CBA, which will run out at 11:59 p.m. on Dec. 1, after which the owners are expected to lock out the players until a new deal is reached. Over the summer, the league proposed limiting free agency contracts, an offer that the players' union quickly disavowed, and the owners' demand for a salary cap is the underlying throughline of every negotiation. Perhaps that means Skubal will rush to sign on the dotted line before new rules are in place. Perhaps that means teams will wait out the negotiations until they know how much they have to spend -- and how they'll be punished if they do so.

Regardless, CBS Sports' MLB experts, three people who are very much not involved in contract negotiations, have gathered to predict where Skubal lands by the time Opening Day rolls around.

Mike Axisa: I'll go off the board a bit and say the Padres. The new ownership group didn't pay $3.9 billion for the franchise only to cheap out in their first offseason. They're moneyed and motivated, and that's usually enough to land the top free agents. It should appeal to Skubal too. The Padres are in the postseason most years, they play in a great (and largely pitcher-friendly) ballpark, and it's San Diego. How can you not love San Diego? Skubal to the Padres because the new owners want to make a big splash in their first offseason. That's my prediction.

Dayn Perry: I'll say the Mets top all offers by a margin sufficient to overcome their lack of appeal compared to the usual suspects (meaning, mostly, the Dodgers). They definitely need a stabilizing force in the rotation outside of Nolan McLean, and they also need a vibes shift after the deeply disappointing 2026 campaign. Landing the biggest fish of all on the market would provide all that and meet a clear need. The Mets will already be rebound candidates in 2027, and signing the likes of Skubal would position them as contenders. Obviously, the structure of the next CBA has bearing here, but maybe this all comes together before the lockout shuts it all down for an indeterminate period of time.

Matt Snyder: I'll go with the easy and obvious answer and say the Dodgers. I don't think the owners win the fight for a salary cap, but there'll be enough push from the Dodgers' end before the CBA talks shut down free agency to snatch up all the talent they can to get his contract grandfathered before a new agreement.

#2643. How Victor Wembanyama's improved shot diet is leading him to historic heights

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

After Victor Wembanyama authored the worst shooting game of his career on opening night, a 1-for-13 showing in a loss to the Thunder, I wrote that the Spurs' honeymoon was over. It was dramatic by design -- a play on the early-season, and in this case single-game, overreactions we always get at the start of every new campaign.

But there was truth in it. Last year, everything the Spurs did was on house money. Winning 62 games. Eliminating the defending champion Thunder on the road in Game 7 of the conference finals. Holding the lead vs. the Knicks for 72% of total minutes played in the Finals. Wembanyama unanimously winning Defensive Player of the Year and finishing third in MVP voting. All prologue, no expectations.

This year, the real story starts, and we knew the benefit of the doubt would be gone. When Wembanyama laid that opening-night egg, the chatter started. He was crowned too soon. He doesn't have a go-to shot or spot. After that game, Wembanyama had no need for the critics. He was his own biggest critic, lamenting his hesitancy and overthinking, saying he needed to "go back to playing the basketball I like."

"I got no reason to be hesitant, no reason to not be myself," Wembanyama said. "For me, it's as simple as that. I'm good when I have fun."

Suffice it to say, he's been having plenty of fun since. Over his last seven games, Wembanyama is averaging 31.4 points, 12.2 rebounds and 4.3 blocks on 52% shooting. After opening 0-2, San Antonio has won six straight, with the latest being Wednesday night's 112-111 thriller over the Mavericks, who erased a 19-point deficit to tie the game with under two minutes to play.

In the end, Wembanyama was just too much. He scored the Spurs' final seven points and 11 of their last 13 and hit the game-winning free-throw. When it was all said and done, the box score read like something out of a video game: 52 points, 24 rebounds and eight blocks as he became the first player to hit those marks since Bob McAdoo more than a half century ago.

CAREER NIGHT FOR VICTOR WEMBANYAMA 🚨🤯 52 PTS (CAREER-HIGH)🤯 24 REB (CAREER-HIGH)🤯 8 BLKFIRST PLAYER WITH 50+ PTS, 20+ REB, 5+ BLK SINCE BOB MCADOO IN 1974. pic.twitter.com/lHzUhYYSTz

Actually, that's selling Wembanyama short. McAdoo only had seven blocks in that 1974 game against the Celtics. Filter it for at least 50, 20 and eight blocks, and only Wilt Chamberlain has done it, and that was before blocks became an official stat. The dude had 29, 15 and five in the first half, for crying out loud. No player in the last 30 years has registered that halftime line.

OK, so Wembanyama is a beast. We all knew this. He's going to have a lot of historic-number games. But what's interesting about the anatomy of this one is where the production came from on the floor, which has quietly been the story of his season.

Wembanyama's shot diet became one of the seminal stories of last year's postseason. He's a relatively random player on the offensive end, and there were stretches when his ability to dance on the perimeter and shoot from range was becoming too easy of a crutch. He's a fine shooter and has a capable handle; for his size, he's extraordinary. But when the listed 7-foot-4 guy who is probably closer to 7-foot-6 is camping out around the 3-point line, it's a win for the defense, particularly at scale.

We saw both sides of this dynamic throughout the playoffs as Wembanyama waffled between a perimeter- and paint-based structure almost from game to game. We saw it against Minnesota in the second round. We saw it again against Oklahoma City in the conference finals when Wembanyama dominated Game 1 at the rim only to be literally pushed out to the perimeter in the following games by Isaiah Hartenstein.

Over the first two games of the Finals, Wembanyama took more shots from outside the paint (22) than he did inside (20), a win for the Knicks, who went up 2-0. In Game 3, he flipped the script, taking 13 of his 18 shots from inside the paint as the Spurs won in a blowout.

There won't always be a direct correlation between Wembanyama's shot diet and the Spurs' outcomes; they're going to win most of their games on sheer talent, and Wembanyama is going to pile up massive numbers for the same reason. But the details matter at the highest level, and so far this season Wembanyama is operating closer to the hoop with greater intention.

Through these first eight games, Wembanyama is taking five more shots a night than he did last year. Nearly all of them are coming from inside the paint, as you can see in the table below highlighting his field-goal attempts from each area.

As a matter of percentage, Wembanyama is taking 42% of his shots from inside three feet this year, up from 33% last year. Those 5.1 dunks per game put him on pace for more than 400 this season, which would obliterate Rudy Gobert's NBA record of 302.

How is Wembanyama doing this? It's not a traditional thing where he's just posting up lower (which he isn't yet strong enough to do on demand and may not ever be), and there still isn't a specific spot or shot he is establishing as the go-to move everyone is clamoring for. It's just the intent to get down there, whether it's by rim rolls, crashing the offensive glass, or forgoing some of the settle 3-pointers for show-and-go drives.

Look at the clip below. He could've taken this initial 3, but he didn't. Instead, he got off the ball to establish himself 10 feet closer to the hoop, where he's now one cut away from a dunk as the Spurs have five 3-point threats on the floor who have collectively pulled every defender away from the basket.

Stephon Castle ⬆️ Victor Wembanyama 👽🤝🏰#NBAHighlights pic.twitter.com/NUX2JAQQ3G

That is what a concerted effort looks like. The seas may not always part like that, but Wembanyama is making it a point to occupy lower positioning more often, where he's ready and able to strike when the slightest crack presents itself. In many cases, Wembanyama is just hanging out beneath the basket or in the dunker's spot along the baseline from the start, rather than having to fight down there after he's started the possession 30 feet away.

One thing the Spurs are doing is initiating pick-and-rolls lower on the floor, so that Wembanyama, with his length, is a single turn from the front of the rim rather than having to navigate all the way from the 3-point line, which gives defenses time to clog his path.

HE'S GOT 47 PTS! 📺 ESPN, @DAZN, @CW35SA pic.twitter.com/ck0iYgngLs

This isn't rocket science. Wembanyama can go up so much higher than everyone else that it's simply a matter of him being near the rim. From there, the Spurs are just throwing it up as you would to an adult playing with kids.

Where Wemby catches the ball for this alley oop is ABSURD pic.twitter.com/azoeaeWUyv

Even the off-the-backboard lobs that Wembanyama is throwing to himself are more than a social media highlight. Note where he's catching the ball: at the free-throw line. When Wembanyama is one step from the rim, just about anything is at his disposal.

WEMBY IS SCARY 😧 pic.twitter.com/A4tPuDvQoa

De'Aaron Fox has talked about running these pick-and-rolls with Wembanyama where he's popping into the free-throw area for soft-spot jumpers, which are going to be there any time he wants as defenses sag back in an attempt, to whatever degree possible, to discourage dunks.

Those shots are about as close to a guaranteed clean look that Wembanyama can get from inside the arc. They are not going in at the moment. He's just 28% from 10-16 feet. But these are the stations from which he can play entirely on his terms. The 3-pointers, particularly the pull-up ones, are on the defense's terms, though he can make them and on plenty of nights will.

So far this year, Wembanyama is making just 24% of his 3s. That will go up, and the threat of him making that shot serves San Antonio's spacing well. He shouldn't, and won't, quit taking them. When they start going in, it could get flat-out unstoppable. But it's a fine balance, and Wembanyama is rightfully erring more on the lower side of the floor this year.

When Wembanyama scored his previous career high of 50 points in 2024, he did so on the strength of eight made 3s. On Wednesday, he only made one 3, while making 15 of his 20 shots from inside the arc. By aggressively going into the paint, he's also in position to draw more fouls, and indeed he made 19 free throws against the Mavs.

That is old-school center stuff. Just flat-out dominating inside. Wembanyama can obviously get buckets either way, but the closer-to-the-hoop way is the better bet all things being equal. On some level, this is pretty simple for a player this size, and you can see Wembanyama starting to figure that out.

#2642. Former Longhorn makes history for Green Bay Packers

On Saturday afternoon, Matthew Golden and Christian Watson tormented the Patriots secondary. The duo combined for 335 receiving yards while finding the end zone twice. As they led the Packers to an impressive win over the Patriots, they also made history.

The Packers' wide receivers became the first pair of wide receivers in team history and the first in the NFL since 2023 to have at least 150 receiving yards and a touchdown in a game. Regardless of who was covering them, they found a way to make plays and combined for 17 catches.

For Golden it was another stellar performance in what has been a career year. The former Longhorn has set new career highs this season in receiving yards (783), which is the fourth most in the NFL, and touchdowns (five). In his second season, Golden is averaging 14.8 yards per catch and has four games with over 100 receiving yards.

As Golden has frustrated defensive coordinators, he has become a vital piece of the Packers passing game. He is second on the team behind Christian Watson in receiving yards, touchdowns and yards per game. That is not a bad place to be following a rookie season full of up and downs and a few frustrating moments.

With the season far from over, Golden is on pace to easily reach the 1,000-yard mark. That would be a massive jump from the 2025 campaign, as Golden finished his rookie season with 361 yards. With Golden now comfortable in an NFL offense, he has shown no signs of slowing down.Over the next few month, the Packers star will be a player to watch. On a team with playoff aspiration Golden has shown that he can be a key contributor as he sets new career highs on a weekly basis.

#2639. Bronny James faces uncertain NBA future after Lakers assign him to G League

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The Los Angeles Lakers assigned Bronny James and rookie Cameron Carr to the G League on Thursday, the team announced. James is no stranger to the Coachella Valley Lakers, having spent time with them across his first two seasons. Still, such an early G League assignment isn't exactly an encouraging start to his third NBA campaign.

James, the 22-year-old son of LeBron James, played for the Lakers in the playoffs last season out of desperation due injuries, but when the team has been closer to full strength, he has failed to earn more than spot minutes in his first two NBA seasons. He struggled mightily in the preseason this year, as he shot just 4 of 16 from the field. And while he has always been a defense-first player, his size -- 6-foot-2 and 210 pounds -- has limited his upside on that side of the floor.

"I thought he had a really nice September and a good summer with us, but I don't think he's played well in the four preseason games," Lakers coach JJ Redick said in October.

Despite those preseason struggles, James survived final cuts as the Lakers ultimately waived former No. 17 overall pick Dalton Knecht to get their roster down to 15 players. The move was relatively surprising considering their draft status. While both Knecht and James have fallen short of the team's hopes for them, Knecht was a former first-round pick who had at least held a consistent rotation role early in his rookie season. He fell off after a failed trade to the Charlotte Hornets, but teams typically like to give their own first-round picks as many opportunities as possible to succeed.

Knecht has since signed a two-way contract with the defending NBA champion New York Knicks. He appeared in his first game on Wednesday, a blowout win over the Chicago Bulls, and he notched 10 points in 16 minutes. By comparison, James has scored four points in 12 minutes spread across five appearances this season.

James was drafted in 2024 and became the first player in NBA history to share the court with his father. Now the elder James is a member of the Philadelphia 76ers, and both teams are doing well after their separation. The 76ers have the NBA's best record at 8-1, and the Lakers aren't far behind at 7-2. But with his father gone and the Lakers thriving in his absence, the younger James is in a somewhat precarious position moving forward. His name carries less weight with the organization than it once did, and a team with championship ambitions isn't going to be willing to wait on the development of a second-round pick forever.

James' contract is guaranteed through the end of this season, but not guaranteed afterward. If he doesn't show progress quickly, he could be a trade candidate at the deadline or simply not retained after the season.

According to Sacha Tavolieri, the Ibrahim Maza situation at Bayer Leverkusen has seemingly taken a new turn behind the scenes.

Even after Paris Saint-Germain, with Luis Campos, returning to the negotiating table, a transfer appears to be out of the question.

The Algerian player’s camp and Leverkusen is said to have ultimately put the decision-makers from the French capital club off the deal.

Accordingly, Maza’s father and Leverkusen wanted to bypass the original framework of the talks and re-establish contact with Paris.

The intention was to communicate through the Stellar agency to “test” whether the Ligue 1 club’s interest in Maza was genuine.

However, this move is said to have displeased Luis Campos. PSG’s sporting adviser is said to have then decided to end the talks.

The approach did not reflect the way Paris wants to handle its transfer business – the Maza deal is definitively off the table for PSG.

Furthermore, Paris is said to have reiterated its position: PSG had never itself made a concrete approach to sign the player.

The club had merely explored making an approach after it emerged that Maza’s father was open in principle to a meeting.

For Ibrahim Maza, the door to Paris therefore appears to have closed for now. However, a future move can't be written off completely.

#2636. Contemporary Baseball Era Committee unveils eight Hall of Fame candidates: Dusty Baker, Bruce Bochy, more

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The National Baseball Hall of Fame in Cooperstown on Monday announced eight candidates for election on the 2027 Contemporary Baseball Era Committee ballot. The non-player ballot includes four former managers and four former executives: Sandy Alderson, Dusty Baker, Bruce Bochy, Joe Maddon, Lou Piniella, Brian Sabean, Ted Turner, and Bill White.

The non-player ballot includes managers, executives, and umpires. On an alternating basis, the Era Committee also evaluates a ballot consisting of former players. As for the qualifications and criteria, the Hall of Fame describes it thus:

"The eight Contemporary Baseball Era finalists were selected by the BBWAA-appointed Historical Overview Committee from all eligible candidates among managers, umpires and executives whose most significant career impact was realized since 1980. Eligible candidates include managers and umpires with 10 or more major league seasons and retired for at least five years (candidates who are 65 years or older are eligible six months following retirement); and executives retired for at least five years (active executives 70 years or older are eligible for consideration regardless of the position they hold in an organization and regardless of whether their body of work has been completed). All candidates must not be on Baseball's Ineligible List."

As for those figures on the Era Committee ballot for 2027, here's a quick rundown:

Alderson built a powerhouse and won a World Series as general manager of the Oakland A's. He later earned multiple playoff berths and a pennant as GM of the New York Mets.

One of the winningest managers of all time, Baker guided five different clubs to the playoffs and won three pennants and a World Series. His success in the dugout came after a long and distinguished playing career as an MLB outfielder.

Bochy as a manager led three different clubs to the postseason and is one of just six managers ever to win at least four World Series. Three of Bochy's rings came with the San Francisco Giants, and the final one came with the Texas Rangers in 2023.

Maddon won more than 1,300 games as a manager for three different franchises. He also won a pennant as manager of the Tampa Bay Rays, and in 2016, he led the Chicago Cubs to their first World Series title in more than a century.

After an 18-year playing career, Piniella racked up more than 1,800 wins as a big-league manager. He led three different clubs to the playoffs, won a World Series as manager of the 1990 Cincinnati Reds, and in 2001 helmed the Seattle Mariners to a record 116 wins during the regular season.

After filling a key role in the New York Yankees front office, Sabean joined the Giants as their general manager. Under his guidance, the Giants won the World Series in 2010, 2012, and 2014.

The only posthumous candidate on the ballot, Turner owned the Atlanta Braves for two decades. Along the way, he innovated the distribution of televised baseball games and oversaw a dynasty. Under Turner's stewardship, the Braves claimed 14 straight division titles and won the World Series in 1995.

A five-time All-Star and Gold Glove first baseman as a player, White after his playing days were over served as president of the National League. White was also the first Black play-by-play broadcaster in MLB history, and his leadership of the NL made him the first Black president of a major sports league.

The results of the committee vote will be announced on MLB Network at 8 p.m. ET on Sunday, Dec. 6. As with the BBWAA ballot, a candidate must be named on at least 75% of ballots in order to earn election. A 16-member committee will vote on the candidates.

The more traditional BBWAA ballot, in which candidates are voted on by writers and other media members, will be revealed on Nov. 16. Results of the 2027 BBWAA ballot will be announced in January, at which point we'll know the full Hall of Fame class for 2027.

#2634. Commanders GM Adam Peters: Ball needs to go in the end zone on final play

The Commanders' operation at the end of games came under the microscope again in Week 9.

Washington was down 20-13 with the ball at the Rams' 31-yard-line with three seconds left and their final play saw quarterback Jayden Daniels hit tight end Chig Okonkwo with a short pass. Okonkwo got down around the 10 before he attempted to lateral to a teammate. The attempt at a Stanford band-esque ending fizzled out from there and the Commanders fell to 2-5-1 on the season.

The Commanders were in position to lose due to several things that went wrong over the first 59 minutes and 57 seconds of play, but they still had a chance to tie or win the game, which is one that General Manager Adam Peters said they should have taken during a Wednesday appearance on 106.7 The Fan.

"There's a couple things on that, but I think the bottom line is the ball needs to get in the end zone there," Peters said.

Last Sunday's ending may not have been as egregious an error as the one Daniels and head coach Dan Quinn made at the end of their tie with the Giants, but it was enough of an error that the case for changing those in charge of the on-field operation is even stronger heading into Week 10.

#2633. Connor Hellebuyck trade: Jets send star goalie to the Devils in exchange for four players, two draft picks

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Connor Hellebuyck is a now a Devil. The star goalie for the Winnipeg Jets is on the move after being traded to New Jersey on Friday in exchange for four players and two future draft picks. the teams announced the move with the Jets receiving Dawson Mercer, Nick Bjugstad, Nico Daws and Alexander Command, plus a 2027 seventh-round pick and a 2029 second-round pick.

Hellebuyck expressed his desire to be traded in the offseason when he formally requested a move in August. He said at the time that he had made the request months earlier and tried to keep the situation private.

Hellebuyck has spent his entire career with Winnipeg after being drafted by the Jets in 2012 at No. 130 overall. He's recognized as one of the best goalies in the league as a three-time Vezina Trophy winner. He also helped carry the United States to its first gold medal since 1980 at the 2026 Olympics in February with some incredible saves against Canada in the final game.

After trading Jacob Markstom in the offseason, the Devils had a clear need in goal, and this splashy move certainly fills that need. With a talented young core already in place, New Jersey's Stanley Cup window is wide open.

RAISE HELLE!Connor Hellebuyck is a New Jersey Devil: https://t.co/HCehRGOQI5 pic.twitter.com/dZGNQR16m1

For the Jets, it must be a hard pill to swallow when a franchise icon decides to walk out they door, but this trade package should help them as the enter a new era and revamp the roster. Winnipeg got a former first-rounder in Mercer to try and add to a rebuild as well as a veteran presence in Bjugstad. They also acquired a younger goalie in Daws who could fill the role of Hellebuyck at just 25 years old.

Goaltending has been an issue in New Jersey for a while now -- even after the team acquired Markstrom from the Calgary Flames in 2024. Markstom never really panned out, and his 13.6 goals allowed above average, per Natural Stat Trick, were a big reason why the Devils missed the postseason last year.

In the early portion of this season, it was clear that New Jersey needed to make a move to upgrade in the crease. Daws and veteran Jake Allen simply aren't a tandem suitable for a Stanley Cup contender, and the numbers backed that up. New Jersey ranks 24th in team save percentage at .877, and the duo of Daws and Allen combined to surrender 2.99 goals above average.

Once Hellebuyck gets up to game speed, that shouldn't be a problem anymore.

In the three-season stretch from 2023-26, Hellebuyck led the NHL with 73.42 goals saved above average, which is 20 goals higher than the next closest netminder. Over that span, Hellebuyck also posted a standard save percentage of .914 and an astronomical high-danger save-percentage of .832.

Hellebuyck carried less talented teams to the playoffs multiple times in his career. Now on a team loaded with weaponry in their prime -- Jack Hughes, Jesper Bratt and Nico Hischier to name a few -- Hellebuyck could be the final piece to the championship puzzle.

In terms of the acquisition cost, it was probably an easy deal for Devils general manager Sunny Mehta to make. The 2029 second-round pick is useless for a team that should be all-in now, Bjugstad is simply a depth piece and Daws now has no path to a starting role with Hellebuyck in town.

The most interesting trade chips are Mercer and Command. Mercer flashed major upside with 56 points in his second NHL season, 2022-23, but he hasn't really come close to hitting those heights again. Still, even if he has plateaued, Mercer remains a strong middle-six forward rising into his prime.

Although Command had his detractors -- and may have been over-drafted at No. 12 overall -- he was a consensus first-round pick last summer. That gives Winnipeg a potential franchise forward it can build around long-term, but New Jersey already has one of the deepest forward groups in the league, especially with the emergence of Arseny Gritsyuk and the acquisition of Luke Evangelista.

If we're looking for a 3-D chess angle of this deal, it only makes the Devils more appealing for a certain Minnesota Wild defenseman whose brothers just happen to play in New Jersey already. Grade -- A+

Let's get the obvious out of the way first: The Jets were never going to get fair value for Hellebuyck because, at his best, he's the No. 1 goaltender in the world with no equal. That type of excellence can't be replaced.

That said, Winnipeg did fairly well given the circumstances. Hellebuyck made a public trade request, and he wasn't even with the team after sitting out for the entirety of training camp. The entire league knew the Jets had to trade him.

Hellebuyck's talent created a decent market anyway, but most of the suitors were bona fide Stanley Cup contenders with little in the way of valuable draft capital, and they weren't going to knee cap the roster by sending a key player back in return.

With all that taken into consideration, Kevin Cheveldayoff got a solid return. Although Mercer's ceiling may be lower than initially thought, he's a 24-year-old forward who banks roughly 20 goals and 20 assists every season. The kicker with Mercer will be Winnipeg's ability to re-sign him before he hits restricted free agency next summer.

The addition of Command means Winnipeg now has two forwards selected in the top 12 of the 2026 NHL Draft after taking center Viggo Bjorck themselves. If both of those players deliver on their first-round pedigrees, they could be a terrific one-two punch for the team long-term.

Daws was a third-round pick in 2020, and despite playing just 13 NHL games since the start of the 2024-25 season, he should give Winnipeg a solid back up option behind Stuart Skinner. It certainly helps that Skinner is off to a great start with his new team -- and if Daws develops into a true No. 1 -- it'll be gravy.

If there's any reason to critique this deal from the Jets' side of things, it's that they didn't get premium draft capital or a surefire up-and-coming prospect. Maybe Command develops into a star, but there's no guarantee he becomes a top-six stud in the NHL.

The Jets got a lot of good stuff, but they didn't really get anything great, at least not based on what we know in the moment. Because of that, I have to ding Winnipeg a little bit. Grade: B

#2632. Eight MLB players tagged with $23.15M qualifying offer: Randy Arozarena, Seiya Suzuki, Jake Bauers, more

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Eight MLB free agents were extended a one-year, $23.15 million contract offer on Monday that, if declined, could fetch their old teams draft-pick compensation. That group includes Randy Arozarena and Seiya Suzuki.

This is one of the smallest groups of qualifying offers ever. Only six players got one in 2020. There were 13 last offseason, and we've seen as many as 20. From 2012 to 2025, 157 qualifying offers were made and only 18 accepted, including a record four last year.

Each offseason, certain free agents are eligible for the qualifying offer (QO). Those eligible free agents have never before received the QO and who spent the prior season with only one team (in other words, players traded during the season cannot receive the QO). The QO is set as the average of the top 125 salaries for a given year, and for the 2026-27 offseason it's a record $23.15 million.

Eligible players who accept the QO will play the 2027 season under that salary for their 2026 team, while those who turn it down become free agents, albeit with the QO compensation attached. That attachment means that the free agent's former team is entitled to an additional draft pick. The position of that draft pick depends upon the team's status when it comes to the luxury tax and revenue-sharing debits or credits.

On the other side, a team that signs a free agent with a QO attached is penalized with the loss of a draft pick, depending again upon the signing team's classification when it comes to the luxury tax and revenue sharing.

Most QO decisions are obvious. Premium free agents receive one without much thought, just as the much less coveted class of free agents do not. It's in the middle ground that interesting decisions lie -- first on the club side and then, if offered, on the player side. That's even more the case this year, when the expiring CBA and negotiations toward a new one have already included talk of a salary cap and restrictions on free agent contracts.

Players presented with a QO this offseason will have until 4 p.m. ET on Nov. 17 to accept or reject the offer.

Below you'll find a rundown of the eight players who received a QO. Do note the players are listed in order of their free agent ranking.

One of the top relievers in baseball over the last three seasons, Morejón gains attractiveness on the open market due to having an effective four-pitch arsenal. That means it's possible he and the team he signs with will want him to convert to a starting pitcher. He could stay in relief, too, where it's likely he'd continue to dominate. A path needs to be chosen, but this guy is a special talent.

Rogers was traded to the Orioles in 2024 and struggled to the point that he needed a trip to the minors. Once he returned in 2025, he was outstanding, pitching to a 1.81 ERA in 18 starts. He struggled to start last season, but made some adjustments and had a 2.90 ERA in his last 20 starts. He's the fallback option to Tarik Skubal, who wasn't eligible for a qualifying offer after a midseason trade.

The power-speed threat posted his sixth straight 20-20 season in 2026 along with an excellent .381 on-base percentage and career-best 5.7 WAR. He's hitting free agency at the right time, though he heads to his age-32 season with sustainability questions, not to mention a few under-the-hood reasons to worry about things going downhill moving forward. Still, it's a weak class for big bats and he'll get paid.

Thanks in large part to huge improvements on defense, Suzuki posted a career-high 5.1 WAR in 2026. His batting average and slugging percentage were right in line with his established career marks and he improved his walk rate to rock a higher OBP. The best path forward is probably to ignore the defensive gains and realize there's a high floor here with the bat for another several years.

There were trade rumors about Jeffers last July, but the Twins hung around in the playoff race and ended up being buyers. Injury limited Jeffers to just 92 games, but on a rate basis he's been a very good hitting catcher for four years, along with being a quality backstop as well.

The NLCS MVP and World Series champion is coming off a career year at the plate. He had a 140 OPS+ and 3.3 WAR in 144 games and 578 plate appearances, serving as the two-hole hitter for the Brewers throughout the playoffs. He heads to his age-31 season, and this might well be the opportunity of his lifetime for one huge payday.

Lowe just posted a career-high 5.4 WAR in 150 games in his first season with the Pirates, topping 30 home runs for the third time in his career, and he averages 35 homers per 162 games. Are the defensive gains real or a one-year outlier? Will his struggles against lefties prevent a long-term deal?

While there has been some inconsistency (he was brutal for some of 2024, for example), Bednar is coming off a big 2026 season. He was one of the best closers in baseball and showed with the Yankees he can handle a high-profile closing job. He also has a good playoff track record. There isn't much of a top-level closer market in free agency, so he's surely turning this down.

#2631. NBA relegation zone predictions: Ranking the 7 worst teams in the race to avoid the bottom of the standings

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

When the NBA reformed the draft lottery, it did so with the hopes that all 30 teams would be somewhat competitive. But two weeks into the 2026-27 season, that isn't proving true.

Five teams have just a single win so far this season, and in many cases, those wins are only coming when they play one another. The Los Angeles Clippers have only beaten the Sacramento Kings. The Chicago Bulls have only beaten the Milwaukee Bucks. The Kings' only win came when the Dallas Mavericks rested Kyrie Irving.

No matter how the incentive structures are designed, the NBA will always have a handful of very bad teams. Some teams are poorly run. Some teams are besieged by injuries. Some teams are simply in transitional stages of their roster builds. The old NBA was designed to make bad teams good quickly. The new one is designed to make it harder for teams to bounce back from the bottom.

As part of last spring's lottery reform, the three worst teams in the league are now punished for losing. In the new 3-2-1 lottery format, the seven best teams to miss the Play-In Tournament get three lottery balls each out of the 37 available ones, while the three worst teams each get only two. In theory, that should create an all-out war to avoid the bottom three. In practice, well, we'll get into that shortly.

For now, as the bottom of the league is starting to take shape, let's take a look at our relegation zone candidates. While injuries could certainly create more of them as we go, seven teams stand out as reasonable threats for a bottom-three record so far this season. We're going to rank them from least to most likely to land in the relegation zone, with the top three teams being our official picks to take that lottery hit in May.

Remember, this is not merely a ranking of the NBA's worst teams. It's who is likeliest to land in the bottom three of the standings, a necessary distinction for reasons you're about to find out.

There isn't a more dumbfounding team to watch in the NBA right now than the Jazz. For four years, Utah was a smart, well-run team that lost because the front office did everything in its power to deprive its coach of talent. Well, coach Will Hardy is allowed to win now. It just isn't happening.

The inventive, flowing offense of years past is sputtering. No. 2 overall pick Darryn Peterson isn't making jumpers and can't get to the rim. Players needed for size and defense -- like Josh Okogie and Jaxson Hayes -- are killing the offense. Everything is running through Keyonte George because he's the only player on the floor creating consistent advantages. He's not a true point guard, and the lack of passing on the floor right now is palpable. Their lone victory came by a single point at home against the New Orleans Pelicans. Not exactly inspiring.

Any dreams of a 50-win, top-six seed season died with the Walker Kessler trade. This team is screaming for anyone who can screen and rebound. Getting Jusuf Nurkić back will help, and eventually, Jaren Jackson Jr. will take the floor again, too. You'd hope Peterson eventually figures some things out. He's a No. 2 overall pick. He's too talented to struggle this much unless the medical issues that plagued him at Kansas are persisting. There are reasons to believe this will get better. The Jazz should eventually be at least competitive.

But we're barely into November and even their more modest, post-Kessler Play-In ambitions already seem to be on life support. The Western Conference is far deeper than it looked a month ago and the Jazz are digging themselves a hole they're going to struggle to climb out of. This is a bad defensive roster even at full strength, and if the offense is this disjointed, the postseason just isn't on the table. After a four-year tank, that's a real concern in Utah. Even sniffing the relegation zone, given the time spent even getting to this point, is a borderline disaster.

The Suns come in ahead of one-win Utah -- and the two-win Orlando Magic they just beat -- because those teams have more substantial reinforcements incoming. The Suns will benefit greatly from the eventual return of Mark Williams, if only because, at this stage, Khaman Maluach just is not ready to play serious NBA minutes. But Williams isn't, say, Jaren Jackson or Paolo Banchero. Phoenix's problems are internal.

They were the first team of the season to leak displeasure to the press, with Chris Haynes reporting that the locker room is frustrated over the lack of a point guard. There's a fair bit of statistical evidence suggesting the Suns could address that problem by benching Jalen Green for Collin Gillespie. Eventually, Green's performance will force the issue. If your value is derived entirely from scoring and you're averaging 12 points on 41-22-69 shooting splits, you won't be long for anyone's starting lineup.

The bigger problem here is the loss of last year's defense-and-hustle identity. The Suns only just surrendered the NBA's 30th defensive ranking to another team on this list, and their deflections, loose ball recoveries and offensive rebounding are way down. As of this writing, they're the worst rebounding team in the NBA. Many of the players responsible for last year's identity are playing less than they did last year. Green simply isn't a defense and energy player. Neither is Miles Bridges, who they gave up yet another unprotected first-round pick to get.

Devin Booker is slipping. The shotmaking bar on superstar-level value for a guard who never makes plays nor gets to the rim at an elite level is almost impossibly high. He basically has to be a high-volume 3-point shooter making close to 40% of his attempts to justify his supermax deal. He hasn't come close to that in years. He doesn't quite have his old burst, either, and after the Bridges trade, the Suns are down to very few remaining draft assets with which they can improve. There's probably enough talent here that the Suns will eventually be able to eke their way to 30 or so wins, but the early returns here are pretty discouraging.

Here's where we take our first real step down in terms of roster talent. The bottom five teams are simply worse than the remaining 25. There's no All Star-level talent here, like George in Utah or Booker in Phoenix. Michael Porter Jr. made his case a year ago, but his volume is down with Julius Randle on the roster. With the Nets, Randle has been largely inefficient and is turning the ball over more than ever. Only three teams turn the ball over more frequently than they do.

They're attempting to sacrifice high opponent 3-point volume for minimizing attempts at the rim. It's working in terms of volume, but once anyone does get to the rim, they're scoring there with impunity because Brooklyn simply doesn't have a reliable, individual rim protector. They're among the most frequent fouling defenses in the NBA. Last year's No. 8 overall pick, Egor Dëmin, is already hurt and has all but abandoned shooting inside the arc. Young guards, no matter how much promise they show, are usually bad. The goal of this season is to develop several of them. Mikel Brown Jr. and the improving Nolan Traore are years away from what they'll eventually become.

Here's where we really have to start talking about incentives. Brooklyn owes its first-round pick to the Houston Rockets. Now, the Jazz and Suns owe their first-round picks out as well, but under different circumstances. The Suns won't control their own pick again until the actual sun burns out, so what happens to their picks isn't really their concern. The Jazz have picked in the top five two years in a row, so their pick, currently owed to the Memphis Grizzlies, can't land there again, and will therefore have a clean slate next year. But the Nets, who are several years away from winning meaningfully barring something unforeseen, probably want to avoid having their pick land in the top five, as teams are forbidden from ending up there three years in a row, or, in the worst-case scenario, coming in at No. 1, which would bar them from picking there in 2028.

The Nets are, in other words, incentivized to lose, which is exactly what this system was supposed to prevent. Now, they can't go about it as brazenly as tankers of the past have, as commissioner Adam Silver now has expanded powers to punish teams for tanking. But the NBA can't stop them from, say, trading useful veterans like Porter at the deadline. Brooklyn didn't do so a year ago when it should have, so this will be something to watch when February rolls around. If the Nets keep Porter, they're probably good enough to duck the relegation zone. If they move him, well, getting in there may not be the goal, but it would be a potentially helpful byproduct.

Considering the Nets traded for Randle in June, though, it seems as though Brooklyn, to the delight of Houston (which walks away with six lottery balls between Brooklyn and Phoenix in this scenario), intends to try to win. There are possible reasons for that ranging from culture-building to job security, but until the Nets show their hand, we'll leave them out of the bottom three for now.

Here's a sobering thought: of the seven teams we're covering in this space, the Kings are the only one that fits into the relegation zone system as intended. They don't owe their pick out to another team. They aren't on any consecutive high picks clock. They're just a bad team trying to rebuild organically. They want high draft picks, which means they don't want to be in the bottom three.

They might even be willing to trade a small asset to improve at the deadline for this purpose if necessary. If nothing else, they have the salary to do so. Between Zach LaVine and De'Andre Hunter, they have over $70 million in expiring money to dangle if doing so makes sense. Wins tend to be elusive in Sacramento, but the Kings actually want them.

They are unfortunately ill-equipped to get them. The 2026-27 Kings are quite frankly one of the strangest teams ever assembled. Former All-Star Domantas Sabonis is playing 36 minutes a game and attempting fewer shots than Precious Achiuwa. Darius Acuff Jr., meanwhile, has the second-highest usage rate any rookie has posted in NBA history, behind only Joel Embiid. He has higher usage this season than Cade Cunningham and Jalen Brunson.

The Kings aren't playing like a team whose goal is to win. They are playing like a team whose sole goal is to fast-forward through Acuff's developmental curve. That's not a crazy decision given their circumstances, but as we've addressed with Brooklyn, young guards can be productive without being especially helpful when it comes to winning. Acuff is taking shots that players like Brunson and Cunningham spend whole careers earning the right to attempt, and he is understandably far worse at actually converting them. Veteran teammates don't tend to enjoy watching rookies chuck bad shots, and without a good defender in sight, it's not as though the Kings can win on the other end of the floor. They're going to be on the bubble here. We just have three better candidates.

The ball-handling deficit here is bleak. Only the Charlotte Hornets are turning the ball over more, and nobody is even close when it comes to points allowed off turnovers. Considering Darius Garland's perpetual issues staying on the court, things are only going to get harder from here. Getting Brandon Ingram back from his partially torn Achilles will help, but he's much more of an individual shotmaker than someone who can lift an entire offense. They're struggling to generate anything near the rim as well, ranking 24th in paint points thus far. They're defending better than most of this group, a byproduct of Jeff Van Gundy's presence on their bench, but even that is at risk because of those pesky incentive structures.

The Clippers obviously owe their own first-round pick to the Oklahoma City Thunder. That isn't especially relevant, but we should note that the Clippers owe their top-three protected pick to the Philadelphia 76ers in 2029 through swap rights, and they'd probably prefer to avoid starting that top-five clock now because consecutive top-five picks would ensure they have no chance of keeping their 2029 selection.

More importantly, though, the Clippers were just stripped of five first-round picks for circumventing the salary cap. That puts them at an enormous draft capital deficit moving forward. There's no way the Clippers can recoup all of that lost value, but it makes plenty of sense for them to trade veterans for whatever value they can get in the name of setting up their future. Players like Brook Lopez, Kris Dunn, Max Strus, Derrick Jones Jr. and Rui Hachimura are all in their primes and could net positive value back in the right trades.

Since the Clippers have nothing to lose by getting relegated this year, it would likely behoove them to cash in these players for whatever value they get. If they do so, they're going to wind up in pretty rough shape down the stretch.

From a team we know circumvented the cap to a team we think very well might have. The Bucks are currently being investigated for the contract they gave Gary Trent Jr. over the summer. And the fact that he has now been DNP-CD'd in six of Milwaukee's eight games certainly doesn't help their case. If they lose picks, they're incentivized to try to make those up by trading away players they don't intend to keep long-term.

Even as it stands, the Bucks are just a bad team. They're a bottom-five offense and defense with no notable injuries. The roster mix is what you'd expect out of a team that just traded the best player in franchise history without receiving a premium asset in return: a jumbled mess. Half of the roster is comprised of shooting guards. They're thin enough at forward that they're still forced to start Kyle Kuzma, and their $108 million starting center, Myles Turner, is averaging single digits. The young players are years away. The old players are years away from the versions of themselves that warranted the minutes and money they're currently receiving.

None of this is especially surprising. It's the first year of a rebuild, and the Bucks won't control their own pick again until 2031. They're in no rush here, and the Pelicans, who control Milwaukee's pick this year, stand to lose draft value because of it.

The Bulls have been the NBA's worst team this season by a pretty comfortable margin. A brutal early schedule is somewhat to blame, of course, but they have nearly a five-point net rating gap between themselves and the No. 29-ranked Kings. They're a bottom-five defense in terms of both points in the paint allowed per game and 3-pointers made per game.

Only the Clippers give up more points off of turnovers. They rank 27th in rebounding rate. Years of steady scoring growth from Josh Giddey have seemingly been undone in two weeks. Matas Buzelis is both playing and shooting less than he did a year ago. Caleb Wilson is exploring the studio space in all of the messy ways you want a top rookie to do so. They're shooting just over 27% from 3-point range.

So the Bulls have the basketball end of the equation covered... but they also have the incentive side to consider. Remember, Wilson was the No. 4 overall pick in June. That means that another top-five pick in 2027 locks them out of the top five in 2028. The 2027 class is considered historically weak, but 2028 is expected to be stronger. Realistically, the Bulls probably don't expect to be any good next year, either. The last thing they should want is to risk getting stuck with a middling 2028 pick because they land at No. 5 in 2027.

Chicago is already terrible and has good reason to try to stay that way. Wilson has an incredibly bright future, but the present is understandably bleak.

#2629. Pete Crow-Armstrong, Jacob Misiorowski, more named finalists for MVP, Cy Young and Rookie of the Year awards

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Major League Baseball, in conjunction with the Baseball Writers Association of America (BBWAA), has announced the finalists for the 2026 major awards: Most Valuable Player, Cy Young, Rookie of the Year, Reliever of the Year and Manager of the Year.

As a reminder, the voting was completed before the playoffs even started. In fact, ballots were due before the first pitch of the playoffs. That means these are regular-season awards. Further, there's no voting after finalists are announced or anything like that. The word "finalists" is kind of misleading, too. The ballots have already been tabulated and the league office is simply revealing the top three vote-getters for each award to create a buzz before the winners are announced.

Take note that the BBWAA has added a new award this season: Relief Pitcher of the Year for each league. MLB has been naming the Mariano Rivera American League Reliever of the Year and Trevor Hoffman National League Reliever of the Year, but this is the first time the BBWAA has added an award for a relief pitcher.

Monday, Nov. 9: Jackie Robinson Rookie of the Year Awards

Tuesday, Nov. 10: Manager of the Year Awards

Wednesday, Nov. 11: Relief Pitcher of the Year Awards

Thursday, Nov. 12: Most Valuable Player Awards

Yordan Alvarez, Astros: He stayed healthy for a full season and was every bit as good as we all thought he'd be. In 158 games, Alvarez had 34 doubles, 42 homers, 106 RBI, 105 runs and led the majors in all three slashes: .316/.432/.601 (190 OPS+). He also led the majors in walks and intentional walks.

Junior Caminero, Rays: At age 22, he played all 162 games, leading the Rays to the best AL record. He hit .276/.360/.524 (144 OPS+) with 42 home runs, 101 RBI and 100 runs, posting a 5.7 WAR. He's already made history, too, as the Rays had previously never had a player finish in the top five of MVP voting.

Bobby Witt Jr., Royals: This is now Witt's fourth straight season in the top seven and third straight season in the top four. He finished second in 2024. This season, he hit .281/.359/.441 (125 OPS+) with 33 doubles, 18 homers, 54 RBI, 94 runs, 45 steals and 6.7 WAR.

Dylan Cease, Blue Jays: In his first season after signing a big deal with the Jays, Cease was one of the few bright spots for the disappointing ballclub. He went 11-6 with a 2.40 ERA (184 ERA+), 1.10 WHIP and 239 strikeouts in 169 innings, finishing with 5.5 WAR. He was the All-Star Game starter.

Parker Messick, Guardians: In 32 starts, Messick was 12-9 with a 2.56 ERA, 1.06 WHIP and 193 strikeouts in 186 ⅓ innings, helping the Guardians win the AL Central for the third straight season. Fun fact: Eight pitchers in history have won the Rookie of the Year and Cy Young. Fernando Valenzuela in 1981 is the only one to win both in the same year.

Cam Schlittler, Yankees: Fresh off a great half season and playoffs in 2025, Schlittler just kept impressing. In his age-25 season, he was 14-6 with a 1.95 ERA, 0.92 WHIP and 239 strikeouts in 193 ⅔ innings, holding the Yankees rotation together despite several key injuries. He led the AL in WAR and ERA.

Kevin McGonigle, Tigers: A first-round pick out of high school in 2023, McGonigle made the Tigers out of spring training and took the league by storm. He returned home to Philadelphia for the All-Star Game and finished with an AL-best 7.1 WAR. In 707 plate appearances, he hit .278/.376/.420 (126 OPS+) with 28 doubles, five triples, 18 home runs, 72 RBI, 97 runs and 12 steals, all the while playing good defense at both shortstop and third base.

Parker Messick, Guardians: The southpaw got his feet wet in 2025, but the workload was low enough that he maintained rookie status for 2026, during which he excelled. In 32 starts, Messick was 12-9 with a 2.56 ERA, 1.06 WHIP and 193 strikeouts in 186 ⅓ innings, helping the Guardians win the AL Central for the third straight season.

Payton Tolle, Red Sox: The 6-foot-6 lefty was a second-round pick in 2024 and debuted last season, though he didn't even work 20 innings and struggled. This time around, he was ready. In 26 starts, he was 9-6 with a 3.03 ERA (135 ERA+), 1.10 WHIP and 171 strikeouts in 148 2/3 innings.

Bryan Baker, Rays: After dabbling in relative obscurity for parts of five seasons, Baker broke out at age 31 this year. He led the majors with 41 saves while pitching to a 1.44 ERA and 0.91 WHIP with 63 strikeouts in his 62 ⅓ innings for the best team in the AL.

Cade Smith, Guardians: Tied with Baker for the MLB lead in saves with 41, Smith was nails in his first full season as closer. He had a 1.95 ERA, 0.96 WHIP and 107 strikeouts in 74 innings for a playoff team.

Louis Varland, Blue Jays: In his fifth MLB season, Varland really found something and finished with a 1.27 ERA, 1.00 WHIP and 97 strikeouts in 78 innings. By late April, he was the Jays' closer, finishing 35 of 37 save chances.

Kevin Cash, Rays: The Rays missed the playoffs in 2024 and 2025 and returned to the Trop after hurricane damage left them without a home in '25. They went out and won 98 games and took one of the toughest divisions in baseball, finishing as the best team in the AL.

Chad Tracy, Red Sox: Tracy took over as manager after the Red Sox got off to a 10-17 start. He went 77-58, making the playoffs. The turnaround featured an absurd stretch during which the Red Sox won 32 of 37 games.

Will Venable, White Sox: Venable became a first-time manager for the 2025 season, taking over a team that lost a modern MLB-record 121 games the previous year. They lost 102 in 2025, but this season improved by 24 games and made the playoffs. This wasn't based much on huge free agency additions or trades for a lot of outside help. It was mostly internal improvement.

Pete Crow-Armstrong, Cubs: We'd seen flashes of the upside before, but PCA put everything together in 2026. He finished a .280/.372/.570 (156 OPS+) hitter with 31 doubles, five triples, 45 home runs, 107 RBI, 119 runs and 9.8 WAR. He led the majors in WAR, runs, home runs and led the NL in slugging percentage, OPS and OPS+. He became the seventh player ever to join the 40-40 club, too.

Shohei Ohtani, Dodgers: The four-time MVP looked like he was going to win a fifth for the first half of the season, but injuries caught up to him late. Still, at the plate, Ohtani hit .275/.377/.512 with 26 doubles, four triples, 30 home runs, 81 RBI, 89 runs, 11 steals and 3.2 WAR. On the mound, he was 8-2 with a 1.79 ERA, 0.95 WHIP and 95 strikeouts in 85 ⅔ innings with 3.2 WAR.

Brice Turang, Brewers: Nationally underrated, Turang still hasn't made an All-Star Game, though he did start 2026 as a member of Team USA in the World Baseball Classic. In the regular season, Turang hit .268/.366/.450 (124 OPS+) with 37 doubles, three triples, 21 home runs, 100 RBI, 102 runs and 7.3 WAR, rating out as one of the best defenders in baseball.

Jacob Misiorowski, Brewers: There was upside to dream on here entering the season and it became a dream season. In 30 starts, Miz posted a 1.80 ERA, 0.80 WHIP and 252 strikeouts in 174 ⅔ innings. He went 16-5 for the team with the best record in baseball and led the majors in ERA, WHIP and strikeouts, among other things.

Chris Sale, Braves: The spindly left-hander won his first Cy Young at age 35 in 2024. He was only able to make 27 starts this season, but he was better in a few rate stats. Overall, he was 14-9 with a 2.16 ERA, 0.98 WHIP and 200 strikeouts against only 31 walks in 162 ⅔ innings.

Cristopher Sánchez, Phillies: Early in the season, Sánchez moved to the front of the line after a scoreless streak of 50 ⅔ innings. At midseason, he started the All-Star Game in Philly. He finished the season 18-7 with a 2.91 ERA, 1.20 WHIP and 231 strikeouts in 207 innings. He led the majors in pitcher WAR at 8.1.

Carson Benge, Mets: The 2024 first-rounder made the team out of spring training and hit .282/.346/.430 with 20 home runs, 22 steals and 4.3 WAR.

Sal Stewart, Reds: It's a fight of Old School vs. New School. Stewart only posted 1.8 WAR, but he had 32 home runs and 111 RBI, putting him in rarefied air for a rookie. He's one of just 15 rookies ever with at least 30 homers and 100 RBI. The last eight players to do so won Rookie of the Year. The only ones who didn't win came before there was an award or someone else did it in the same season (two rookies in 1950 got to 30-100).

JJ Wetherholt, Cardinals: Defensive metrics love Wetherholt and help push him to 4.5 WAR in 139 games. He hit .242/.339/.365 with 17 homers, 14 steals and 89 runs.

Jhoan Duran, Phillies: In his first full season with the Phillies, Duran closed down 33 of his 35 save chances with a 1.82 ERA, 0.99 WHIP and 84 strikeouts in 59 ⅓ innings.

Mason Miller, Padres: In 70 innings across 66 appearances, Miller pitched to a 1.67 ERA, 0.90 WHIP and struck out 129 hitters. He won five games and converted 38 of his 41 save chances.

Trevor Megill, Brewers: Though the Brewers didn't always employ a traditional closer, Megill was the closest thing to it, securing 30 saves in 33 chances with a 2.63 ERA, 0.89 WHIP and 69 strikeouts in 61 2/3 innings.

Don Mattingly, Phillies: Mattingly started the season as the bench coach before taking over a 9-19 team for the fired Rob Thomson. Immediately, the Phillies got hot. They ended up going 79-55 under Mattingly, making the playoffs yet again despite starting 10 games under .500.

Pat Murphy, Brewers: Managers almost never win this award in back-to-back seasons because it's generally given to the guy whose team most exceeded expectations. How could that possibly happen two straight years? Well, Murphy now is going for three. In 2025, the Brewers set a franchise record with 97 wins and had the best record in baseball. In 2026, they set a franchise record with 103 wins and had the best record in baseball.

Walt Weiss, Braves: In 2025, the final season of Brian Snitker's career, the Braves were a disappointing 76-86. Weiss was hired in the offseason and went 94-68, getting the Braves back on top in the NL East after a two-year hiatus.

#2628. Russell Wilson shares what he found ‘surprising’ about Carson Wentz’s performance vs Buffalo Bills

The Minnesota Vikings suffered just their second defeat of the 2026/27 NFL season on Monday when they took on the Buffalo Bills.

The Vikings have relied heavily on their defence this term and for the most part, it has worked out.

But they struggled to deal with Josh Allen and the rest of the Bills this week, losing 23-6.

On the back of their defeat, former NFL player Russell Wilson has been speaking about Carson Wentz.

He suggested that 'Justin Jefferson is arguably the best receiver in football' but was left surprised at how much Wentz seemed to get 'in his own head' when trying to find Jefferson, labelling the situation a 'surprising moment'.

Speaking on the 'Set, Hut!' podcast, Wilson said: "If I'm the Minnesota Vikings, if I'm their GM, if I'm Nolan, if I'm KOC, if I'm those guys, we got to figure out this quarterback.

"Because at the end of the day, you're also going to frustrate your main player, Justin Jefferson. Justin Jefferson is arguably the best receiver in football and has been for a long time. I mean, they showed a picture of Justin Jefferson, and here comes Randy Moss right afterwards.

"And you're talking about two all-time greats. You know, that's the level of play that he makes. He almost made that one-handed catch yesterday.

"He's landed on his head, landed on his shoulder. I mean, that's the player that he is. And to me, you know, seeing Carson Wentz throw balls over his head and the balls in the dirt, that was just disappointing. That was a surprising moment for me, just because I feel like he got in his own head. And sometimes, I feel like he was trying to convince himself that he could still do it or whatever in his own mind."

The Vikings are currently managing 266.8 net yards per game this season, which is the second lowest in the league.

Meanwhile, Wentz ranks 39th for passing yards in the NFL this year with 357.

#2626. Robinson Canó Jr., son of eight-time MLB All-Star, agrees to $1 million deal with Marlins, per reports

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The Miami Marlins have reached a preliminary agreement with 16-year-old Robinson Canó Jr. that stands to make him part of the club's 2028 international signing class. The agreement is worth $1 million, reports Mike Rodriguez.

MLB rules state that an international amateur free agent player is eligible to sign with an MLB organization between Jan. 15 and Dec. 15 of his signing class year. He must turn 17 before Sept. 1 of the year in which he signs.

Canó Jr., a highly regarded shortstop out of the Dominican Republic who bats right-handed, is the son of former MLB great Robinson Canó. The elder Canó spent parts of 17 seasons in the majors, the majority of which came with the New York Yankees. Over that span, Canó earned eight All-Star selections and three Gold Gloves; racked up 2,639 hits and 335 home runs; and won a World Series ring as a member of the 2009 Yankees. He went on to sign a large free-agent contract with the Seattle Mariners, where he played from 2014-18.

Canó's career total of 68.7 WAR would under normal circumstances make him a strong candidate for election to the Baseball Hall of Fame. However, two suspensions for positive PED tests make it unlikely he'll get a plaque, at least while he's on the BBWAA ballot. He last appeared in the majors in 2022 as a member of the Atlanta Braves.

Canó Jr. is also the grandson of José Canó, who appeared in the majors with the 1989 Houston Astros, which puts him in line to be a third-generation major leaguer.

#2622. Tarik Skubal contract predictions: Ace's new deal could break multiple MLB records for a pitcher

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Tarik Skubal is about to become a very, very rich man. The two-time Cy Young winner and arguably the best pitcher in baseball hits free agency this winter, and it stands to reason that he'll break the record for highest-paid pitcher in MLB history, both by total value and average annual value.

By total value, Dodgers ace Yoshinobu Yamamoto currently holds that record thanks to the 12-year, $325 million contract he signed ahead of the 2024 season (we're eliminating Shohei Ohtani from the running for obvious reasons, though his 10-year, $700 million deal would clearly lead the list).

As for AAV, Ohtani again tops the class at $70 million a year, but for those who only pitch, Max Scherzer and Justin Verlander share the record at $43.33 million annually.

The expectation is that Skubal will break both records, even as the owners try to tamp down on spending in the ongoing CBA negotiations. Just how high could those figures go? CBS Sports experts pulled out their calculators.

Mike Axisa: Seven years and $325.5 million. That's $46.5 million per season and it would break the records for average annual value (Max Scherzer's and Justin Verlander's $43.3 million) and total guarantee (Yoshinobu Yamamoto's $325 million) for a pitcher. I would expect there to be an opt out because those are just the cost of doing business these days. Maybe even multiple opt outs. Scott Boras loves to break records, though, and this contract allows him to break two.

Dayn Perry: I'll say eight years, $350 million. Likewise, that sets the record for total contract value and AAV for a pitcher. Normally, I'd ding him a bit for those elbow problems in his walk year, but he was mostly dominant after returning ahead of schedule. I also think Skubal will benefit from an aggressive pre-lockout market and from a pretty thin free agent class overall.

Matt Snyder: Eight years, $400 million. This gets him the record deal for pitchers both in terms of the guarantee and the average annual value. I'm probably going too low on the years, but I feel like teams have been burned so many times before on the length of pitcher deals due to injury that this holds down the market a bit. Ever so slightly. I do think there will be opt outs after years three and five.
