#2620. Doc Rivers says 'difficult' Giannis Antetokounmpo 'didn't want to be the bad guy' while forcing Bucks exit

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Former Milwaukee Bucks coach Doc Rivers said Giannis Antetokounmpo was difficult to coach and "didn't want to be the bad guy" amid the saga that ultimately led to his trade to the Miami Heat this summer.

Rivers, who coached the Bucks for two and a half seasons from 2024-26, said on "The Bill Simmons Podcast" that the ordeal dragged on for so long because Antetokounmpo "kept yo-yoing" with his desire to leave Milwaukee. Antetokounmpo never publicly requested a trade.

Like any small-market star, Antetokounmpo had been the subject of trade rumors since he emerged as an MVP-caliber player, but the questions about his future really amped up in recent years as the Bucks' title window closed and he moved closer to unrestricted free agency.

The Bucks had the opportunity to trade Antetokounmpo after the 2024-25 season, which ended with another first-round exit after Damian Lillard tore his Achilles tendon. Instead, Milwaukee waived Lillard and stretched his contract, which will now be on their books until 2030, and signed Myles Turner to a four-year, $108 million deal in a desperate attempt to keep Antetokounmpo around. The plan did not work; the Bucks missed the playoffs last season for the first time since 2016, and eventually traded Antetokounmpo when it became clear that he would not sign an extension.

"In [Bucks general manager Jon Horst's] defense, I thought Giannis kept yo-yoing," Rivers said when discussing what went wrong in Milwaukee over the last few seasons. "When I look back on that whole situation, Giannis wanted out, but he was a Buck. He didn't want to be the bad guy. He wanted Jon and [co-owner Wes Edens] and those guys to say, 'We're trading you,' instead of him asking for a trade. To me, that was the game that was being played."

Everyone could see that Antetokounmpo, who led the Bucks to the 2021 NBA championship, was torn about leaving the only franchise he had ever known, and the city where he had spent nearly half of his life, but it's still notable to hear Rivers confirm it.

Rivers' more interesting comments were about how hard it was for him to coach Antetokounmpo:

"He's not easy. He plays at this crazy downhill pace. He's really a difficult guy. I was telling someone this. He has this great passing ability, but he doesn't necessarily have a super IQ at the same time. It's really a strange thing. And he really has only one way -- downhill, force, force, force. Every play, he wants to force it. I wish he'd learned how to execute better.

"He's one of those guys, you get a lot of them from the U.S., AAU guys that have never needed to execute, because they can do it on their own. But that doesn't help the team. I told Giannis this: The thing he still needs to learn is the value of execution. How important it is, when you're in practice and at shootaround, to lock in on execution. Now he has a coach who's as good as there is in execution."

Antetokounmpo is a unique player and, like many all-time greats, incredibly stubborn. Those qualities helped him grow into a two-time MVP and lead the Bucks to their first title in 50 years. They also made it challenging to build a roster around him and led him to play through injuries that should have kept him on the sideline.

There are certainly aspects of Antetokounmpo's style and approach that would make life difficult for any coach, but Rivers has been making excuses about his time with the Bucks since his introductory press conference, when he said, "I wouldn't wish this on anyone," about taking over a team with Antetokounmpo, Lillard and Khris Middleton mid-season.

It was also a bit strange to hear Rivers say that Antetokounmpo, who scored 50 points in a title-clinching game on 16 of 25 from the field and 17 of 19 from the free-throw line, needs to learn the value of execution.

Rivers was not retained after the 2026 season and Antetokounmpo, along with Bobby Portis, was traded to the Heat in June. In return, the Bucks received Tyler Herro, Kel'el Ware, Jaime Jaquez Jr., Kasparas Jakucionis, three first-round picks, a second-round pick and a pick swap.

Both teams are off to rough starts this season. While the Bucks are 1-7 as they begin their rebuild, the Heat are 3-6. Antetokounmpo is averaging 27.3 points, 12.7 rebounds and 5.6 assists per game.

#2619. Why MLB could see an early free agency frenzy before the potential Dec. 1 lockout

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Most of the season, my assumption was that November would be a slow month for the hot stove. There is a new collective bargaining agreement coming, likely after a lockout, and I figured teams would not want to commit significantly to future payroll without first seeing what the new CBA would bring. Salary cap, stiffer competitive balance tax penalties, whatever.

A perfectly reasonable stance, that is, and I say that as someone who is happy to call out teams and owners who do not appear to be putting forth the best effort to contend, if you catch my drift. My assumption was November would be slow. I am here now to tell you why my assumption not just may be wrong, but likely is wrong, and the hot stove will burn bright in November.

The CBA expires at 11:59 p.m. ET on Dec. 1, or four weeks from Tuesday. Here now are four reasons why MLB clubs could be active between now and then.

MLB teams committed more than $1.7 billion to free agents in November 2021, just before the last CBA expired and the owners locked out the players. That includes the Rangers, who spent more than $560 million on Jon Gray, Corey Seager, and Marcus Semien. Those three later helped the Rangers win the franchise's first World Series title in 2023. Five players signed nine-figure contracts in the weeks leading up to the last lockout.

It is not only the teams we must consider here. More than 140 players became free agents the day after the World Series, and you can be sure many (most?) of them would prefer to sign before the lockout. They want to get their contract locked in and know where they'll play next season so they can find a place to live, get the kids enrolled in school, etc. Peace of mind during the lockout will go a long way.

MLB's owners did not propose a salary cap during the last round of labor negotiations, but there was similar uncertainty about what the upcoming CBA would bring, and teams spent lots of money anyway. Past behavior can inform us about what to expect in the future and what we saw leading into the last lockout suggests it will be a busy four weeks.

During the last lockout, MLB amended its posting agreement with Japan's Nippon Professional Baseball league and paused the 45-day negotiating window during the lockout. Seiya Suzuki was posted on Nov. 22, 2021, his 45 days were paused when the lockout began on Dec. 1, then they resumed when the lockout ended on March 10, 2022. Suzuki signed with the Cubs on March 18.

NPB players will not have the same luxury this year. MLB has declined to amend its posting agreement this offseason, according to The Athletic, so NPB players potentially face a hard Dec. 1 signing deadline even though they were officially posted on Nov. 1. They won't get the full 45 days because players cannot sign MLB contracts during the lockout. Their posting window is really 30 days.

This applies to three of our top 50 free agents: Hanshin Tigers third baseman Teruaki Sato (No. 4), Seibu Lions righty Kaima Taira (No. 19), and Hokkaido Nippon Ham Fighters righty Hiromi Itoh (No. 26). All three were posted on Nov. 1 and their 45-day posting window should run through Dec. 16. Instead, they must sign by Dec. 1 with the lockout looming, or return to Japan for 2027.

Tarik Skubal, far and away the best free agent on the market, is expected to sign before the lockout, reports ESPN. There is always a bit of a domino effect with top free agents. Several big spenders (Blue Jays, Cubs, Dodgers, Mets, etc.) are expected to pursue Skubal, and the teams that lose out could quickly pivot to their secondary targets to avoid being left empty-handed.

We saw a good example of this domino effect last offseason. The Dodgers beat out the Mets for Kyle Tucker and agreed to terms with the outfielder on Jan. 16. The Mets quickly pivoted and agreed to a contract with Bo Bichette just a few hours later. They had money to spend and a void in the lineup, and after losing out on their top target, New York quickly pivoted to Plan B.

The sooner Skubal signs, the sooner second-tier free agent starters like Freddy Peralta and Trevor Rogers will come off the board. Teams need pitching, always and forever, and once the best available starter comes off the board, there figures to be a rush to get whoever's left. Skubal is expected to sign before the lockout. Other starters won't be far behind then.

Even if the MLB Players Association relents and agrees to a salary cap, it is unlikely the cap will be fully implemented in 2027. MLB has expressed a willingness to phase in a salary cap over some number of years and, honestly, it's a must. It will be impossible for big payroll clubs like the Dodgers, Mets, and Yankees to trim payroll and get cap-compliant immediately after the lockout.

November may be the last chance for all teams, not just those with deep pockets, to spend freely and have contracts grandfathered into whatever economic system the new CBA brings. Spend now, deal with the consequences later. That kind of thing. It may sound foolish -- the bill will come due eventually, right? -- but rarely is the hot stove league and free agency rational.

"You prepare under the current system, and then you adjust along the way," Blue Jays president Mark Shapiro told Sportsnet last month. "Any new system adopted, there will be a timeframe for adjustment into that system. I don't think any new system adopted would cause for immediate action."

#2618. Nikita Kucherov trade request: Five potential landing spots for the reigning NHL MVP

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

One of the greatest players in Tampa Bay Lightning history may soon be wearing a different jersey. According to Sportsnet, Nikita Kucherov has told the Lightning he won't sign a contract extension and has requested a trade.

Kucherov, a two-time Stanley Cup champion and two-time Hart Trophy winner as league MVP, is one of the best players of his era. The 33-year-old just passed the legendary Steven Stamkos for the all-time franchise lead in points and has shown no signs of slowing down.

Just last season, Kucherov posted 44 goals and 86 assists en route to his second Hart Trophy win. His underlying numbers were even better with a five-on-five goal differential of plus-38 and an expected goals share of 57.0 percent. Only a select few players can drive play from the wing like Kucherov, and that makes him a unicorn of sorts.

Kucherov is in the final year of a contract that pays him $9.5 million per season, and with the salary cap rising rapidly, he's due for a gargantuan raise next summer. It sounds like Kucherov and the Lightning were too far apart on that number, so the superstar winger has shifted his focuse to a change of scenery.

It's important to note that Kucherov has limited trade protection in the form of a 10-team trade list, but that should be more than enough for the Lightning to find a suitable trade partner. With that in mind, let's take a look at five teams that would be ideal fits for Kucherov as he prepares for the next chapter of his illustrious career.

Right out of the gate, this is the most natural fit of all the potential landing spots. General manager Kent Hughes has done a superb job of locking down his young core on team-friendly contracts, and as a result, the Canadiens have nearly $30 million in projected cap space for next season. They also have a glaring need in their top two lines, and I'd say the reigning Hart Trophy winner would fill that role quite nicely.

Montreal's moment to strike is now. It's an ascendant team with a great salary cap situtation and assets to spend. It's time to make a splash, and this would be a tsunami. Just imagine Kucherov on a power play unit with Nick Suzuki, Cole Caufield, Lane Hutson and Ivan Demidov. Kucherov would also be coached by former Lightning teammate Martin St. Louis, so a rapport would already exist between player and coach. I expect the Canadiens to do everything in their power to land Kucherov.

We already know the Wild are big-game hunting at forward because they've been heavily linked to former Detroit Red Wings captain Dylan Larkin. If I were advising general manager Bill Guerin -- and I'm certainly not -- I would recommend Minnesota package whatever assets it has offered Detroit and redirect them to Tampa Bay. No, Kucherov is not a center,  and that's the Wild's biggest need.

However, Kucherov is a rare breed of winger in that he can drive play better than most first-line centers from the wing. Put him on a line with Kirill Kaprizov, and the only time opponents will touch the puck is when they're pulling out of the net.

With Quinn Hughes also on an expiring contract, acquiring Kucherov would be a risky move for the Wild. What if they give up premium assets only to lose Kucherov and Hughes next summer? I don't think fear can dictate Minnesota's decisions. The team has a top-two defenseman in the world on its roster right now, and it has the opportunity to acquire a top-five forward. Worry about next summer when the time comes. Go all in to win the Cup while you have a chance.

It was no secret that the Hurricanes were in on the Connor Hellebuyck sweepstakes but just missed out. So, if they can't get better at preventing goals, why not get much better at scoring them? Carolina doesn't exactly need any help offensively, but adding Kucherov would go a long way to helping the team repeat as Stanley Cup champions. Besides, Kucherov would provide another level of playmaking and finishing that the Canes don't currently have on their roster.

Carolina has a good chunk of cap space available already, and it wouldn't need to shed much in order to make room for Kucherov. The Canes also have some enticing young players on their roster that might appeal to the Bolts, and they have three first-round picks over the next two drafts. Why not take a shot at landing a superstar winger?

Similar to the Hurricanes, the Mammoth were in the mix to acquire Hellebucyk, and for good reason. The goaltending tandem of Karel Vejmelka and Sebastian Cossa has not been good, so Utah may have to outscore its problems until one of the goalies finds a groove. Offense may be the best defense for the Mammoth -- and if that's the case -- then Kucherov should be in the mix for the Norris Trophy. There is a great young core of forwards in Salt Lake City, and I think Kucherov would be a perfect fit alongside Logan Cooley, who is emerging as a franchise center.

Utah also has plenty of draft capital with which to work, and it's projected for just over $25 million in salary cap space next season. The Mammoth don't have any major pending free agents on their cap sheet, so they're a suitor capable of signing Kucherov to a long-term extension.

Allow me to get a little bold on the fifth and final destination. The Stars have already failed to sign 27-year-old winger Jason Robertson to a long-term extension once. The two sides agreed to a one-year deal worth $12 million prior to the season, but Robertson's future with the team is still very much in doubt. What if Dallas and Tampa Bay executed a true "hockey trade" -- one player for one player?

Dallas would get the better player in Kucherov, but there are no guarantees regarding an extension. The Stars are in win-now mode, and Kucherov could help them get over the Cup hump immediately. Tampa Bay would get a younger player in Robertson, and although he doesn't have the elite playmaking ability of Kucherov, he's still an exceptionally talented scorer. Perhaps the Bolts could get him to join the team's core and sign a multi-year contract. This deal could work for both sides.

After a colossally disappointing 2026 season, the Seattle Mariners are bringing in a first-time manager. The Mariners have named Chicago Cubs director of player development Jason Kanzler their new manager, the team announced Tuesday. Seattle fired manager Dan Wilson after the season.

"Our goal in this process was finding a manager with the ability to challenge all of us to improve," president of baseball operations Jerry Dipoto said in a statement. "Jason has the mindset, expertise, communication skills, and intensity to help create a championship standard here in Seattle."

The Mariners will be Kanzler's first managerial job at any level. At 36, he will be the second-youngest manager in baseball, older than only 34-year-old Washington Nationals skipper Blake Butera.

Bringing in a manager with zero previous managerial experience at any level is a rare move, certainly, though it is not unprecedented. Most notably, the New York Yankees hired Aaron Boone straight from the broadcasting booth in 2018. Boone had no managerial or coaching experience at any level. He's led the Yankees to the postseason eight times in nine seasons.

"I am thrilled to join the Mariners organization and I'm looking forward to hitting the ground running," Kanzler said in a statement. "This team has an immense amount of talent in all facets of the game, and my coaching staff and I are excited to access and unlock this team's full potential."

Kanzler may have no prior managerial experience, but this will not be his first time on a big-league staff. He was a major-league coach with the Houston Astros in 2022 and their assistant hitting coach in 2023, and had coached in their farm system previously. The Cubs hired Kanzler to oversee their player development in 2024.

Former Astros manager Joe Espada was reportedly the other finalist for the Mariners job.

The Mariners went 76-86 this past season and finished five games back in the woebegone AL West. A year ago, they went to Game 7 of the ALCS and were five outs away from their first-ever trip to the World Series. Seattle entered 2026 as a trendy World Series pick and instead fell flat, mostly because so many core hitters underperformed.

Kanzler will be the team's third manager since Dipoto was hired to run baseball operations in September 2015, joining Scott Servais (2015-24) and Wilson (2024-26).

The New York Knicks have released a statement supporting Taylor Swift's fandom after recent comments from reserve guards Tyler Kolek and Deuce McBride.

Earlier this month, Kolek called Swift's fandom "a little performative" on an NBA 2K League video. Kolek and McBride were playing a game called "Deflected," where they have to compete in NBA 2K to avoid answering awkward questions. After McBride scored on the game, Kolek had to answer: "Who's the fakest celebrity fan you've seen sitting courtside in an NBA game?"

"At the Knicks games, I would say it's very performative," Kolek said. "Because they just want to be seen at the game; they're not necessarily fans. Maybe Taylor Swift?"

"I don't know if I've seen her at any other games," Kolek said.

"Swifties not gonna like that answer," McBride replied.

"No, I'm gonna get some hate from the Swifties," Kolek acknowledged. "I get she's got a lot going on, so she can't come all the time, but it's a little performative."

This is not the first time Swift's Knicks fandom has been questioned. "She's not a Knicks fan. Get outta here, girl," broadcaster Monica McNutt said in June after Swift sat courtside during Game 4 of the 2026 NBA Finals, which the Knicks won with a historic 29-point comeback. McNutt later apologized for the comments.

Swift was born and raised in Pennsylvania, but has been a Knicks fan since moving to New York over a decade ago. Here's an excerpt from an interview with Time Magazine in 2014:

You recently moved to New York. Are you a Knicks fan now?

I love them, though. Why does that matter? So you run into a bunch of different, interesting types of people at the Met Ball. I've gone the last four years. And the most normal people at that event, every single time, are Amar'e Stoudemire and his wife Alexis. I talk with them and hang with them every time I'm there. So I've always had this sort of love of the Knicks, just because Amar'e is so cool. And also I performed at the Knicks'—at Madison Square Garden's—Kids Talent Competition at halftime when I was 12 or 13. And ever since then I've had this kind of sparkly, magical opinion of Madison Square Garden and the Knicks, since they let me sing when I was a little kid.

Swift and Kansas City Chiefs star Travis Kelce were married at Madison Square Garden during a lavish wedding in July.

#2611. Jordan Davis trade grades: Eagles kickstart rebuild, Jaguars push for 2026 AFC and Super Bowl titles

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The Jacksonville Jaguars capped their flurry of activity on the eve of the NFL's 2026 trade deadline with a blockbuster: they traded a 2027 first-round pick and a 2029 second-round pick for Philadelphia Eagles defensive tackle Jordan Davis.

Davis was the 13th overall pick in the 2022 NFL Draft out of Georgia and was also a starter on the Eagles' Super Bowl LIX title team in the 2024 season. Jacksonville doesn't have to worry about a long-term contract with Davis since Philadelphia extended Davis on a three-year, $78 million extension this past offseason. On Monday, the Jaguars have relinquished a 2027 first-round pick, a 2027 second-round pick, a 2028 fifth-round pick, a 2028 sixth-round pick and a 2029 second-round pick for the services of Davis, Atlanta Falcons Pro Bowl safety Jessie Bates III and New Orleans Saints defensive tackle Davon Godchaux.

Meanwhile, the Eagles now have 10 draft picks in the first two rounds of the NFL Draft across the next three years. They have their own first-round pick and second-round pick, plus the Jaguars' first-round pick in 2027. They have their own first-round pick and own second-round pick plus the New England Patriots' first-round pick (A.J. Brown trade) and the Baltimore Ravens' second-round pick (Cam Jurgens trade) in 2028. In 2029, they have their own first-round pick, their own second-round pick and the Jaguars' second-round pick (Jordan Davis trade).

So how does each side grade out in Monday evening's blockbuster deal? Let's dive in.

The Jaguars are right to go all in for the 2026 season. The Buffalo Bills (6-1) have one of the leakiest secondaries in the NFL, allowing 254.7 passing yards per game (the third-most in the entire NFL). The Denver Broncos (7-2) have offensive inconsistency issues because of quarterback Bo Nix, whose 5.6 air yards per pass attempt is the second-worst among 31 qualified quarterbacks this season. Nix's 5.6 air yards per pass attempt is mere decimal points ahead of Kansas City Chiefs (6-2) quarterback Patrick Mahomes' 5.6 air yards per pass attempt to avoid being dead last in the league. Mahomes' league-worst air yards per pass attempt figure has more to do with the Chiefs' limited passing game options than an unwillingness to throw the ball downfield like Nix.

The AFC North-leading Pittsburgh Steelers (6-2) have Aaron Rodgers at quarterback, and he will be 43 years old by the time the playoffs begin. Jacksonville beat the Cincinnati Bengals (6-2) in a narrow, one-score game earlier this season, and the New England Patriots (5-4) just got decimated at home (45-27) by quarterback Jordan Love and his Green Bay Packers.

Jacksonville's timing is right, but the price they paid for Davis is not. A first-round pick and a second-round pick for Davis isn't all that different from what the Chicago Bears gave up (2027 and 2028 first-round picks plus a 2027 fourth-round pick) for All-Pro defensive tackle Jeffery Simmons, the best defensive tackle in football at the moment. Sure, the Jaguars were never going to get Simmons since he was on an AFC South division rival, the Tennessee Titans, but couldn't they have gotten Davis for a slightly cheaper price? The Bears are getting a player whose 17 sacks over the last two seasons are the most in the league among defensive tackles, while Davis has just 9.5 career sacks.

Yes, Davis can be incredibly impactful in the run game just because of his frame (6-feet-6-inches tall while weighing 336 pounds), but one would think that the Jaguars would have been able to acquire a more well-rounded defensive tackle at the price point of a 2027 first-round pick and a 2029 second-round pick. Davis will certainly help Jacksonville, but what they gave up for him was a little rich.

Hats off to Eagles general manager Howie Roseman because he's done it again. He recognized that the 2026 season was dead with quarterback Jalen Hurts (blood clots) sidelined, and the team was on a seven-game losing streak, putting their record at 2-7 through nine games. Roseman also extended two-time Pro Bowl defensive tackle Jalen Carter on a four-year, $152 million extension last offseason, and it was clear that Philadelphia likely wouldn't be able to keep both Carter and Davis for years to come in order to have a well-balanced roster.

Roseman was able to trade away the lesser player of the two, and he recouped first-round and second-round draft capital in the deal. He couldn't have asked for anything more, and he'll be able to rebuild the Eagles in no time with 10 picks in the first two rounds of the draft across the next three years.

#2609. MLB CBA negotiations timeline: League proposes delaying salary cap for 'smoother transition'

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

As the 2026 Major League Baseball offseason continues to unfold, something vitally important to the future of the sport quietly hums in the background: the ongoing negotiations over a new collective bargaining agreement.

The collective bargaining agreement, or CBA (or Basic Agreement, as it's known in a formal sense), is the negotiated accord between players and clubs -- i.e., the team owners and commissioner Rob Manfred, who represents their interests -- that governs the working relationship between the two parties, typically for a period of five years. It covers things as mundane as players' meal allowances and travel protocols and as vital as minimum salaries, the structure of free agency, revenue-sharing specifics, and roster sizes. Every CBA can be distilled down to a fight over money, or, more specifically, how the league's revenues will be divided between players and team owners.

The first CBA covered the 1968 and 1969 seasons and was the first in professional sports history. That was the handiwork of Marvin Miller, the pioneering head of the Players Association (i.e., the players union) and belated Hall of Famer. It was Miller's organizing skills, foresight, and training as a union economist that allowed him to make the Players Association a viable and effective labor organization. Every CBA negotiation from 1972 through 1994-95 resulted in some form and scale of labor stoppage, whether a players' strike or an owner-implemented lockout. After the cancellation of the 1994 World Series because of the worst labor stoppage in the sport's history, a long run of peace followed. That peace lasted until the prior CBA negotiations, which resulted in a 99-day lockout forced by team owners and delayed the start of the 2022 season.

The current CBA negotiations have been underway for some time, and not surprisingly, the two sides remain far apart on several key issues. The biggest fight will be over the owners' renewed desire to implement a salary cap, which the union continues to view as a non-starter. The push for a cap has less to do with the notions of competitive balance and more to do with the ownership's internal belief that being the only non-salary-capped league among the major North American sports is harming franchise values. The cap, though, is but one of many pressing issues on which players and owners must find congruity.

Moving forward, the process will be uncertain and rife with posturing and pointed public comments from both sides. The hope, though, is that a new CBA will be agreed to before the middle of March 2027, at which point there's a high risk of having the 2027 season delayed or even abbreviated.

To keep you informed of the twists and turns along the way to a new CBA, we've provided a detailed timeline of negotiations. That timeline will illuminate the important and finer points of the talks and, along the way, explain the implications of the various proposals coming from each side. The hope, of course, is that all of it culminates in a timely agreement that permits a fully intact and on-time 2027 season.

To allow for a "smoother transition" to a salary cap/floor system, MLB proposed delaying its implementation until 2028. That would give teams time to prepare and get their payrolls in order, and allow for a full offseason heading into the system. The current competitive balance tax and revenue sharing system would remain in place in 2027.

"We recognize that clubs will need a full offseason to prepare to operate within the cap and floor system. Therefore, with this offseason already underway, we proposed today to begin the cap and floor system in 2028," MLB spokesman Glen Caplin said in a statement. "This proposal would allow a smoother transition into the cap and floor system."

MLB also upped its salary cap/floor proposal to $258.3 million and $180.2 million, respectively. Back in June, the league proposed a $245.3 million cap and $171.2 million floor. It says it is willing to discuss further phase-in scenarios for a salary cap/floor system.

In its latest proposal, MLB proposed reducing the regular season from 162 games to 154 games, and adding a standard off day to every week. The league also proposed extending the Division Series from a best-of-five to a best-of-seven, and allowing higher seeded teams to select their opponents in the Wild Card Series and Division Series. As with every MLB proposal to date, the 154-game schedule and changes to the postseason format are contingent on the MLBPA accepting a salary car/floor system.

If labor strife lops off 60 or more games from the 2027 MLB season, then the consequences could be significant. The Athletic recently reported that if the forthcoming lockout extends into late May or so and costs at least 60 games, then most of the league's national broadcast and streaming contracts would be extended for another year, through 2029. That's significant because commissioner Rob Manfred hopes to bundle and centralize team streaming rights and share those revenues equally, and the current timeline would theoretically allow that to happen at the same time the national contracts are up for renegotiation. Tacking on another year to those national contracts would push back the significant windfall that owners and the league are expecting from that new media rights structure. As such, this is a heavy incentive, at least on the league side, to not let any labor stoppage drag into June.

A poll of current MLB players across the full spectrum of salaries and service time conducted by ESPN showed strong resistance to the payroll cap and floor being demanded by ownership and league and being put forth as a precondition to every proposed change from that side. An excerpt:

How open are you to a salary cap?NL starting pitcher entering arbitration: Not open.

NL infielder making eight figures annually: Zero. No chance.

NL infielder on two-year contract: Zero. Absolute zero.

NL pre-arbitration journeyman: From what I've been told, I don't think it's good for the game. I just don't know if I know all the pros and cons of it. But, from everything we've been told, it doesn't sound like it's a good thing.

NL reliever on multiyear contract: With the right criteria, I'd be open to it.

AL starting pitcher in arbitration: I don't want it. In '94, they canceled the World Series, so if those guys can miss over half a year and miss the World Series, I think we're fully prepared to hold out for sure.

AL catcher entering arbitration: I need more information, but perhaps I would listen on it.

That's mostly strong sentiment that aligns with the MLBPA position on the cap, but it's not ironclad. MLB in negotiations and its public statements is seeking to tap into any existing divide between, broadly speaking, lower-salaried players with not much service time and more tenured veterans in their higher-earning years. There is a bit of a schism there, but it would take a substantial one to shift, in any exploitable way, the union's long-standing opposition to a cap-and-floor system. The ESPN piece covers an array of CBA topics. With the two questions related to the proposed cap, the responses can be broken down as 16 in mostly firm opposition to a cap and five not necessarily in favor but open to further discussions and reflection.

MLB proposed a series of changes to current roster rules that, in a statement, the league says are aimed at "creating more stability in rosters, getting the best players to the Major Leagues more quickly, and accelerating the pace of the offseason." Among the rule changes included in MLB's proposal are:

All the proposed roster rule changes are contingent on the MLB Players Association agreeing to a salary cap-and-floor system.

During a negotiating session with the league, the players' union puts forth its own proposed changes to the MLB Draft -- changes that are, in essence, a rejoinder to the drastic overhaul earlier put forward by MLB. Among the changes the MLBPA proposes are:

Additionally, the union proposes increasing the money payable to draftees under the incentive bonus plan and eliminating, according to the MLBPA, "the current practice of clubs deducting certain bonuses from players' continuing education benefits."

The timing of the draft has actually been a concern for front offices for years, since it was shifted later in the calendar to coincide with the All-Star break in 2021. Holding the draft in July crams both that and the trade deadline into just a few weeks and making it more difficult to allocate resources.

Commissioner Rob Manfred and interim union head Bruce Meyer each hold press conferences on the day of the All-Star Game in Philadelphia. "I think that I have an ownership group that is more united than any group in my entire time of baseball," Manfred says, referring at least obliquely to the league's push for a salary cap. "They are a group that believes in what I am arguing for."

"The supposed stewards of the game have spent an inordinate amount of time trying to convince those same fans that they don't have hope or they shouldn't have hope or that the product that they're paying to consume in record numbers is somehow broken," Meyer says of MLB's efforts to highlight perceived competitive-balance issues in the face of increasing attendance and television ratings. "I think it's perverse."

The MLBPA puts forth multiple proposals, many of them dealing with procedural matters for purposes of player health, safety, and wellness. They include:

The union's latest proposal is a reminder of the breadth of CBA discussions. Most issues are not the big-ticket items like a salary cap or lack thereof or revenue sharing structure but instead are somewhat esoteric matters that strike most fans as mundane. To players and teams, though, they're important considerations and in some instances may even provide a foundation of common ground moving forward.

More face-to-face negotiations take place, and MLB proposes more changes to the free-agency system, among other asks. MLB's latest proposal includes the following, all of which depend upon the union's acceptance of a payroll cap:

MLB in a prior proposal called for a cap on team payrolls of $245.3 million starting in 2027 and a payroll floor of $171.2 million. The league issues a statement that reads in full:

"The biggest issue baseball fans want solved to strengthen the game is fixing the payroll disparity that leaves too many fans without hope of their team competing for a World Series title. Every other major U.S. sport has tackled this problem, and every year more small market teams in those leagues have a chance to win. The salary cap and floor proposal levels the playing field, allowing us greater flexibility to address longstanding player priorities while sharing baseball revenue with the players 50/50.

"Today, in addition to proposing the largest ever increase in the minimum salary, earned by over half of MLB players, we accepted two landmark changes to free agency that have been in place for 50 years. We agreed to both the MLBPA's proposal to provide earlier access to free agency, and their proposal to eliminate the qualifying offer system, a provision players view as a drag on free agency. We also proposed to eliminate deferred compensation and to create a new 'Cornerstone Player' provision similar to the NBA's 'Bird Rights' to give every team a fair shot at retaining their fans' favorite star players.

"We will continue working with the MLBPA during the bargaining process to improve the game for teams, players and fans."

"After making a series of proposals to reduce player compensation by billions of dollars, eliminate fundamental rights with a salary cap, and destroy the amateur entry process, Major League Baseball and team owners are now attempting to distract from the true impact their plan would have on baseball. These misleading offers are designed to look like 'improvements' but are of little or no value, given they are expressly conditioned on agreement to the league's cap system which eliminates the free market, and ensures gains for one player only come at the expense of another.

"The league also introduced a litany of additional restrictions on player rights — limiting salaries, contract length, performance, award, and signing bonuses. While MLB claims to be acting in the interest of fans, their proposals thus far are entirely consistent with owners' long-held goals: suppressing player salaries and maximizing club profits.

"Owners' attempts to pit players against players are nothing new, but they've failed in the past and will fail again now, because PA members remain unified. We are committed to achieving a fair deal that protects the rights of all players, promotes competition, and leaves our game better for future generations."

Lacking from the league's latest proposal, at least on the public-facing side, is any revisiting of the recent changes to the draft and any mention of prior proposed changes to the league's revenue-sharing system.

During these same face-to-face sessions, the MLBPA proposes a ban on prop bets placed on individual players, ESPN reports. The idea is to preempt harrassment of players by gamblers. The proposed ban would extend to bets placed on individual player performance prior to and during any MLB game. The MLBPA also requested that players be permitted to engage in paid endorsements and sponsorships with sportsbooks and prediction markets.

MLB and the MLBPA meet for face-to-face negotiations, and owners propose sweeping changes to the draft and also push for an international draft. As for the MLB Draft, formally known as the First-Year Player Draft, MLB pushes for the following changes:

"Over the last several years, college baseball has undergone a remarkable transformation," MLB says in a statement. "Expanded scholarships, NIL opportunities, revenue sharing and significant investments in facilities and player development have made college baseball an increasingly important pathway that is producing major league-ready talent at an accelerated rate. Today's top programs provide players with resources, competition and national exposure that were unimaginable a decade ago. Our proposal is designed to build on that momentum to benefit the game at the college, minor-league and major-league levels. By creating a draft system centered around college-aged players and making most college players eligible one year earlier, more players will benefit from both a college education and an elite development environment while reaching professional baseball -- and ultimately the major leagues -- more quickly. We believe these changes will strengthen college baseball and deepen fans' connection to the next generation of major league stars. We look forward to working with the MLBPA throughout the bargaining process to modernize the domestic amateur system in a way that benefits players, clubs, and fans."

As for the international draft, MLB proposed making players outside of the U.S., Puerto Rico, and Canada (who are already included in the standard draft) subject to a similar system. The international draft would, as with the proposed changes to the MLB Draft, come with a $200 million bonus cap. At present, international amateurs may sign with any team under the international free agent system, although teams do have hard budget caps each year.

The MLBPA also issues a statement in response to MLB's proposals:

Today, MLB made another set of proposals that are flat out bad for baseball, ones that would cripple the next generation of players and damage the future of our game. They would, among other things:

Players remain committed to bargaining in good faith and leaving baseball better than they found it -- the league's proposals fall woefully short.

U.S. President Donald J. Trump publicly supports MLB's efforts to implement a salary cap. "If you don't have a salary cap, you don't have a sport, because they can't help themselves," Trump says. "Football has a salary cap. They should have done it a long time ago.

"It's shocking, frankly, that they didn't put a cap on many years ago," he said, possibly referencing the 1994-95 strike. "They had a chance to do a cap, but they blew it."

Speaking to reporters following the owners' quarterly meetings, Manfred addresses the luxury-tax system he and the owners seek to replace with a cap. "We have tried mightily over several rounds of bargaining to use a competitive balance (luxury) tax to address competitive concerns," Manfred says. "And sometimes you've got to admit you failed.

"We made a proposal on one set of topics. At the outset of negotiations, I went and said myself, 'We're open to whatever ideas people have, but we need a realistic framework that addresses the fans' concerns about competitive balance.' You just can't ignore that financial penalties have not gotten it done for us."

In a call with reporters, MLBPA interim executive director Bruce Meyer addresses the owners' proposals. "Using MLB's definition of revenue and player share as set forth in their proposal and their presentation to us, player share under their proposal would go down," Meyer says. "Player share for this season, 2026, is projected to be well over 50 percent, using, again MLB's definitions of revenues and what counts against player share.

"Had MLB's proposal been in place in 2026, players, we estimate, would lose over half a billion dollars."

Meyer also refers to a salary cap as "a form of institutionalized collusion."

"Our salary cap-and-floor proposal addresses our fans' concerns by leveling the playing field while sharing baseball revenue with the players 50-50 like the other leagues," MLB spokesperson Glen Caplin responded on behalf of the league. "Under our proposal, major-league players will receive more compensation in year one of the system than in 2026. We are ready to listen if the MLBPA wants to counter our proposal at the bargaining table."

MLB and the owners publicly announce their first formal CBA proposal. Chiefly, they propose:

Using competitive balance tax (CBT), or luxury tax, payrolls as a guide, since they include benefits expenses, nine teams at present would be above the proposed cap line, while 12 teams would be below the floor. However, as Craig Goldstein points out, the amount needed to get all these teams below or above the relevant payroll thresholds amounts to an $18.7 million loss in aggregate player salary overall. Another sticking point will be how league revenues are defined. Owners no doubt seek to carve out things like real estate developments surrounding ballparks and ownership stakes in regional sports. As well, MLB's working definition of league revenues includes many expense deductions.

On another level, the fact that Manfred is able to persuade large-market, high-revenue clubs to agree to equal sharing of all local revenues is a notable development. However, such a concession by those large-market clubs may be contingent upon the implementation of a cap.

Another sticking point is that the league proposes an escrow system, as is used in the NBA and the NHL. This would mean a percentage of player salaries is withheld. If revenues fall short of projections, some of that money in escrow goes back to the league. If revenues are higher than projected, that excess is shared with the players. The MLBPA opposes the escrow system on the grounds that it undermines the notion of guaranteed player salaries.

The MLBPA makes an opening suite of proposals to the league, including:

"Today, the MLBPA (Major League Baseball Players Association) presented a comprehensive set of economic proposals designed to advance the rights and benefits of players at all levels," Meyer says in a statement released by the union. "Our goal is to preserve and improve baseball's market system, rewarding competition on and off the field. Additionally, the players' proposals provide increased revenue sharing initially guaranteeing every small market club a minimum of $240m in revenue every season. This enhanced revenue sharing includes added protections to ensure clubs prioritize winning over profiteering. Ultimately, our proposals are designed to build upon the incredible momentum and popularity of our sport world-wide."

"We appreciate the union making a set of proposals and we look forward to continuing the bargaining process and working towards solving the competitive balance problem our fans are telling us needs to be addressed," Caplin says in a statement. "We understand their proposals are designed to benefit players. Unfortunately, they do not address and in fact exacerbate the competitive balance problem our fans are telling us we must address. The MLBPA's proposal would reduce the amount transferred to lower-revenue Clubs, weaken the Competitive Balance Tax, and lead to even more payroll disparity than exists today. For example, under the Union's proposal, the Dodgers would pay less in luxury tax payments, giving them an additional $70 million to spend on payroll."

Negotiations on a new CBA formally begin between teams and players. Among the key issues to be discussed will be the league's desire for a salary cap, drastic changes to the revenue sharing system, league expansion, possible further playoff expansion, and an international draft.

The 2022-26 Basic Agreement is set to expire at 11:59 p.m. ET, at which point owners are expected to lock out the players in the absence of a new agreement.

Porziņģis has not played for the Warriors this season and reports earlier this week indicated that the team is withholding payments from him. He signed a two-year, $40 million deal with the Warriors in free agency this summer, but the second year of the deal only has a $3 million guarantee.

Here is Porziņģis' full statement announcing his decision to step away from basketball:

This season I was really looking forward to running it with this group, but as I ramped up, my body didn't respond the way I anticipated.

I'm thankful to my family and close ones for always being there. Much appreciation to all of you for the support.

Porziņģis' career has been defined by health problems. He's played more than 57 games just three times since he was drafted No. 4 overall by the New York Knicks in 2015, and has dealt with significant injuries, including a torn ACL that cost him the entire 2018-19 season. In recent years, he's been limited by this mysterious illness that first became an issue in Boston during the 2024-25 season.

Porziņģis started dealing with extreme fatigue and previously disclosed a diagnosis of postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome, or POTS, which is characterized by rapid changes in heart rate when a person stands up and can lead to exhaustion and dizziness.

"You know how people say, 'Oh, I'm so fatigued.' I've never used those words. I don't even like to speak in those terms, but I really was like that," Porziņģis said ahead of last season. "At that time, I could just lay on the couch and be a house cat."

Over the last three seasons with the Celtics, Atlanta Hawks and Warriors, Porziņģis has only played 74 games. He has been away from the Warriors since late September and released a previous statement in mid-October shutting down rumors that he had been diagnosed with HIV or AIDS. At that point, the Warriors said Porziņģis would be out indefinitely.

"Hello people, I'm working with doctors and experts to figure out how to be fully back to good health asap. Honestly, I'm getting better and better. I just have to stay patient, and I believe I'll be feeling great again soon," Porziņģis wrote. "It has definitely been frustrating dealing with some health stuff that you can't exactly pinpoint, on top of injuries throughout my career, so it has added up for sure, but we will get through it. Health is wealth. Thank you for all the support."

The Warriors hoped that Porziņģis would play a big role this season as a floor-spacing big, especially while Jimmy Butler (torn ACL) and Moses Moody (torn patellar tendon) remain sidelined. Instead, it seems more likely that he will never play for the franchise again.

The Warriors have reportedly been trying to trade Porziņģis to use his $20 million cap figure, as explained by CBS Sports' Sam Quinn:

While he would not have trade value as a player given his health status, he is essentially an expiring contract with only that small $3 million guarantee on the books for next season. That could potentially make him valuable to a team looking to move off of longer-term money, or the Warriors could entice another team into a trade using draft picks with Porziņģis serving only as the matching salary.

Despite Porziņģis' absence, the Warriors are off to a 6-3 start, putting them in seventh place in the extremely crowded Western Conference standings. Rookie big man Yaxel Lendeborg has stepped up in Porziņģis' place and provided a major boost on both ends of the floor.

Through nine games, Lendeborg is averaging 21 points, 7.1 rebounds, 4.1 assists and 1.1 steals while shooting 49.2% from the field, including 39.6% from 3-point range.

#2599. The numbers behind Luka Dončić's historic start are entering the realm of ridiculous

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Luka Doncic delivered another casual masterpiece with 53 points in a 124-118 Lakers victory over the Trail Blazers on Friday night. He outscored Portland by himself 20-15 in the third quarter. He dropped a three-quarter-court buzzer-beater to end the first half. He added five rebounds and five assists for fun. And the Lakers are now atop the Western Conference standings at 8-2.

If the season were to end today, Dončić would be the runaway MVP, maybe joining 2015-16 Stephen Curry as the second unanimous winner in NBA history. His box scores will always be somewhat skewed given his usage, but that context notwithstanding, these numbers are downright stupid.

Luka Doncic this season:28 PTS | 8 REB | 7 AST23 PTS | 6 REB | 7 AST52 PTS | 8 REB | 10 AST41 PTS | 5 REB | 9 AST37 PTS | 7 REB | 5 AST45 PTS | 15 REB | 6 AST42 PTS | 7 REB | 13 AST40 PTS | 9 REB | 7 AST53 PTS | 5 REB | 5 ASTMVP? pic.twitter.com/2qjWxSo3E0

Let's dive a little deeper into the numbers behind Dončić's historic start.

Dončić has become the third player in Lakers history to score at least 35 points in seven straight games, joining Kobe Bryant and Elgin Baylor.

Dončić is just the fourth Lakers player to put up four straight 40-point games, joining Bryant, Baylor and George Mikan. You'll notice names like LeBron James, Shaquille O'Neal, Kareem Abdul-Jabbar and Magic Johnson missing from these lists. Some franchise marks are oversold. Not when it comes to the Lakers.

Dončić has made at least five 3-pointers in seven straight games. If he continues that streak for another five games, he will break James Harden's NBA record of 12 straight.

Dončić is currently averaging six made 3-pointers per game. He has played in nine of the Lakers' 10 games. Meaning, if he stays on this pace of six 3s per game while playing in 90% of L.A.'s games, he would end up making 426 3s, which would break Curry's single-season record of 402.

Staying on six, Dončić also owns the non-Wilt Chamberlain NBA record with six 40-point games in his team's first 10 games.

Dončić has now logged seven straight games with at least 35 points, five assists and five rebounds, tying Oscar Robertson for the longest such streak in history.

Dončić is currently attempting 13.7 3-pointers per game. If that volume holds up, it would break Harden's NBA record of 13.2 attempts per game in 2018-19. But Harden only made 36.8% of his 3s that year. Dončić, as you'll see shortly, is blowing that number out of the water.

LUKA DONCIC FROM 3/4 COURT TO END THE HALF. OMG 🤯 pic.twitter.com/6MZGtF5ahY

With two 50-point games so far and just 11% of the schedule completed, Dončić is currently on pace to cook up 16 50-burgers this season, which would shatter Bryant's non-Chamberlain record of 10 in a single season. Chamberlain, for the record, had 45 50-point games in 1961-62, which is just absurd.

After Friday's performance, Dončić is now averaging 40.1 points per game. The only other player in history to average 40 through the first nine games of a season is Chamberlain, who is basically a category unto himself in these statistical side-by-sides. The most Michael Jordan ever averaged through the first nine games of a season was 38.6 in 1986-87.

Dončić is shooting 41.9% from 3 to start the year. That isn't likely to continue. Like Harden, he's been a volume marksman to this point as a career 35% 3-point shooter. But right now he is absolutely dialed, particularly with his step-back, which, according to NBA.com shot tracking, he entered Friday night knocking down at a Curry-like 43% clip.

Luka made 8 of his first 9 three-point attempts last night against the Raptors. Almost all contested step-backs or pull-ups. Crazy level of shot making... pic.twitter.com/K5GWhxXq2x

Dončić is reading the game on autopilot at this point in his career. If you double him, he's zipping the right pass. If you single cover him, he's either powering his way into the paint or, more often, getting right into this step-back as a matter of routine. And when he's making it, there's nothing any defender in the world can do about it.

The Lakers' 110.2 defensive rating with Dončić on the court would register as a top-10 mark. For all the talk about Dončić's poor defense, he hasn't been nearly as bad with the Lakers as he was with the Mavericks (especially in the 2024 Finals, the clips from which are going to haunt him forever), and he's been downright good so far this season.

It's early, yes, and individual defensive stats can be deceiving, but nonetheless Dončić is tied for sixth league-wide with 15 steals (he's been a genuine ball hawk early), and he's tied for the league lead in charges with four.

And get this: Opponents are shooting just 32.3 percent so far with Dončić as their defender, which is the best mark in the league among all players who are defending at least 12 shots per game. Better than Victor Wembanyama!

Again, these can be deceiving markers. Dončić obviously isn't an elite defender, and that opponent shooting percentage is going to vary wildly on Dončić simply being the closest defender on misses rather than the one genuinely forcing someone into a bad shot. Also, he's defending perimeter shots, so on some level, shooters are just missing a lot of shots with him nearby so far.

But the 3-pointers are the ones where he's just the guy closing out a lot (which is still important). Inside the arc, you're much more responsible for effecting misses, and have a look at this entering the Portland game.

SURPRISE LEADER ON DEFENSE: LUKA DONČIĆOpponents have made only 21.9% of their two-point attempts against Luka Dončić this season. No player in the league has allowed a lower mark among those who have defended at least 30 of them.The top 10:Luka Dončić: 21.9%Miles Bridges:… pic.twitter.com/RCnWEqMHg3

Bottom line, a 110.2 defensive rating with Dončić on the floor is what it is. At the very least, he hasn't been a liability, which, given his offensive production, is a major win.

The Lakers' offensive rating with Dončić on the floor this season, which would be an NBA record. When he isn't on the floor, the offense falls to a 99.1 rating, which would rank as the worst in the league by a long shot. As Austin Reaves is finding out in the non-Luka minutes, life is mighty difficult without one of the greatest offensive players in history out there to command all the attention and still break defenses down like a cardboard box.

Including Friday night, the Lakers have won Dončić's on-floor minutes this season by a total of 140 points and lost his bench minutes by 63.

Do the math, and he has single-handedly represented a 203-point swing so far. If you are looking for one MVP number, this might be it.

If Minshew is sidelined, Carson Beck would be the next man up. Beck would be the third quarterback to start for the Cardinals this season. Jacoby Brissett began the year as their starter before being benched and traded to the Baltimore Ravens earlier this month.

Since Beck would be the team's only QB on the depth chart if Minshew is out for the year, team reportedly acted fast to get some backup. On Monday, the team signed Josh Johnson off the Cincinnati Bengals practice squad, according to ESPN. This marks Johnson's 15th NFL team in 14 seasons.

Beck was drafted in the third round of the 2026 NFL Draft at No. 65 overall. The two-time College Football Playoff national champion has yet to make an appearance in the NFL. He would be the third rookie quarterback to start a game this season, joining Tampa Bay Buccaneers undrafted free agent Jalon Daniels and Washington Commanders seventh-rounder Athan Kaliakmanis.

The 24-year-old spent five years at Georgia and his last collegiate season with Miami (FL). He finished with 338 completions, a conference high, for 3,813 yards, 30 touchdowns and 12 interceptions last season. His 72.4 completion percentage was also a conference high.

In 55 total college games, he had 966 completions for 11,725 yards, 88 touchdowns and 32 interceptions.

After Brissett's eight games, the team made a change at QB during the third quarter of their Nov. 1 game against the Cowboys, putting in Minshew. Beck was promoted to backup quarterback, with Brissett demoted to the third-string QB shortly before his exit from Arizona.

Minshew played two games, with a 71.7 completion percentage, 354 yards, three touchdowns and no interceptions, going 0-1 in starts.

The Cardinals currently sit at 3-6 and are in fourth place in the NFC West.

#2596. MLB proposes delaying salary cap in new negotiations as Dec. 1 CBA expiration inches nearer

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Major League Baseball has proposed delaying the implementation of a salary cap/floor system until 2028 as part of its latest collective bargaining agreement proposal, the league announced Tuesday. MLB says the delay is intended to provide a "smoother transition" to a salary cap/floor system and give teams more time to prepare and get their payrolls in order.

"We recognize that clubs will need a full offseason to prepare to operate within the cap and floor system. Therefore, with this offseason already underway, we proposed today to begin the cap and floor system in 2028," MLB spokesman Glen Caplin said in a statement. "This proposal would allow a smoother transition into the cap and floor system without delaying key player benefits, including earlier free agency, a $1 million minimum salary, a 30% increase to the pre-arbitration bonus pool, and transactional reform that will reduce roster churn."

The league also newly proposed a $180.2 million salary floor and a $258.2 million salary cap. Those numbers are up from $171.2 million and $245.3 million, respectively, in the league's previous proposal in June. The $1 million minimum salary would only apply to players with at least two years of service time. The minimum salary would be $900,000 for all other players.

Four teams currently have more than $258.2 million on the books for 2027 (including arbitration projections) and 20 teams have less than $180.2 million on the books, according to FanGraphs' calculations. The current competitive balance tax and revenue sharing system would remain in place in 2027 before the transition to a salary cap/floor system in 2028.

The collective bargaining agreement expires at 11:59 p.m. ET on Dec. 1, and the owners are expected to lock out the players at that time. The previous lockout ended on March 10, then there was a three-week spring training leading up to Opening Day. If there is a similarly lengthy lockout, it would be impossible for clubs to become salary cap-compliant in such a short period of time.

The MLB Players Association has repeatedly insisted it will not accept a salary cap/floor system, and has instead proposed a revised revenue sharing system that would funnel more money from big-market teams to small-market teams. In a statement following the league's proposal on Tuesday, the MLBPA accused owners of continuing to "propose blowing up the current system and replacing it with one designed to line their pockets and increase their franchise values." The union also said that even with a delayed implementation, the league's proposal of a salary cap maintains the same "negative impacts," including a "massive reduction in player compensation" and the "elimination of fundamental player rights, including guaranteed contracts."

MLB says its push for a salary cap/floor system is intended to improve competitive balance. The small-market Milwaukee Brewers defeated the small-market Tampa Bay Rays in the World Series last week and swept big-market teams (Los Angeles Dodgers and New York Yankees) en route to the Fall Classic.

#2595. Can Carson Beck convince the Cardinals not to draft a QB? He has eight games to make his case

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Carson Beck wasn't supposed to be the Cardinals' starting quarterback in 2026. But after Jacoby Brissett was benched-and-then-traded to Baltimore following Week 8's loss, and then, seven days later, Gardner Minshew suffered an elbow injury that could require season-ending surgery, those best-laid plans have suddenly changed.

Now the third-round rookie is in line to make his NFL debut against the Rams this Sunday. And Beck will have eight games to convince the Cardinals they don't need to use what will almost certainly be a top-10 pick on another quarterback next spring.

(I say "almost certainly" because while the Cards are currently 3-6 and everything appears to be going wrong, a year ago at this time, the Saints were 1-7, turned to Tyler Shough to finish 5-4 and ended up with the eighth pick instead of something higher. Shorter version: We'll see.)

That's a potentially franchise-changing opportunity for the 65th overall pick, but what exactly would success look like?

Back in June, I wrote that Beck might be the safest quarterback in the 2026 draft class. The former Georgia and Miami QB had started 43 games, was a quick processor, took care of the football and kept the offense on schedule. His 38.6% first-down rate ranked in the 95th percentile among draft-eligible quarterbacks from 2015-26.

But there was a catch. Beck faced pressure on just 19.1% of his college dropbacks, the lowest rate among quarterbacks going back more than a decade, and more than 32% of his throws were screens. He was rarely asked to make something happen when everything around him fell apart because it so rarely did.

That was a big question entering the NFL: Was Beck's high floor the product of his talent, his surroundings or some combination of both? Well, we're about to find out.

Since 2007, 24 quarterbacks drafted in the third round or later made their first NFL start after Week 7 of their rookie seasons. (This is through the 2024 draft class so we can look at Year 2 production, as well.)

Of those 24, only eight started at least four games as rookies. And just three of those eight – Nick Foles, Desmond Ridder and Brock Purdy – started at least eight games the following season. Sam Howell was the only quarterback with fewer than four rookie starts to do so.

How late-starting rookie QBs drafted in Round 3 or later fared in Year 2

What's interesting is that six of those eight quarterbacks improved their yards per attempt between their first two and final two rookie starts. But that improvement didn't necessarily translate to long-term success.

Ridder, for example, went from 5.3 yards per attempt in his first two starts to 7.0 in his final two, with two touchdowns and no interceptions. Atlanta handed Ridder the starting job in 2023 but benched him twice that season before trading him to Arizona the following March. The Falcons then drafted Michael Penix Jr. eighth overall in 2024.

Purdy, obviously, was very different. He averaged 8.6 yards per attempt with four touchdowns and no interceptions in his first two starts, then maintained that production over his final two. He didn't need to improve dramatically because he'd already shown he could play. Now he's one of the league's best quarterbacks.

Five of those eight teams didn't draft a quarterback the following spring. But several drafted one within the next year or two, and where they picked tells us plenty about the decisions they made.

The Cardinals know this story better than most. Injuries forced them to start rookies John Skelton in 2010 and Ryan Lindley in 2012, but neither was viewed as the long-term answer. Arizona took Patrick Peterson fifth overall in 2011, passing on quarterbacks Jake Locker, Blaine Gabbert and Andy Dalton, then selected Jonathan Cooper seventh overall in 2013, ahead of Geno Smith. Instead of drafting a quarterback, the Cardinals traded for veterans Kevin Kolb and Carson Palmer in those respective offseasons.

That's why draft position matters. Tennessee had the No. 2 overall pick in 2015 and used it on Marcus Mariota after Zach Mettenberger's six rookie starts. St. Louis took Sam Bradford first overall in 2010, but Keith Null had only started four games because injuries forced the Rams to turn to their sixth-round rookie.

San Francisco's situation was different. The 49ers traded up to draft Trey Lance third overall in 2021, but he suffered a season-ending ankle injury in Week 2 of '22. Jimmy Garoppolo took over, then broke his foot in Week 13, giving Purdy, the final pick of the 2022 draft, his opportunity. Purdy won all five of his regular-season starts, then two playoff games, and by the following season he'd taken the job Lance was drafted to fill.

If there's a recent example Beck should hope to follow, it's Tyler Shough. The Saints selected him 40th overall in 2025, and he took over the starting job in Week 9, giving New Orleans nine games to evaluate him.

Shough went 5-4, but it was how he played that mattered. He completed nearly 68% of his passes, made smart decisions and showed he could run the offense without the Saints having to protect him. It wasn't always pretty, but it was enough for New Orleans to pass on drafting another QB in 2026 and enter the season believing Shough could be its long-term answer.

That's the goal for Beck. He doesn't need to become a superstar overnight, but he does need to give Mike LaFleur enough confidence to build around him instead of looking for his replacement – which is exactly what the Saints did in April when they used the No. 8 pick on wide receiver Jordyn Tyson.

And there's reason to think this offense should suit him. Arizona has attempted 58.8% of its passes within five yards of the line of scrimmage, while the offensive line has allowed pressure on 31.1% of dropbacks – the fifth-lowest rate in the NFL, according to TruMedia. Beck's accuracy, anticipation and ability to play on time should, in theory, translate. (The game, I need to remind myself, is not a theoretical exercise, so … we'll see.)

But Arizona also ranks 28th in yards per play, and Brissett and Minshew had not consistently turned those manageable throws into meaningful production. Beck's challenge is to turn those short throws into more first downs and points.

In my preseason projections for the 2026 rookie quarterbacks, I had Beck averaging 6.9 yards per attempt with an 85.8 passer rating – solid numbers that would be an improvement over Arizona's quarterback play to date. But just as important will be whether Beck gets better over the next two months.

The Cardinals don't need to reel off eight straight wins, but they do need to see how Beck responds when defenses take away the easy throws. Can he push the ball downfield, keep drives alive under pressure and avoid costly mistakes?

At Miami last season, Beck showed that he can be an efficient game manager – and his preseason debut suggested those skills could translate. Now comes the part that actually matters: proving he can do it against NFL starters, week after week, when opponents know exactly what he wants to do.

And with a possible top-10 pick awaiting Arizona in April, there's a lot at stake – for the rookie quarterback and an organization that last had a winning season in 2021 (and before that, 2015). Beck doesn't have to prove he's a franchise quarterback during his two-month audition, but he does have to give the Cardinals a reason to believe he could become one.

#2592. MLB offseason bold predictions: Tarik Skubal breaks records, World Series champ gets a deal, a FA frenzy, more

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

With the Brewers crowned World Series champions, the 2026-27 offseason is underway. We're still waiting for the first significant free agent signing or trade, which isn't unusual less than a week into the offseason. Give it another week or so and the action will pick up. Before the hot stove really gets burning, here are 10 bold predictions for the 2026-27 offseason. Remember, all geniuses were called crazy at first.

Yoshinobu Yamamoto's $325 million deal with the Dodgers is the largest pitching contract in history, and our first bold prediction says Tarik Skubal, this offseason's undisputed No. 1 free agent, will beat that. Specifically, he'll sign a contract that is closer to $400 million in value than $300 million, which is another way of saying he'll clear $350 million and break Yamamoto's record for total dollars by a good bit. Scott Boras, Skubal's agent, likes to break contract records with room to spare, not just by a tiny bit. Skubal is the best free agent starter since Yamamoto, and the best free agent starter with MLB experience since Gerrit Cole in 2019. It's a very thin free agent class with few places to (wisely) spend money. The bet here is a team steps up and gives Skubal a record deal.

Milwaukee's thing over the last few years has been trading its top players a year before free agency (Corbin Burnes, Freddy Peralta, Devin Williams, etc.) and obviously it has worked for them. William Contreras is at that point now: he's scheduled to hit the open market next offseason. This next bold prediction says the Brewers will buck that trend and instead sign the World Series MVP to a long-term extension that keeps him in Milwaukee for at least another few years, if not the rest of his career. How does six years at $24 million a pop sound? That would be $144 million total and the richest contract given to a catcher in the last 13 years, clearing Will Smith's $140 extension with the Dodgers. The World Series champs keep their most irreplaceable player. It has been foretold.

Every offseason is important, and this one is extra important for new Astros GM Randy Flores, who must figure out what to do with third baseman Isaac Paredes and shortstop Jeremy Peña, both a year away from free agency. Keeping Peña and trading Paredes, and installing Carlos Correa at the hot corner, is the sensible move. This bold prediction says the opposite will happen. The Astros will trade Peña and keep Paredes, and figure out their 2027 infield alignment later. Houston needs help up and down the roster, particularly on the mound, and I think the offers for Peña will simply be too great for Flores to ignore. It will be similar to the Kyle Tucker trade two years ago. The Astros don't have to move Peña, but the offers will get to a point where they just can't say no.

On one hand, keeping the offense intact and adding some pitching would be a viable offseason plan for the Braves. On the other hand, can they really run it back with the same offense that flatlined after June 1 and in the NLDS? It might be time to shake things up a bit, and I boldly predict it will happen. Ronald Acuña Jr., Drake Baldwin, Michael Harris II, and Matt Olson aren't going anywhere. No team will take the current version of Austin Riley and the six years (!) remaining on his contract. That leaves Ozzie Albies and I suppose Sean Murphy, though the latter is well into role player status now. Does that make this bold prediction a "the Braves will trade Albies" prediction? Yeah, I guess it does. It feels like things are getting a little stale in Atlanta and it's time to change up a core.

You could argue Freddy Peralta is the second-best free agent starter behind Skubal. You could also argue it's Trevor Rogers, who doesn't have Peralta's pedigree or track record, but has strong under-the-hood performance indicators, the kind that project well into the future and get players paid. So, for this bold prediction, I'll say that Rogers signs a richer deal than Peralta, even though the latter is the more famous player and has been better in their careers to date. It'll be close. I can see Rogers getting something in the $125 million range and Peralta signing for right around $120 million, but, in the end, Rogers will sign for more guaranteed dollars because he's a year and a half younger and teams love nothing more than players they believe have untapped upside. That's Rogers, not Peralta.

After the Dodgers swept in the NLCS, there were calls to infuse some youth into the roster, and, honestly, they need it. Fortunately, Los Angeles has one of the best prospects in the game in the precocious Josue De Paula, who was so impressive late in the season. Trading an outfielder to clear a spot for De Paula seems like such an obvious move that I'm not sure this prediction qualifies as bold. Andy Pages and Kyle Tucker aren't going anywhere, which leaves Teoscar Hernández. How about a trade that sends Hernández back to the Blue Jays? It's a one-year commitment, the Blue Jays badly need over-the-fence power, and the fan base already loves the guy. Teoscar to Toronto as what amounts to their George Springer replacement. I boldly predict it.

Every offseason, there are two teams that appear to match up so well that a trade feels inevitable. Last offseason, it was the Brewers and Mets for a Freddy Peralta deal. This offseason, it's the Cubs and Yankees. The Cubs need rotation help and have some young position players to spare (like Matt Shaw). The Yankees need infield help and have starting pitching to trade (like Will Warren). I'm not saying Shaw for Warren will happen or even should happen. I'm just saying Chicago's and New York's trade chips and roster needs align very well, and when that happens, a trade typically comes together. This bold prediction says the Cubs will send a position player to the Yankees for a starting pitcher, with maybe some other pieces involved on both sides.

There are trade rumors involving a Mariners starting pitcher every offseason and there's a good reason for that. They have a lot of really good starters and teams want them. The Mariners currently have Kade Anderson, Logan Gilbert, Emerson Hancock, George Kirby, Bryce Miller, and Bryan Woo lined up for their 2027 rotation. They could keep them all because pitching depth has a way of disappearing, sure, but Seattle needed another bat even before Randy Arozarena became a free agent. This next bold prediction says the Mariners finally trade one of their starters in an arm-for-bat deal. I'll say Kirby, who is two years away from free agency, is the one to go. Gilbert is a one-year rental but the better pitcher. The others all have longer control than Kirby.

After coming out of the gate so well in April and May, Munetaka Murakami finished right where the pundits expected. He hit .207 and had the highest strikeout rate among qualified hitters, but he also slugged 35 home runs in only 127 games. Hanshin Tigers third baseman Teruaki Sato, who will be posted for MLB teams this offseason, is similar to Murakami as a strikeout-prone lefty with huge power. This bold prediction says Sato will double Murakami's contract with the White Sox (two years and $34 million) because he's a better bet to stay at third base, a position that is barren in free agency, and because Murakami provided proof of concept. He showed that a player with big contact concerns in Japan can indeed succeed stateside, even if it is an eyesore at times. Four years and $68 million for Sato, perhaps with an opt out that makes the $68 million not really $68 million.

Dec. 1 is of course when the collective bargaining agreement expires and the owners are expected to lock out the players. My final bold prediction says free agents and teams will get out ahead of the potential lockout and sign in November. Players won't want to wait until who knows when to sign and teams will want to lock in contracts so they can be grandfathered into whatever the next CBA brings. MLB free agency tends to be slow-moving. Last offseason, only one of our top 10 free agents signed in November, and that was Shota Imanaga taking the qualifying offer. Only three other top 10 free agents signed in December. The other six signed on Jan. 14 or later. This offseason will be the opposite, I boldly predict. There will be a flurry of activity in November and at least seven of our top 10 free agents will put pen to paper before a potential lockout.
